findings.suggested_fix: Search m=(T.Name, T.Keyword, T.Wildcard) or handle function keywords

findings.explanation: Only already-grouped sql.Over is included; if grouping order leaves OVER as Keyword + Parenthesis it is omitted from the Function.
findings.suggested_fix: Also detect Keyword 'OVER' followed by Parenthesis and include it in eidx

findings.explanation: token_next defaults may not skip comments, so name /* comment */ ( ... ) fails to group.
findings.suggested_fix: Use tlist.token_next(tidx, skip_ws=True, skip_cm=True)

findings.explanation: has_create, has_table and has_as are computed but never used, so a table name followed by a column-definition parenthesis in CREATE TABLE is grouped as a Function (e.g. CREATE TABLE foo (id INT)), corrupting the parse tree.
findings.suggested_fix: Use the flags in the loop to skip grouping the CREATE TABLE table name (ideally only that name, continuing to group real functions after AS), e.g. do not call group_tokens for the table-name token when has_create and has_table indicate a DDL statement.

findings.explanation: Keywords are matched by value alone without checking ttype, so plain identifiers/names whose text is CREATE, TABLE or AS (e.g. a column or table named 'table' or 'as') falsely set the flags and would wrongly suppress function grouping once the flags are used.
findings.suggested_fix: Require the token to be a keyword first: check tmp_token.ttype in T.Keyword before comparing tmp_token.value.upper().

findings.explanation: token_next() defaults to skip_cm=False, so a comment between a function name and its parenthesis (foo /*c*/ (...)) or between the parenthesis and OVER (count(*) /*c*/ OVER (...)) prevents the function/OVER clause from being grouped.
findings.suggested_fix: Pass skip_cm=True (along with skip_ws=True) to tlist.token_next() calls on lines 16 and 18.

findings.explanation: tmp_token.value can be None and non-keyword values (strings, identifiers) are matched with .value.upper() == ...
findings.suggested_fix: check tmp_token.is_keyword and tmp_token.normalized == 'CREATE'/'AS' instead of value.upper()

findings.explanation: Requires TABLE to skip CREATE; CREATE FUNCTION/VIEW/PROCEDURE without AS is then wrongly grouped and logic diverges from has_create and not has_as.
findings.suggested_fix: if has_create and not has_as: return (drop has_table)

findings.explanation: Only T.Name matches function names, misses placeholders, symbolic names and keyword function names.
findings.suggested_fix: use t=(T.Name, T.Name.Placeholder, T.String.Symbolic) or include T.Keyword/T.Wildcard as upstream does

findings.explanation: Condition uses or so any following token is swallowed into the Function instead of only sql.Over.
findings.suggested_fix: if over is not None and isinstance(over, sql.Over): eidx = over_idx else: eidx = nidx

findings.explanation: When no Parenthesis follows, no grouping occurs and search restarts from same tidx, returning same token forever.
findings.suggested_fix: advance search with idx=nidx (next index) instead of idx=tidx

findings.explanation: token_next() without explicit skip_ws/skip_cm handling groups across or fails across comments inconsistently.
findings.suggested_fix: use tlist.token_next(tidx, skip_ws=True, skip_cm=True) for name->paren and paren->over checks

findings.explanation: Using 'or' makes any truthy following token count as a window clause, so e.g. 'func(a), x' or 'func(a) + y' groups the comma/operator token into the Function and corrupts the token stream; the isinstance check is also rendered meaningless.
findings.suggested_fix: Use 'if over is not None and isinstance(over, sql.Over):' (i.e. replace 'or' with 'and').

findings.explanation: CREATE/TABLE/AS are detected purely by token text regardless of token type, so identifiers or other tokens whose value happens to equal those words (e.g. columns named 'create'/'table') can set the flags and trigger the early return, causing legitimate function calls in the statement to never be grouped.
findings.suggested_fix: Check token type as well, e.g. 'tmp_token.ttype == T.Keyword and tmp_token.normalized == "CREATE"' (same for TABLE/AS).

findings.explanation: token_next() by default skips whitespace but not comments, so a window function written as 'count(*) /*c*/ OVER (...)' does not see the Over token as the immediate next token and the OVER clause is left outside the grouped Function.
findings.suggested_fix: Skip comments when looking past the parenthesis, e.g. call tlist.token_next(nidx, _skip_cm=True) if supported, or scan forward past Comment tokens.

findings.explanation: Loop exits on EOF without finding R_PAREN and code still builds an Operator, silently accepting unterminated '(' instead of raising an error.
findings.suggested_fix: After the inner loop check if R_PAREN was actually matched and return error / break if not, e.g. if not matched raise ParseError.

findings.explanation: Empty parentheses '()' leaves op as empty string but code still creates exp.Operator with empty operator.
findings.suggested_fix: Validate `if not op: break/return this or raise error` before building Operator.

findings.explanation: Result of _parse_bitwise() is used unconditionally; if right operand is missing it is None, creating an invalid Operator or crashing later.
findings.suggested_fix: Check `rhs = self._parse_bitwise(); if not rhs: return error/None` before constructing Operator.

findings.explanation: When `this` is None there is no left operand, but code still tries to parse '(op)' and builds Operator(this=None).
findings.suggested_fix: Add `if not this: return this` at start.

findings.explanation: Loop requires a spurious OPERATOR token after each '(op) expr' so chained '(op)' operators are never parsed, and a trailing OPERATOR is consumed and lost even when not followed by '(' .
findings.suggested_fix: Remove OPERATOR match and loop solely on L_PAREN, e.g. `while self._match(TokenType.L_PAREN): ...`, without consuming extra token.

findings.explanation: The first parenthesized operator is parsed without requiring or consuming an OPERATOR token, while subsequent operators do require one, so ordinary parenthesized input can be misparsed as a custom operator and the first OPERATOR token is handled inconsistently.
findings.suggested_fix: Require and consume TokenType.OPERATOR before every '(' (or document/enforce that the caller consumed only the first one and do not silently treat bare '(' as an operator).

findings.explanation: If EOF is reached before ')', the while loop simply exits and an Operator node is built anyway, silently accepting malformed input such as 'x OPERATOR(+'.
findings.suggested_fix: Track whether R_PAREN was matched and call self.raise_error('Expected ) in OPERATOR(...)') if it was not.

findings.explanation: An empty pair of parentheses produces op == '' and is still turned into an exp.Operator with an empty operator string instead of being rejected.
findings.suggested_fix: Validate that op is non-empty before constructing exp.Operator and raise an error otherwise.

findings.explanation: Every token up to the first ')' is concatenated into the operator name regardless of type, so strings, numbers, keywords, commas, or a subquery are invented into an operator, and a nested '(' is truncated by the inner ')' leaving the remainder to be misparsed.
findings.suggested_fix: Only accept valid operator/identifier/dot tokens, reject nested parentheses and other token types, and preserve/validate qualified operator structure instead of blindly concatenating curr.text.

findings.explanation: Concatenating token text discards the original separation and token types, so distinct token sequences can collapse into a different operator name than the one written in the source.
findings.suggested_fix: Build the operator from the validated token sequence with its original lexemes/types, or accumulate the raw source slice for the parenthesized operator.

findings.explanation: comments is taken from self._prev_comments after consuming everything through ')', so comments belonging to tokens inside the parentheses (or the closing paren) are attached to the whole Operator expression instead of comments preceding the operator construct.
findings.suggested_fix: Capture the relevant comments before consuming the OPERATOR/'(' tokens and pass those to self.expression.

findings.explanation: Neither the left operand 'this' (declared nullable) nor the result of _parse_bitwise() is checked, so inputs like a leading '(op) x' or 'x (op)' / 'x (op) )' create an Operator with None operands that can crash or corrupt later generation/transform stages.
findings.suggested_fix: Return/raise an error when this is None or when _parse_bitwise() returns None instead of constructing exp.Operator.

findings.explanation: The right-hand side is parsed only at _parse_bitwise level, so comparison, range, and boolean operators following a custom operator are not bound into the RHS and the resulting tree's precedence/associativity differs from a normal binary-operator parse.
findings.suggested_fix: Parse the RHS at the precedence level intended for this operator (e.g. the same level other binary operators use) or re-dispatch through the normal expression parser with the Operator node as the left operand.

findings.explanation: If OPERATOR is matched but is not followed by '(', the next loop iteration breaks at the L_PAREN check after OPERATOR has already been consumed, silently dropping the keyword and returning a partial expression instead of reporting malformed syntax.
findings.suggested_fix: After matching OPERATOR, require L_PAREN explicitly and raise an error (or restore the index) when it is absent.

findings.explanation: On failure to match L_PAREN no token was consumed so no retreat is needed, and _retreat(self._index - 0) is a no-op that suggests a mistaken -1 which would corrupt the index.
findings.suggested_fix: Remove the _retreat call and just return None when L_PAREN is not matched.

findings.explanation: Loop concatenates every token until R_PAREN into op, so the inner operand is swallowed into the operator string instead of being parsed as an expression.
findings.suggested_fix: Only consume operator tokens for op and parse the operand separately, e.g. stop at whitespace/expression start or parse inner expression before consuming R_PAREN.

findings.explanation: If EOF is reached before R_PAREN the loop exits via not self._curr and code still returns an Operator instead of backtracking/failing on unterminated paren.
findings.suggested_fix: After loop check that R_PAREN was actually matched; if self._curr is None and no R_PAREN found, retreat to start and return None.

findings.explanation: Empty parens () yields empty operator string op == '' but still builds an Operator node instead of returning None.
findings.suggested_fix: If not op: retreat to start index and return None.

findings.explanation: R_PAREN is consumed in the loop then _parse_bitwise parses tokens after the closing paren, so operand comes from outside the parens and inner tokens are lost.
findings.suggested_fix: Parse the bitwise expression inside the parens before matching R_PAREN, then match R_PAREN and build Operator with that inner expression.

findings.explanation: comments is taken from _prev_comments after consuming R_PAREN, so attached comments are those before ) not those for the whole operator expression.
findings.suggested_fix: Capture comments before parsing (at function entry / after L_PAREN) and pass those to self.expression.

findings.explanation: When L_PAREN is not matched, retreating to self._index is a no-op, so the previously consumed OPERATOR token is lost instead of being restored for alternative parsing.
findings.suggested_fix: Use self._retreat(self._index - 1) before returning None.

findings.explanation: Operator token text is appended without uppercasing, so alphabetic operators are not normalized to the canonical form expected by expression equality and SQL generation.
findings.suggested_fix: Use op += self._curr.text.upper().

findings.explanation: Comments are captured after the parenthesized operator has been consumed, so _prev_comments belongs to the closing parenthesis or last operator token rather than the OPERATOR token, attaching the wrong comments to the Operator node and losing its original comments.
findings.suggested_fix: Capture comments = self._prev_comments at function entry, before matching L_PAREN, and pass that value to self.expression.

findings.explanation: If EOF is reached before R_PAREN, or the parentheses are empty, the loop silently ends and an Operator is returned with a missing closing parenthesis or an empty operator string instead of reporting malformed syntax.
findings.suggested_fix: Track whether R_PAREN was matched and op is non-empty; otherwise raise a parse error or return None after retreating.

findings.explanation: On failed L_PAREN match _match did not advance, so no retreat is needed, and 1 - self._index computes a negative/wrong absolute index.
findings.suggested_fix: Remove the _retreat call entirely.

findings.explanation: Returning None discards the already-parsed left side `this`; parse helpers taking `this` must return `this` when their syntax is absent.
findings.suggested_fix: return this instead of None

findings.explanation: Loop exits on EOF with no R_PAREN check, so unterminated OPERATOR( creates an Operator anyway instead of failing/returning `this`.
findings.suggested_fix: Track if R_PAREN was matched and if not return this.

findings.explanation: OPERATOR() yields op=="" but still builds exp.Operator with empty operator, accepting invalid syntax.
findings.suggested_fix: if not op: return this

findings.explanation: Result of _parse_bitwise() is used unconditionally, so missing right operand builds Operator with expression=None instead of returning `this`/raising.
findings.suggested_fix: Parse to variable, if falsy return this.

findings.explanation: Concatenating raw token texts collapses whitespace/separators and accepts arbitrary tokens as operator.
findings.suggested_fix: Validate/split operator tokens and preserve exact form or reject invalid.

findings.explanation: The retreat target is computed as 1 - self._index instead of self._index - 1, producing negative or otherwise wrong token indexes for almost every position and corrupting or crashing subsequent parsing.
findings.suggested_fix: self._retreat(self._index - 1)

findings.explanation: If the closing parenthesis is missing, the loop consumes tokens until EOF and the method still builds an Operator instead of reporting an error or rewinding, silently swallowing the rest of the statement.
findings.suggested_fix: Track whether R_PAREN was matched; if EOF is reached first, raise a ParserError (or retreat to the start and return None) instead of constructing the node.

findings.explanation: An empty operator such as () is accepted with operator="", and a missing right-hand side makes _parse_bitwise() return None for a required expression, producing an invalid Operator node rather than a parse error.
findings.suggested_fix: Validate that op is non-empty and that the parsed right-hand expression is not None; otherwise raise a ParserError.

findings.explanation: self._prev_comments is read only after the parenthesized operator tokens have been consumed, so it reflects comments inside/before the closing parenthesis rather than comments preceding the operator, attaching the wrong comments to the Operator node and losing the original ones.
findings.suggested_fix: Capture the relevant comments before matching L_PAREN/advancing through the operator tokens and pass that saved value to self.expression(...).

findings.explanation: When called with this=None and input has no left operand, _parse_bitwise can return None yet the code still builds exp.Match(this=None,...).
findings.suggested_fix: Guard with `if this is None: return super()._parse_range(this)` or only enter MATCH branch when `this is not None`.

findings.explanation: Left side is parsed via _parse_bitwise which consumes leading NOT as unary, so `NOT col MATCH 'q'` becomes `(NOT col) MATCH 'q'` instead of `NOT (col MATCH 'q')`.
findings.suggested_fix: Parse left without unary NOT or handle leading NOT before parsing left, e.g. parse with lower precedence.

findings.explanation: Result of _parse_string() is not validated; if it returns None an invalid Match with expression=None is still created.
findings.suggested_fix: Check `if not expression: return super()._parse_range(this)` or retreat and delegate.

findings.explanation: Analyzer parsed with any_token=False rejects keyword-named analyzers and code continues building Match with analyzer=None even if raise_error does not raise.
findings.suggested_fix: Use `_parse_id_var(any_token=True)` / `_parse_var` and return None or retreat after failed analyzer parse.

findings.explanation: The MATCH branch does not check that `this` is not None, so an expression beginning with e.g. `MATCH_ANY 'x'` builds a Match node with a missing required left operand instead of producing a parse error, which can break generation or downstream processing.
findings.suggested_fix: Add `this is not None` to the condition, or raise an error if `this` is None before constructing exp.Match.

findings.explanation: Wrapping the Match in exp.Not and then passing it to super()._parse_range() lets a following range operator such as BETWEEN bind to the whole Not(Match) expression (e.g. `a NOT MATCH_ANY 'x' BETWEEN ...`), producing a wrong/invalid AST instead of rejecting or correctly scoping the range.
findings.suggested_fix: Return the Not(Match) directly when negated, or only delegate to super()._parse_range() for the non-negated Match case.

findings.explanation: After USING ANALYZER, raise_error() does not necessarily abort parsing, yet the code still builds and returns a Match with analyzer=None, silently dropping the analyzer clause and continuing with an incorrect AST.
findings.suggested_fix: Only construct the Match when an analyzer was parsed; otherwise return None / propagate the error instead of building an incomplete Match.

findings.explanation: _parse_id_var(any_token=False) rejects analyzer names that are tokenized as keywords or are quoted/back-quoted identifiers, causing valid USING ANALYZER clauses with such names to fail or be dropped.
findings.suggested_fix: Parse the analyzer with a more permissive identifier parser (e.g. any_token=True or accept quoted identifiers / _parse_table_parts-style handling).

findings.explanation: Requiring token_type == TokenType.VAR misses operator spellings that the tokenizer emits as a keyword token or as a quoted identifier token, so a valid MATCH/MATCH_* predicate in those forms silently falls through to unrelated parsing (alias/range handling).
findings.suggested_fix: Match by curr text against MATCH_OPERATORS without restricting to VAR, while keeping the following-STRING guard to avoid swallowing plain identifiers.

findings.explanation: VAR operator is tested but never consumed, so _prev.text is the previous token (left operand or NOT) not the operator, producing wrong kind and leaving operator unconsumed.
findings.suggested_fix: Consume the operator, e.g. use _match_texts/_match or _parse_var before reading _prev.text.

findings.explanation: Condition accepts any VAR as a MATCH operator, so implicit aliases like `SELECT a b` are misparsed as Match(a, b) instead of alias.
findings.suggested_fix: Only enter branch when current text is MATCH or in MATCH_OPERATORS.

findings.explanation: NOT is matched unconditionally even when this is None, so a leading prefix NOT is mistaken for infix NOT MATCH and corrupts `NOT x MATCH y`.
findings.suggested_fix: Only match infix NOT when this is not None.

findings.explanation: Direct access to _curr.token_type and _prev.text crashes at EOF/BOF when _curr or _prev is None.
findings.suggested_fix: Guard with `self._curr and` / check _prev is not None.

findings.explanation: After raise_error for missing analyzer name execution continues and builds a Match with analyzer None instead of aborting/retreating.
findings.suggested_fix: Return None or re-raise after raise_error; do not build Match on failure.

findings.explanation: Due to short-circuit `or`, when the current token is a VAR the `_match_texts(self.MATCH_OPERATORS)` call is never evaluated, so the MATCH operator is not consumed and `self._prev` is not the operator. `kind` is therefore derived from the preceding column token and `_parse_bitwise()` parses the operator itself (e.g. MATCH_ANY) as the search expression, leaving the real search term unconsumed or misparsed.
findings.suggested_fix: Check membership and consume explicitly, e.g. `if self._curr and self._curr.text.upper() in self.MATCH_OPERATORS: self._advance(); kind = ...` or use only a consuming match that verifies the text.

findings.explanation: The condition accepts any VAR token, not only MATCH_OPERATORS, so ordinary implicit aliases or identifiers after an expression (e.g. `SELECT a b`, `a NOT b`) are treated as a MATCH operation and turned into `exp.Match(this=a, expression=b)` instead of being left for alias/range parsing. The missing-expression retreat does not help because the alias parses successfully as `expression`.
findings.suggested_fix: Gate the branch on the current text actually being one of MATCH_OPERATORS (and consume it), otherwise fall through to `super()._parse_range(this)`.

findings.category: null dereference at end of input
findings.explanation: `self._curr.token_type` dereferences `_curr` without a None check; `_curr` is None at EOF or after truncated input (e.g. a statement ending right after an operand, or `col MATCH_ANY` handled through other paths), causing AttributeError instead of a parse error or clean return.
findings.suggested_fix: Use `if self._curr and (self._curr.token_type == TokenType.VAR or self._match_texts(...))` or a safe helper.

findings.explanation: When USING ANALYZER is present but no analyzer name can be parsed, `raise_error` only records the error and execution continues, silently building and returning a Match node with `analyzer=None` and generating SQL that drops the analyzer clause instead of aborting/retreating.
findings.suggested_fix: After raising the error, retreat to `index` and delegate to `super()._parse_range(this)`, or return None / avoid constructing the Match node.

findings.explanation: `_parse_id_var(any_token=False)` rejects analyzer names tokenized as reserved/keyword tokens, and neither `_parse_string()` nor `_parse_id_var` accepts backtick/quoted identifiers, so valid Doris analyzer references such as `USING ANALYZER `my_analyzer`` spuriously trigger the 'Expected an analyzer name' error.
findings.suggested_fix: Parse the analyzer with `_parse_var_or_string()` / `_parse_identifier()` (handling quoted identifiers) and normalize it, rather than string-or-id_var only.

findings.category: negated MATCH wrapping and re-entry into range parsing
findings.explanation: For `col NOT MATCH_ANY 'x'` the code wraps the whole Match in `exp.Not`, whose generator emits `NOT (col MATCH_ANY 'x')` rather than the Doris `col NOT MATCH_ANY 'x'` form, and then feeds that boolean Not node into `super()._parse_range(this)`, which can mis-associate any following range operator with the negated boolean instead of the match result.
findings.suggested_fix: Represent negation on the Match node itself (or generate NOT MATCH) and return the match expression directly without re-entering `_parse_range` on the Not wrapper.

findings.explanation: Condition is inverted: raises on valid analyzer and silently accepts missing analyzer.
findings.suggested_fix: Change to `if not analyzer: self.raise_error(...)`

findings.explanation: If left side `this` is None a Match with null `this` is built instead of delegating to super.
findings.suggested_fix: Only build Match if `this` and `expression` exist, e.g. `if not this: return super()._parse_range(this)`

findings.explanation: The condition is inverted: a successfully parsed analyzer triggers an error, while USING ANALYZER with no analyzer name is silently accepted with analyzer=None.
findings.suggested_fix: Change to `if not analyzer: self.raise_error("Expected an analyzer name after USING ANALYZER")`.

findings.explanation: self._curr can be None when the preceding expression is at end of input, so accessing self._curr.token_type raises AttributeError instead of returning the parsed expression.
findings.suggested_fix: Guard the check: `if self._curr and self._curr.token_type == TokenType.VAR and ...`.

findings.explanation: The plain MATCH keyword is tokenized as TokenType.MATCH rather than TokenType.VAR (unlike underscored MATCH_ALL/MATCH_ANY variants), so the VAR-only guard skips plain `col MATCH 'text'` even though MATCH is in MATCH_OPERATORS and kind=None is explicitly handled.
findings.suggested_fix: Allow both token types: `self._curr.token_type in (TokenType.VAR, TokenType.MATCH)` before calling _match_texts.

findings.explanation: If FILTER has no WHERE clause expression.expression is None, .this raises AttributeError.
findings.suggested_fix: Guard: where = expression.expression; cond = where.this if where else None; fallback if None.

findings.explanation: agg.expression can be None when WITHIN GROUP has no ORDER BY, so .expressions crashes; also IFF built without false branch.
findings.suggested_fix: Check agg.expression exists; use exp.If(this=cond.copy(), true=key.copy(), false=exp.null()).

findings.explanation: Unsupported WITHIN GROUP case warns but returns sql(agg) silently dropping the FILTER condition.
findings.suggested_fix: Do not silently drop filter; return original FILTER SQL or raise.

findings.explanation: Only COUNT(*) is mapped to COUNT_IF; COUNT(DISTINCT x) FILTER loses DISTINCT and other *-args fall through to invalid IFF(cond, *, NULL).
findings.suggested_fix: Handle Distinct/Star explicitly; never wrap Star in IFF.

findings.explanation: exp.Order stores keys in expressions, not this, so agg_arg.this is None/wrong and ordering is lost or crashes.
findings.suggested_fix: Do not unwrap via .this; handle Order node by rewriting its Ordered expressions.

findings.explanation: Only Order-outside-Distinct is handled; Distinct-outside-Order and multi-arg DISTINCT wrapped per-arg changes DISTINCT semantics.
findings.suggested_fix: Handle both nestings and single-argument case only; mark multi-arg DISTINCT unsupported.

findings.explanation: IFF built as If(this, true) without false=NULL is invalid in Snowflake and mutates the input AST in place causing double-wrap on re-generation.
findings.suggested_fix: Use exp.If(this=cond.copy(), true=target.copy(), false=exp.null()) on a copy of agg.

findings.explanation: This assumes the FILTER expression is always a Where node; a Filter with a missing or directly-stored condition causes an AttributeError instead of generating SQL.
findings.suggested_fix: Handle both cases, e.g. cond = expression.expression.this if isinstance(expression.expression, exp.Where) else expression.expression, and guard against None.

findings.explanation: This assumes the filtered expression always has a single aggregate argument; zero-argument aggregates or aggregates whose `this` is None/string (e.g. Anonymous/custom aggregates) make agg_arg invalid and later crash or misbehave at target.replace.
findings.suggested_fix: Validate that agg is an AggFunc with an Expression argument; handle Anonymous aggregates via their expressions list and bail out with unsupported() when there is no rewritable argument.

findings.explanation: This assumes a WithinGroup percentile/MODE always has agg.expression with an expressions list; if the WITHIN GROUP clause is missing or represented differently, accessing .expressions crashes.
findings.suggested_fix: Guard agg.expression and its expressions, calling unsupported() and falling back when the ORDER BY clause is absent or unexpected.

findings.explanation: For unsupported WITHIN GROUP aggregates it returns the aggregate with the FILTER clause silently dropped, producing results computed over all rows rather than only qualifying rows.
findings.suggested_fix: Do not emit an unfiltered aggregate as if equivalent; preserve/emit the original FILTER expression or raise/fail rather than returning self.sql(agg) without the filter.

findings.explanation: For DISTINCT aggregates, sqlglot stores the first distinct value in Distinct.this and only additional values in Distinct.expressions, so targets misses the main value (e.g. SUM(DISTINCT x) FILTER is returned completely unfiltered, or only secondary columns are wrapped).
findings.suggested_fix: Use targets = [agg_arg.this] + agg_arg.expressions (filtering out None) when agg_arg is a Distinct.

findings.explanation: Order and Distinct are only unwrapped once and in a fixed order, so aggregates where Distinct wraps Order (or other nestings of the two) are not unwrapped correctly and the condition is applied to the wrong node or not at all.
findings.suggested_fix: Loop while agg_arg is an Order or Distinct, collecting the underlying value expression(s) from both node types regardless of nesting order.

findings.explanation: Only agg.this (the first argument) is wrapped, so multi-argument aggregates (e.g. CORR(x, y), COVAR_POP(x, y), or custom aggregates stored in expressions) still consume the unfiltered additional arguments from non-qualifying rows.
findings.suggested_fix: Wrap every input argument of the aggregate (this plus its value expressions), not just the first, while leaving non-value arguments such as separators untouched.

findings.explanation: The rewrite mutates the caller's AST in place via replace(); generating SQL twice from the same parsed tree (or reusing the tree afterward) double-wraps values in nested IFs and permanently destroys the original FILTER structure.
findings.suggested_fix: Work on a copy, e.g. agg = expression.this.copy(), and build the result from the copy instead of mutating the input expression.

findings.explanation: The same in-place mutation and single-argument issues apply to the ordered-set branch: only agg.expression keys are wrapped and the original tree is mutated, so re-generation double-wraps and any other input carried on the aggregate node is left unfiltered.
findings.suggested_fix: Copy the WithinGroup node before rewriting and wrap all relevant input expressions on the copy.

findings.explanation: Wrapping values as IF(cond, x) makes non-qualifying rows NULL, which is only equivalent for aggregates that ignore NULLs; for aggregates such as ARRAY_AGG (and the specially-handled ArrayAgg/GroupConcat path) the NULLs are collected into the result instead of the rows being excluded.
findings.suggested_fix: Only use the conditional-aggregation rewrite for NULL-ignoring aggregates, or use a dialect-supported filtered form for ARRAY_AGG/GroupConcat instead of wrapping their input in IF.

findings.explanation: Assumes Filter always has Where wrapper: expression.expression.this crashes if Where missing and returns wrong node if condition stored directly.
findings.suggested_fix: Unwrap safely: cond = expression.expression; if isinstance(cond, exp.Where): cond = cond.this; check for None.

findings.explanation: Mutates input AST via replace without copying agg first, corrupting cached tree and double-wrapping on re-generation.
findings.suggested_fix: agg = expression.this.copy() and cond = ...copy() before mutating.

findings.explanation: Builds If with only 2 args, missing explicit NULL else-branch, so Snowflake IFF gets wrong arity or wrong semantics.
findings.suggested_fix: exp.If(this=cond.copy(), true=key.copy(), false=exp.Null())

findings.explanation: Same missing else-NULL: IFF(cond, x) instead of IFF(cond, x, NULL) is invalid or mis-compiled in Snowflake.
findings.suggested_fix: exp.If(this=cond.copy(), true=target.copy(), false=exp.Null())

findings.explanation: Comment says COUNT(*/t.*) must use COUNT_IF but code never implements it and falls through to IFF(cond, *, NULL) which Snowflake rejects.
findings.suggested_fix: if isinstance(agg_arg, exp.Star) or star-column: return COUNT_IF(cond) e.g. f"COUNT_IF({self.sql(cond)})"

findings.explanation: exp.Order stores keys in .expressions not .this, so agg_arg.this is None leading to crash on None.replace or dropped argument.
findings.suggested_fix: Handle Order correctly: don't collapse to .this; unwrap Distinct underneath and preserve ORDER BY expressions.

findings.explanation: Rewrites null-preserving aggregates like ARRAY_AGG/GROUP_CONCAT to IFF(cond,x,NULL) which adds spurious NULL rows instead of excluding rows like FILTER does.
findings.suggested_fix: Don't rewrite ARRAY_AGG/GROUP_CONCAT this way or filter NULLs out afterwards; mark unsupported.

findings.explanation: On unsupported WITHIN GROUP it warns but returns plain agg, silently dropping the FILTER condition.
findings.suggested_fix: Fallback to preserving semantics or raise; do not return agg without cond.

findings.explanation: Wrapping each DISTINCT expression separately breaks multi-arg DISTINCT correlation and ORDER BY participation of filtered rows.
findings.suggested_fix: Wrap row as whole or use subquery filter instead of per-column IFF.

findings.explanation: The comment says COUNT(*/t.*) FILTER must use COUNT_IF, but no such branch exists, so a Star target is wrapped as IF(cond, *, NULL), which Snowflake expands/rejects and does not count qualifying rows.
findings.suggested_fix: Before generic wrapping, detect exp.Count whose argument is exp.Star or a qualified star and emit COUNT_IF(cond) instead.

findings.explanation: sqlglot stores a single DISTINCT argument in Distinct.this, with expressions only holding additional arguments, so for COUNT/SUM(DISTINCT x) targets becomes [] and the FILTER condition is silently dropped.
findings.suggested_fix: Use targets=[agg_arg.this, *agg_arg.expressions] (filtering out None), and also unwrap Distinct nested inside/outside Order in either order.

findings.explanation: exp.If is built with only this/true and no false branch; Snowflake's IFF (and IF) conditional requires an else value, so generated SQL is invalid or does not yield NULL for non-qualifying rows. The same bug occurs on line 42.
findings.suggested_fix: Pass false=exp.Null() (or exp.column NULL) explicitly: exp.If(this=cond.copy(), true=key.copy(), false=exp.Null()).

findings.explanation: The non-WITHIN GROUP rewrite also creates a two-argument conditional without an else NULL, which Snowflake rejects and which is needed so non-qualifying rows are ignored by the aggregate.
findings.suggested_fix: Use exp.If(this=cond.copy(), true=target.copy(), false=exp.Null()).

findings.explanation: For unsupported WITHIN GROUP aggregates the code calls unsupported() but still returns self.sql(agg), emitting an unfiltered aggregate and returning wrong results instead of preserving/failing the FILTER rewrite.
findings.suggested_fix: Do not emit a correct-looking unfiltered aggregate; fall back to the original Filter SQL via super().filter_sql(expression) or raise/leave FILTER intact after unsupported().

findings.explanation: The percentile/Mode branch assumes agg.expression exists and has expressions and that each ordered.this is a replaceable expression; a programmatically built WithinGroup without ORDER BY (or with a non-Ordered key) crashes with AttributeError instead of being handled.
findings.suggested_fix: Guard agg.expression/its expressions and ordered.this for None, and route missing ORDER BY cases to the unsupported fallback.

findings.explanation: The code assumes expression.expression.this is a condition and agg.this is always an Expression; FILTER over an aggregate with no argument or an Anonymous/custom function whose this is a string/None makes target.replace fail with AttributeError.
findings.suggested_fix: Validate isinstance(agg_arg, exp.Expression) and the Where/condition shape before replacing, otherwise call unsupported() and fall back to the original expression.

findings.explanation: replace() mutates the caller's parsed Filter/aggregate tree in place, so generating SQL twice or reusing the AST double-wraps arguments in IF(IF(...)) and loses the original FILTER node.
findings.suggested_fix: Work on agg.copy() (and cond copies from it) and generate SQL from the copy instead of mutating expression.this.

findings.explanation: agg.this and expression.expression.this are dereferenced without None checks; FILTER without WHERE, COUNT with no arg, or malformed Filter crashes.
findings.suggested_fix: Guard for None: if agg_arg is None or cond is None: fallback or return self.sql(expression).

findings.explanation: agg.expression is assumed non-null and Ordered.this is assumed non-null; WITHIN GROUP without ORDER BY crashes.
findings.suggested_fix: Check if agg.expression is None before iterating and if ordered.this is None.

findings.explanation: Unsupported WITHIN GROUP case warns but returns self.sql(agg) without the FILTER condition, producing wrong results.
findings.suggested_fix: Preserve semantics or fail: return self.sql(expression) to keep FILTER instead of dropping it.

findings.explanation: ArrayAgg/GroupConcat WITHIN GROUP unwraps agg_arg then falls through to generic rewrite that wraps the aggregate argument instead of the WITHIN GROUP ORDER BY keys.
findings.suggested_fix: Handle ArrayAgg/GroupConcat WITHIN GROUP like Mode/percentiles: rewrite agg.expression.expressions keys and return early.

findings.explanation: Uses `or` so any non-Count SUM(t.*) becomes COUNT_IF, and calls agg_arg.is_star when agg_arg may be None, crashing.
findings.suggested_fix: Use `if isinstance(agg, exp.Count) and agg_arg is not None and agg_arg.is_star:`

findings.explanation: COUNT(expr) and COUNT(DISTINCT expr) FILTER are rewritten to COUNT_IF(cond), dropping expr nullability check and DISTINCT.
findings.suggested_fix: For COUNT with args use COUNT_IF with null check, e.g. COUNT_IF(cond AND arg IS NOT NULL) and preserve DISTINCT or use IFF rewrite.

findings.explanation: exp.Order stores Ordered nodes in expressions, not this, so agg_arg.this is None/wrong and rewrite corrupts or crashes.
findings.suggested_fix: Unwrap Order by iterating agg_arg.expressions and rewriting each ordered.this underneath.

findings.explanation: Only Order-outer/Distinct-inner is handled; DISTINCT-outer with ORDER BY inside wraps whole ORDER/DISTINCT clause yielding invalid IFF(cond, DISTINCT x, ...).
findings.suggested_fix: Recursively unwrap both Order and Distinct in either order before collecting targets.

findings.explanation: exp.If created without false produces 2-arg IF/IFF, but Snowflake IFF requires 3 args, so generated SQL is invalid.
findings.suggested_fix: Add explicit false: exp.If(this=cond.copy(), true=key.copy(), false=exp.null())

findings.explanation: COUNT(x) FILTER (WHERE cond) is rewritten to COUNT_IF(cond), which counts qualifying rows even when x is NULL, whereas COUNT(x) counts only rows where x is not NULL.
findings.suggested_fix: Use COUNT_IF(cond AND agg_arg IS NOT NULL) for non-star COUNT, or rewrite as COUNT(IFF(cond, x, NULL)).

findings.explanation: The COUNT shortcut runs before DISTINCT handling, so COUNT(DISTINCT x) FILTER (WHERE cond) becomes COUNT_IF(cond) and loses both DISTINCT and the counted expression.
findings.suggested_fix: Only use COUNT_IF for plain COUNT(*)/COUNT(1)-style forms; for COUNT(DISTINCT x) rewrite to COUNT(DISTINCT IFF(cond, x, NULL)).

findings.explanation: agg_arg can be None for aggregates with no 'this' argument, so agg_arg.is_star raises AttributeError for non-COUNT aggregates (the COUNT check short-circuits only for Count).
findings.suggested_fix: Guard with agg_arg and agg_arg.is_star, e.g. isinstance(agg, exp.Count) or (agg_arg is not None and agg_arg.is_star).

findings.explanation: agg_arg.is_star triggers COUNT_IF for any non-COUNT aggregate whose first argument is a star, silently replacing that aggregate (and any WITHIN GROUP clause) with a count instead of reporting it unsupported.
findings.suggested_fix: Restrict the star shortcut to exp.Count (including a Count nested in WithinGroup only if handled explicitly); otherwise fall through or mark unsupported.

findings.explanation: For unsupported WITHIN GROUP aggregates the code returns self.sql(agg), silently dropping the FILTER condition and producing unfiltered results instead of preserving semantics or failing.
findings.suggested_fix: Do not emit the bare aggregate; either implement the rewrite for that function or surface an error/unsupported result that cannot be mistaken for the filtered aggregate.

findings.explanation: target.replace mutates the caller's original AST in place (same issue at lines 12-16), so generating Snowflake SQL permanently removes the FILTER semantics from the tree; re-generating for another dialect or re-running generation yields doubly-wrapped IFFs and a still-attached FILTER.
findings.suggested_fix: Work on a copy, e.g. agg = expression.this.copy() at the start of filter_sql, and mutate only the copy.

findings.explanation: Only agg.this (the first argument) is ever wrapped, so multi-argument aggregates such as OBJECT_AGG(k, v), COVAR_POP(x, y) or REGR_*(y, x) FILTER (...) keep later arguments unfiltered; aggregates that do not discard rows solely because the first argument became NULL then compute over unfiltered rows.
findings.suggested_fix: Wrap every per-row argument of multi-argument aggregates with the condition, or restrict the rewrite to single-argument aggregates and mark the rest unsupported.

findings.explanation: Only one level of Order-then-Distinct nesting is unwrapped; a Distinct wrapping an Order (or deeper nesting) leaves targets pointing at the Order/Distinct node itself, generating invalid IFF(cond, DISTINCT ...)/IFF(cond, ORDER BY ...) syntax.
findings.suggested_fix: Unwrap Order and Distinct in a loop until reaching leaf expressions before collecting targets.

findings.explanation: Lookup defs[...] raises KeyError if single-column PRIMARY KEY references unknown, quoted, case-mismatched, or non-column expression.
findings.suggested_fix: Guard lookup: check expression is column and name in defs before moving, otherwise leave table constraint.

findings.explanation: Appends a second PRIMARY KEY constraint without checking if column already has one, producing duplicate PRIMARY KEY.
findings.suggested_fix: Only append if no PrimaryKeyColumnConstraint already present on that column.

findings.explanation: column.constraints can be empty/None for unconstrained columns, so enumerate() fails with TypeError.
findings.suggested_fix: Use `for i, constraint in enumerate(column.args.get('constraints') or []):` or early continue.

findings.explanation: When AUTOINCREMENT exists without PRIMARY KEY, code removes it and never re-inserts, silently dropping the constraint.
findings.suggested_fix: Do not remove when primary_key_index == -1; only reorder when both constraints exist and auto precedes pk.

findings.explanation: defs[primary_key.expressions[0].name] raises KeyError if the primary-key column is absent, differs only in identifier case/quoting, or is wrapped (e.g. PRIMARY KEY(id DESC) / COLLATE), instead of leaving the CREATE unchanged.
findings.suggested_fix: Normalize keys (e.g. upper-case) and unwrap Ordered/Collate to the underlying column, use column = defs.get(key) and bail out if not found.

findings.explanation: If several table-level PrimaryKey constraints exist only the last is remembered and moved; the others remain, producing a table with multiple primary keys.
findings.suggested_fix: Collect all PrimaryKey nodes and handle/remove each, or bail out when more than one is present.

findings.explanation: A new PrimaryKeyColumnConstraint is appended unconditionally, so a column that already declares PRIMARY KEY (e.g. 'id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, PRIMARY KEY(id)') ends up with two primary-key constraints.
findings.suggested_fix: Skip appending if the target column already has a PrimaryKeyColumnConstraint.

findings.explanation: Moving the table primary key discards its attributes: sort order (ASC/DESC), collation, ON CONFLICT clause and any constraint name are lost, changing semantics (e.g. INTEGER PRIMARY KEY DESC is not a rowid alias in SQLite).
findings.suggested_fix: Bail out for non-plain primary keys, or transfer on_conflict/ordering/collation onto the column constraint.

findings.explanation: defs is keyed by column name, so duplicate (or case-colliding) column names overwrite each other; the autoincrement cleanup loop over defs.values() then never visits the overwritten column(s) and the PK may be attached to the wrong definition.
findings.suggested_fix: Iterate schema.expressions directly for the cleanup loop and keep a list of ColumnDefs, using defs only for lookup.

findings.explanation: Only the last AutoIncrement and last PrimaryKey constraint per column are tracked, so duplicate constraints are not normalized: an earlier AUTOINCREMENT on a non-primary-key column (or before the PK) is left in place, yielding invalid SQLite.
findings.suggested_fix: Track and process all AutoIncrementColumnConstraint/PrimaryKeyColumnConstraint instances, removing/moving every one.

findings.explanation: AUTOINCREMENT is kept/moved for any primary-key column regardless of type, but SQLite only allows AUTOINCREMENT on an INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, so e.g. TEXT/VARCHAR PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT is emitted and rejected by SQLite.
findings.suggested_fix: Only retain AUTOINCREMENT when column.kind is an INTEGER type; otherwise drop it (or convert the type).

findings.explanation: AUTOINCREMENT is silently stripped from a column that belongs to a composite (multi-column) table primary key, because such columns have no individual PrimaryKeyColumnConstraint; this silently loses the source auto-increment intent without any fallback.
findings.suggested_fix: Detect membership in a composite primary key and handle it explicitly (e.g. keep_single-column conversion only when safe) instead of dropping based solely on a missing column-level PK.

findings.explanation: Checks len==2 instead of len==1, so single-column PKs are never inlined and 2-column composite PKs are truncated to one column.
findings.suggested_fix: Change to `len(primary_key.expressions) == 1` and do not touch composite keys.

findings.explanation: Direct dict/index access `defs[...]` and `expressions[0]` raises KeyError/IndexError if PK is empty, non-column, or references missing/differently-cased column.
findings.suggested_fix: Guard lookup: get target, normalize case, and return early if not found in defs.

findings.explanation: Appends a PrimaryKeyColumnConstraint without checking if the column already has one, creating duplicate PRIMARY KEY.
findings.suggested_fix: Skip appending if column already has a PrimaryKeyColumnConstraint.

findings.explanation: Overwrites primary_key so only the last PrimaryKey is handled, leaving any earlier ones in schema.
findings.suggested_fix: Collect all PrimaryKey expressions or reject multiple keys instead of keeping last only.

findings.explanation: Loop keeps only last AUTOINCREMENT/PK index, so duplicate constraints leave earlier AUTOINCREMENT before PK.
findings.suggested_fix: Handle all AutoIncrementColumnConstraints, not just the last one.

findings.explanation: The condition requires exactly two PK expressions: a normal single-column table PK (length 1) is never moved, while a two-column composite PK is incorrectly collapsed to a PK on only the first column and the table PK is removed, changing uniqueness semantics.
findings.suggested_fix: Use len(primary_key.expressions) == 1 for the move; leave composite primary keys as table-level constraints.

findings.explanation: defs[...] raises KeyError if the PK references a column not present in defs, e.g. an undefined/externally defined column or a name whose case/quoting differs from the ColumnDef name, crashing the transform instead of leaving the CREATE unchanged.
findings.suggested_fix: Use column = defs.get(key); only transform and remove the table PK when column is found, normalizing identifier case for comparison.

findings.explanation: PK expressions are not guaranteed to be plain Columns; e.g. PRIMARY KEY (id DESC) is wrapped in an Ordered expression whose .name does not yield the column name, causing a KeyError or wrong lookup.
findings.suggested_fix: Unwrap Ordered/expression wrappers (e.g. e.this / find exp.Column or exp.Identifier) before extracting the column name, and bail out if it is not a simple column reference.

findings.explanation: defs keyed by name silently overwrites earlier ColumnDefs with the same (or case-insensitively equal) name, and primary_key overwrites earlier table PrimaryKey nodes; only the last of each is processed/removed, leaving earlier columns un-reordered and duplicate table PKs behind.
findings.suggested_fix: Track all PrimaryKey nodes and handle/avoid duplicate column names, or bail out when duplicates are present.

findings.explanation: A PK column constraint is appended unconditionally, so a column that already declares PRIMARY KEY (in addition to the redundant table-level PK) ends up with two PRIMARY KEY column constraints, producing invalid output.
findings.suggested_fix: Check for an existing PrimaryKeyColumnConstraint on the column before appending; skip the append (but still consider dropping the table PK) if present.

findings.explanation: With duplicate constraints only the last AutoIncrement and last PrimaryKey positions are remembered, so an earlier AutoIncrement constraint that precedes the PK is left before it and is never reordered.
findings.suggested_fix: Collect all AutoIncrement constraints (or handle each occurrence) and move every one that precedes the primary key to after it.

findings.explanation: Wraps str(self) in double quotes without escaping embedded quotes, backslashes, newlines or control characters, producing invalid output and allowing injection/breakout.
findings.suggested_fix: return json.dumps(str(self))

findings.explanation: f'"{self}"' formats self via __format__/__str__, which in parser node classes is typically implemented by calling serialize(), so serialize() recurses indefinitely and raises RecursionError.
findings.suggested_fix: Build the output from the underlying stored value/fields directly instead of formatting self, e.g. return json.dumps(self.value)

findings.explanation: The stringified value is wrapped in double quotes without escaping embedded double quotes, backslashes, or control characters such as newlines, producing invalid/ambiguous serialized output that cannot be reliably parsed back and allows quote injection.
findings.suggested_fix: Escape the contents before quoting, e.g. return json.dumps(str_content) instead of f'"{self}"'

findings.explanation: Rejects any value containing a single quote, even though values containing only a single quote can be serialized with double quotes; only values containing both quote types are unserializable.
findings.suggested_fix: if "'" not in value: return f"'{value}'"; elif '"' not in value: return f'"{value}"'; else raise ValueError(...)

findings.explanation: Any value containing a single quote raises ValueError even when it contains no double quote and could safely be serialized with double quotes; the error message also incorrectly claims both quote characters are present because '"' is never checked.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a branch: elif '"' not in value: return f'"{value}"', and only raise when both quote characters are present.

findings.explanation: Lookbehind (?<=\n) never matches at position 0, so a list break at start of string is missed.
findings.suggested_fix: Use (?:(?<=\n)|\A) instead of (?<=\n)

findings.explanation: If _get_list_break_rules returns empty, regex is empty string which matches everywhere.
findings.suggested_fix: if not pairs: return re.compile(r'(?!)')

findings.explanation: p.replace("3", _repl_w, 1) replaces first '3' anywhere, corrupting \3, {13}, character classes, and misses other occurrences; also ignores leading_width > 3.
findings.suggested_fix: Use a placeholder template e.g. p.replace("{WIDTH}", _repl_w) or parameterized pattern construction

findings.explanation: Negative or zero leading_width produces invalid or degenerate quantifier like {-1} or {0} causing re.error or empty matches.
findings.suggested_fix: Validate leading_width >= 0/int and clamp/handle 0 specially, raise ValueError otherwise

findings.explanation: Rule name is interpolated as (?P<name>) without validation, so invalid Python group names or duplicates raise re.error.
findings.suggested_fix: Sanitize names to valid identifiers or use auto-generated names like (?P<g0>...)

findings.explanation: Direct block.specification[name] indexing assumes key exists and value is str; missing key raises KeyError and non-str value breaks .replace.
findings.suggested_fix: Check membership / isinstance str and raise/skip with clear error

findings.explanation: Replacing the first literal "3" anywhere in a pattern corrupts patterns whose first "3" is not the indentation quantifier (e.g. in a character class, literal, or another quantifier) and is a no-op for patterns written with literal spaces, so those rules keep requiring 3 spaces.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace only the specific indentation token, e.g. p.replace('{0,3}', '{0,%d}' % leading_width) or the exact known width substring for each rule.

findings.explanation: count=1 leaves any additional width-related "3" quantifiers in the same pattern unchanged, producing inconsistent indentation requirements within one rule and wrong list-break matches.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace every intended indentation occurrence for the rule, using a targeted token/regex rather than a single generic digit replacement.

findings.explanation: Negative (or non-integer) leading_width values are passed into the pattern, e.g. producing "{-1}" or invalid quantifiers, causing re.error at compile time instead of being rejected or clamped.
findings.suggested_fix: Validate that leading_width is an int in the supported range (e.g. 0..3) and raise ValueError or clamp before building the regex.

findings.explanation: leading_width greater than 3 is silently ignored, so the compiled rules still only recognise breaks indented up to 3 spaces and can falsely break or fail to break lists with wider leading indentation.
findings.suggested_fix: Apply the same width substitution for leading_width > 3, or document/validate that callers never pass values above 3.

findings.explanation: The (?<=\n) prefix is inside the named group but directly concatenated with the pattern, so for a pattern containing a top-level alternation only the first alternative is constrained to follow a newline; later alternatives can match mid-line.
findings.suggested_fix: Scope the whole pattern: r"(?P<%s>(?<=\n)(?:%s))" % (name, pattern).

findings.explanation: (?<=\n) can never match at the very beginning of the input, so a list-breaking construct on the first line (with no preceding newline) is never recognised.
findings.suggested_fix: Also allow start-of-string, e.g. (?:\A|(?<=\n)) or (?m:^) around the scoped pattern.

findings.explanation: If _get_list_break_rules returns no rules, regex becomes the empty string and re.compile('') matches an empty string at every position, which can make callers treat every position as a list break or loop; a missing name in block.specification also raises KeyError.
findings.suggested_fix: Guard against empty pairs (e.g. compile a never-matching pattern like '(?!)' or raise) and use .get()/validate names against block.specification.

findings.explanation: Rule names are interpolated unchecked into (?P<name>...); invalid identifiers, duplicates, or nested named groups inside a specification pattern raise re.error and crash compilation.
findings.suggested_fix: Validate names are unique valid identifiers and reject/strip named groups in sub-patterns, or use non-capturing groups with an external name-to-index mapping.

findings.explanation: Expression is `pair % template` instead of `template % pair`, so Python raises TypeError for tuple % str.
Lookbehind (?<=\n) never matches at position 0, so a list break on the first line is missed.
findings.suggested_fix: Use (?:(?<=\n)|\A) instead of (?<=\n)

findings.explanation: Rule name is interpolated directly into (?P<name>...); names with hyphens/spaces/duplicates cause re.error.
findings.suggested_fix: Sanitize names to valid unique Python identifiers or use non-capturing groups

findings.explanation: If no break rules are returned, "|".join([]) is "" which compiles to a pattern matching everywhere.
findings.suggested_fix: Return a never-matching pattern like re.compile(r'(?!)') when pairs is empty

findings.explanation: Negative leading_width creates " {0,-1}" which raises re.error, and replace(...,1) rewrites the first occurrence anywhere even for rules with no leading indent.
findings.suggested_fix: Clamp leading_width to >=0 and only rewrite a leading indent prefix, e.g. anchored with startswith/re.sub

findings.explanation: pair is a (name, pattern) tuple, so pair % format-string attempts tuple % str and raises TypeError for every non-empty rule set; the format string must be the left operand.
findings.suggested_fix: regex = "|".join(r"(?P<%s>(?<=\n)%s)" % pair for pair in pairs)

findings.explanation: A negative leading_width produces an invalid quantifier such as {0,-1}, causing re.error when the combined pattern is compiled instead of a controlled validation error or clamping.
findings.suggested_fix: Validate 0 <= leading_width (raise ValueError otherwise) before constructing _repl.

findings.explanation: If pairs is empty, the joined regex is the empty pattern, which matches an empty string at every position rather than never matching, so list-break detection can spuriously trigger.
findings.suggested_fix: Return a never-matching pattern, e.g. re.compile(r'(?!)'), when pairs is empty.

findings.explanation: Only the first literal " {0,3}" is rewritten and rules whose indent prefix uses a different spelling are not rewritten at all, so later or differently-spelled indent quantifiers still allow up to 3 spaces when leading_width < 3.
findings.suggested_fix: Rewrite every leading-indent quantifier occurrence for the rule (or compile rules from a parameterized indent token) and assert each rule was adjusted.

findings.explanation: The (?<=\n) lookbehind requires a preceding newline, so a list-breaking construct at position 0 of the scanned string can never match even though it is at a line start.
findings.suggested_fix: Allow start-of-string as well, e.g. use (?<=(?:^|\n)) or prepend/check a synthetic newline consistently.

findings.explanation: Config default is DEFAULT_CONFIG mutable object shared across calls, so any mutation leaks to future calls.
findings.suggested_fix: Use config: Config | None = None and assign DEFAULT_CONFIG inside.

findings.explanation: Empty input returns False immediately without emitting config.add_imports even when force_adds/add_imports require additions.
findings.suggested_fix: Do not early-return before handling add_imports, or check force_adds/add_imports.

findings.explanation: seek()/tell()/truncate() assumes seekable output_stream and raises UnsupportedOperation on pipes/stdout.
findings.suggested_fix: Guard seek/truncate with seekable() check or try/except OSError.

findings.explanation: and binds tighter than or, so condition is (A and B) or C and any line withpio single quote enters quote parsing even inside comments.
findings.suggested_fix: Use ((not stripped_line.startswith('#') or in_quote) and ('"' in line or "'" in line)).

findings.explanation: split('=') without maxsplit fails to unpack on multiple = and rhs.lstrip()[0] IndexErrors on missing/empty RHS.
findings.suggested_fix: Use stripped_line.split('=',1) with validation and check rhs.lstrip() non-empty.

findings.explanation: strip().split('#')[0] leaves trailing space so '\\ # comment' no longer endswith backslash and parenthesized/comment handling mis-detects continuations.
findings.suggested_fix: Strip after splitting, e.g. line.strip().split('#',1)[0].rstrip() or .strip().

findings.explanation: lstrip(line_separator) treats separator as char set, not prefix, so multi-char endings like \r\n over-strip.
findings.suggested_fix: Use removeprefix() or conditional slicing instead of lstrip(line_separator).

findings.explanation: Substring file_skip_comment in line matches inside strings/code, incorrectly skipping file or raising FileSkipComment.
findings.suggested_fix: Only match in comments, e.g. check stripped_line.startswith('#') or comment portion.

findings.explanation: FILE_SKIP_COMMENTS are searched in every raw line before quote state is updated or checked, so a matching string inside a docstring or other multiline string falsely raises FileSkipComment or suppresses sorting for the rest of the file.
findings.suggested_fix: Only check for file-skip comments when not in_quote/was_in_quote, e.g. guard with `if not in_quote and not was_in_quote:`.

findings.explanation: Due to precedence, `or "'" in line` makes the quote scanner run for any line containing a single quote, including comment lines starting with '#'; an apostrophe in a comment (e.g. "don't") can set in_quote and cause following imports to be treated as inside a string and left unsorted.
findings.suggested_fix: Parenthesize the quote test: `if ((not stripped_line.startswith("#") or in_quote) and ('"' in line or "'" in line)):`

findings.explanation: Any stripped line starting with '__all__' is treated as a reexport assignment, including '__all__x = ...', '__all__ += ...', bare annotations, and comparisons; these are mis-sorted or mangled instead of being left alone.
findings.suggested_fix: Match only a simple assignment, e.g. regex `^__all__\s*=(?!=)` on the stripped line.

findings.explanation: `_, rhs = stripped_line.split("=")` raises ValueError when the __all__ literal contains '=' (e.g. `__all__ = ["a=b"]`), and `rhs.lstrip()[0]` raises IndexError/ValueError for `__all__ =` or a missing '='.
findings.suggested_fix: Use `split("=", 1)`, verify an assignment exists and rhs is non-empty before indexing, e.g. `parts = stripped_line.split('=', 1); if len(parts) < 2 or not parts[1].strip(): not a reexport`.

findings.explanation: For sort_reexports the __all__ section is only terminated by a blank line or EOF, so code immediately following `__all__ = [...]` with no blank line is consumed into code_sorting_section, dropped from its original position, and fed to literal.assignment (likely error/corruption); conversely a blank line inside a multiline __all__ literal terminates it early and sorts an incomplete literal.
findings.suggested_fix: End the reexport section when the assignment's brackets/parentheses balance and the logical line is complete, not on blank lines.

findings.explanation: Code sorting builds its config with `_indented_config(config, indent)` using the stale import-section indent instead of the captured `code_sorting_indent`, so indented __all__/literal blocks (e.g. under `if TYPE_CHECKING:`) are formatted with the wrong indent width.
findings.suggested_fix: Pass `code_sorting_indent` instead of `indent` at both call sites (lines 122 and 238).

findings.explanation: sort_reexports unconditionally calls output_stream.seek()/tell()/truncate(); for non-seekable streams such as pipes or sys.stdout these raise io.UnsupportedOperation, crashing instead of sorting. The max(0,...) clamp does not help since seek itself is unsupported, and tell() is called before any guard.
findings.suggested_fix: Check `output_stream.seekable()` (and try/except UnsupportedOperation/OSError) before seeking/truncating, and fall back to buffering or skipping the rollback for non-seekable/no-op streams. Same fix needed at lines 111-139.

findings.category: non-seekable output stream crash at EOF
findings.explanation: The EOF reexport path has the same unguarded seek/tell/truncate calls, so a file ending in __all__ without a trailing blank line crashes on non-seekable output streams.
findings.suggested_fix: Guard seek/tell/truncate with seekable()/try-except as in the mid-file path.

findings.explanation: The float_to_top pre-pass never tracks in_quote, so lines inside multiline strings/docstrings containing '# isort: off', '# isort: split', or ending with '# isort: split' falsely toggle isort_off or split sections, changing string content handling and import placement.
findings.suggested_fix: Track multiline quote state in the float_to_top loop like the main loop and only honor isort directives outside strings.

findings.explanation: Config default is DEFAULT_CONFIG mutable object shared across calls, so mutation leaks between calls.
findings.suggested_fix: Use config: Config | None = None and assign DEFAULT_CONFIG inside.

findings.explanation: Missing parens makes condition (A and B) or C, so any line with single quote triggers quote parsing even inside # comments.
findings.suggested_fix: if (not stripped_line.startswith('#') or in_quote) and ('"' in line or "'" in line):

findings.explanation: split('=') without maxsplit crashes with ValueError if no = or too many values, e.g. __all__ with = in string.
findings.suggested_fix: _, rhs = stripped_line.split('=', 1)

findings.explanation: Skip requires contains_imports, so a first import with isort: skip is sorted instead of kept in place.
findings.suggested_fix: Check _has_skip_comment(import_statement) without contains_imports gate.

findings.explanation: tell()-len(line) arithmetic is invalid for TextIO where tell is opaque cookie, and seek/tell crashes on non-seekable streams like pipes.
findings.suggested_fix: Buffer reexport output instead of seek/truncate, or guard with seekable() check.

findings.explanation: Uses line_separator.join which is empty string when separator undetected, instead of add_line_separator fallback used elsewhere.
findings.suggested_fix: Use add_line_separator = line_separator or '\n' as in float_to_top path.

findings.explanation: extra_space.replace('\n','',1) leaves stray \r for CRLF files, corrupting line endings.
findings.suggested_fix: Strip one line_separator sequence instead of one \n.

findings.explanation: Backslash continuation at EOF silently accepts dangling backslash while paren continuation raises ExistingSyntaxErrors; also readline while iterating chain can skip data.
findings.suggested_fix: Raise ExistingSyntaxErrors on EOF with pending backslash and iterate via readline consistently.

findings.explanation: Due to precedence, `or "'" in line` is evaluated independently, so a comment containing an apostrophe (e.g. `# don't`) enters quote-scanning and can set in_quote, causing following imports to be treated as quoted text and left unsorted.
findings.suggested_fix: Parenthesize the quote test: `if (not stripped_line.startswith("#") or in_quote) and ('"' in line or "'" in line):`

findings.explanation: `stripped_line.split("=")` without maxsplit raises ValueError when the RHS contains '=' (e.g. a string "a=b"), and `rhs.lstrip()[0]` raises IndexError/ValueError for `__all__` without an inline RHS or for a bare `__all__` reference.
findings.suggested_fix: Use `stripped_line.split("=", 1)`, require an assignment match (e.g. regex `__all__\s*[:=]`), and guard against an empty RHS before indexing.

findings.explanation: Any line starting with `__all__` is treated as a sortable literal assignment, including comparisons (`__all__ == ...`), augmented assignment (`__all__ += ...` which is rewritten as a plain assignment), annotated assignments (annotation dropped on rewrite), and names like `__all__foo`, corrupting such code.
findings.suggested_fix: Only trigger on a plain assignment such as regex `^__all__\s*=`, and skip/handle `+=` and annotated assignments explicitly.

findings.explanation: Once code_sorting is set (including for __all__), every subsequent non-blank line is swallowed into code_sorting_section until a blank line or EOF, so code immediately following a __all__ block (no blank line) is fed to literal.assignment, causing errors or silently dropping/rewriting that code.
findings.suggested_fix: Terminate the section when the literal's brackets balance / the statement ends, not only on a blank line, and flush following code lines normally.

findings.explanation: The backslash-continuation loop never checks for EOF: readline() returning '' silently ends the loop, so an unterminated continued import at EOF is accepted/truncated instead of raising ExistingSyntaxErrors as the parenthesis branch does.
findings.suggested_fix: After each readline() in the backslash branch, `if not line: raise ExistingSyntaxErrors(...)` like lines 307-308.

findings.explanation: The condition is true for every statement whose lstrip starts with 'from' (and any statement lacking 'import'), regardless of a skip comment, so all from-imports are flushed as not_imports and never collected/sorted, breaking normal import sorting and grouping.
findings.suggested_fix: Require a skip comment for this bypass, e.g. `(import_statement.lstrip().startswith('from') or 'import' not in import_statement) and _has_skip_comment(import_statement)`, plus the new contains_imports skip case.

findings.explanation: Clamping the rollback seek to 0 on a real seekable stream (tell() < reexport_rollback for any reason other than check mode) rewinds to the file start and overwrites/truncates earlier content; calling seek() also still raises UnsupportedOperation on non-seekable streams (stdout/pipes), and the `tell() > 0` guard skips truncate() when the write position is 0, leaving stale bytes.
findings.suggested_fix: Only seek/truncate when the stream is seekable and tell() >= reexport_rollback; otherwise buffer/rewrite instead, and call truncate(sorted_position) unconditionally for seekable streams.

findings.explanation: Same flaw at the blank-line flush: max(0, tell()-rollback) can overwrite the beginning of a real stream when rollback exceeds the position (e.g. when the __all__ line was merged into a preceding import section flush, so it is not the last bytes written), seek() crashes on non-seekable outputs, and `tell() > 0` can skip truncation leaving stale trailing content.
findings.suggested_fix: Verify seekability and that the __all__ line was actually the last verbatim output before seeking back exactly reexport_rollback; otherwise avoid seek/truncate and use a buffered rewrite, truncating at the post-write position unconditionally.

findings.explanation: start saves a Token (self._prev) but _parse_as_command expects an index to rewind, so fallback cannot restore position.
findings.suggested_fix: start = self._index - 1  # or self._index as required by _parse_as_command

findings.explanation: Advances on self._next instead of self._curr, so a single trailing action token is never consumed and parser lookup uses the wrong token.
findings.suggested_fix: if self._curr: self._advance()

findings.explanation: The advance to the action keyword is inside the else branch, so ALTER SESSION never advances and _prev still points at SESSION.
findings.suggested_fix: Advance / resolve parser outside the SESSION vs non-SESSION branch.

findings.explanation: Lookup uses only self._prev.text, so multi-word ALTER_PARSERS keys can never match and valid alters fall back to Command.
findings.suggested_fix: Match against ALTER_PARSERS keys and keep the matched key instead of using _prev.text.

findings.explanation: ensure_list(parser(self)) turns parser returning None into [None], which is truthy and later embedded in Alter.actions.
findings.suggested_fix: result = parser(self); actions = ensure_list(result) if result else None

findings.explanation: First action does not handle parser returning exp.Command nor use _try_parse, while later actions do, so a Command first action is embedded in Alter instead of falling back.
findings.suggested_fix: Use _try_parse for first action and if any action is exp.Command return _parse_as_command(start).

findings.explanation: While condition calls _match(COMMA) and _match_texts(ALTER_PARSERS) which consume input even when the whole condition is false, losing a trailing comma/action keyword.
findings.suggested_fix: Look ahead without advancing, only consume comma and action after confirming both match.

findings.explanation: Accesses self._prev.token_type without checking self._prev is not None.
findings.suggested_fix: self._prev and self._prev.token_type == TokenType.COMMA

findings.explanation: Indexes ALTER_PARSERS with _prev.text which may not be a key after _match_texts consumed a multi-word or case-variant match, raising KeyError.
findings.suggested_fix: Reuse the key matched by _match_texts or use .get with fallback to command.

findings.explanation: ensure_list(_try_parse(...)) turns failure None into [None], so `not parsed` never fires and None is appended to actions.
findings.suggested_fix: parsed_raw = self._try_parse(lambda: parser(self)); if not parsed_raw: return ...; parsed = ensure_list(parsed_raw)

findings.explanation: Using `and` stores False instead of None/bool when dialect flag is off, mixing types for cascade field.
findings.suggested_fix: cascade = self._match_text_seq("CASCADE") if self.dialect.ALTER_TABLE_SUPPORTS_CASCADE else None

findings.explanation: Requires exact end-of-input, so valid ALTER with trailing semicolon or extra token is misclassified as Command instead of Alter.
findings.suggested_fix: Allow semicolon / handle trailing tokens instead of `if not self._curr` only.

findings.explanation: The action-token advance is guarded by self._next instead of self._curr, so a statement whose action keyword is the final token is never advanced to and dispatch at line 44 uses the table's last token, incorrectly falling back to Command; it also unconditionally consumes whatever token follows the table even if it is not an action.
findings.suggested_fix: Use `if self._curr: self._advance()` only when the current token is a known ALTER_PARSERS key, otherwise fall back to _parse_as_command(start).

findings.explanation: The first action parser is called directly and its result is not checked for exp.Command, unlike mixed actions at lines 56-58, so an unsupported first action can be embedded as a Command inside exp.Alter or raise instead of falling back to _parse_as_command(start).
findings.suggested_fix: Wrap the first parser in _try_parse and, if the result is empty or contains exp.Command, return self._parse_as_command(start).

findings.explanation: The while condition consumes a COMMA via _match before checking PROPERTY_PARSERS/ALTER_PARSERS, so when the loop is not entered the comma is already lost and lines 62-64 can misparse the following NOT VALID/CASCADE/garbage token as an option instead of treating the statement as unsupported.
findings.suggested_fix: Peek for the comma with advance=False/non-consuming checks, and only consume it after confirming a following ALTER_PARSERS action exists.

findings.explanation: self._prev is dereferenced without a None guard at line 51 and used as a dict key at line 55, so EOF/retreat after a failed or empty action parse can raise AttributeError/KeyError instead of the intended Command fallback.
findings.suggested_fix: Guard `self._prev and self._prev.token_type == TokenType.COMMA` and use ALTER_PARSERS.get(...) with fallback to _parse_as_command(start).

findings.explanation: For SESSION the code does not advance to the action token as the non-SESSION branch does, and exists/only parsing can leave _prev as EXISTS/ONLY, so line 44 dispatches on SESSION/EXISTS/ONLY rather than the actual SET/UNSET action and ALTER SESSION actions fall back to Command.
findings.suggested_fix: Advance to the session action token before ALTER_PARSERS lookup, or dispatch SESSION through a dedicated _parse_alter_session parser.

findings.explanation: NOT VALID, options and CASCADE are only parsed once, in that fixed order, after all mixed actions, so valid forms with NOT VALID or CASCADE attached to an earlier mixed action or CASCADE before trailing options are not consumed and the whole ALTER is demoted to Command at line 83.
findings.suggested_fix: Parse per-action trailing clauses inside the mixed-action loop or accept NOT VALID/CASCADE in either order before/after options.

findings.explanation: Unconditionally advances on `self._next` instead of `self._curr`, so a trailing action keyword is not consumed and any non-action token is silently skipped, making parser lookup on `self._prev` wrong.
findings.suggested_fix: Check `self._curr` and only advance over a known action, e.g. peek `self._curr.text.upper()` in ALTER_PARSERS before advancing.

findings.explanation: Uses `self._prev.text.upper()` without guarding `self._prev` or `text` being None, and calls `parser(self)` assuming keyword already consumed, coupling correctness to the blind advance above.
findings.suggested_fix: Use `self._curr` for lookup or guard: `self._prev.text.upper() if self._prev and self._prev.text else None`.

findings.explanation: Loop condition consumes COMMA and the next ALTER keyword via `_match` before success is known; on failed lookahead there is no retreat so tokens are lost and subsequent parse is wrong.
findings.suggested_fix: Snapshot index with `index = self._index` before matches and retreat on failure, or use `_try_parse` / `advance=False` for the whole guard.

findings.explanation: If `parser(self)` consumes tokens then returns None/[] without raising, `_try_parse` does not roll back, but code only falls back to command on failure, losing precise error location.
findings.suggested_fix: Ensure parsers raise on failure so `_try_parse` retreats, or explicitly retreat to saved index when `not parsed`.

findings.explanation: Requires `not self._curr` to return structured `Alter`; any trailing/unexpected token silently downgrades to `Command` instead of surfacing a parse error, hiding wrong results.
findings.suggested_fix: Validate trailing tokens / raise `ParseError` on unexpected `self._curr` instead of unconditional `_parse_as_command` fallback.

findings.explanation: The action dispatch advances based on self._next instead of self._curr, so when the ALTER action keyword is the final token it is never consumed and ALTER_PARSERS lookup uses the table's last token, incorrectly falling back to Command.
findings.suggested_fix: Use `if self._curr: self._advance()` (or only advance when the current token is a known ALTER_PARSERS key).

findings.explanation: The parser blindly advances one token after the table name even if that token is not an ALTER action (e.g. a property/option keyword or statement terminator), then looks it up in ALTER_PARSERS; valid ALTER forms without an ALTER_PARSERS action therefore get parser=None and degrade to _parse_as_command instead of an Alter node.
findings.suggested_fix: Only advance/dispatch when `self._curr` matches ALTER_PARSERS, e.g. `if self._curr and self._curr.text.upper() in self.ALTER_PARSERS: self._advance()` and otherwise leave the token for options parsing.

findings.explanation: The mixed-action loop requires the next keyword to be in both PROPERTY_PARSERS (checked with advance=False) and ALTER_PARSERS; most alter actions such as ADD/DROP/RENAME/ALTER are not property parsers, so sequences like `ADD COLUMN a INT, DROP COLUMN b` are never consumed, leaving _curr set and causing the whole statement to fall back to Command at line 89.
findings.suggested_fix: Remove the PROPERTY_PARSERS conjunct and dispatch solely on ALTER_PARSERS: `and self._match_texts(self.ALTER_PARSERS)`.
