findings.explanation: Evaluating the while condition calls self._match(TokenType.COMMA) even when the following token is not another alter action, permanently consuming a comma that separates the actions from trailing properties/options; the subsequent options/property parse then starts at the wrong token and the statement can fall back to Command.
findings.suggested_fix: Peek for the comma without consuming it (advance=False / check _curr) and only consume it once an ALTER_PARSERS action has been confirmed to follow.

findings.explanation: `self._prev.token_type` is dereferenced without a None guard (unlike line 46); if the first action parser leaves the parser at the start of input / _prev is None, this raises AttributeError instead of parsing or falling back to Command.
findings.suggested_fix: Guard it: `or (self._prev and self._prev.token_type == TokenType.COMMA)`.

findings.category: valid ALTER rejected on trailing tokens
findings.explanation: A structured Alter is only returned when self._curr is None (exact end of input); a valid ALTER terminated by a semicolon or followed by other tokens that the option parsers don't consume therefore discards all parsed actions and returns _parse_as_command(start), losing the structured result.
findings.suggested_fix: Return the Alter when the remaining current token is a terminator (e.g. SEMICOLON/EOF) or when actions were successfully parsed, rather than requiring _curr to be None.

findings.explanation: alter_token is False/None when no ALTERABLE matches, but code dereferences alter_token.token_type unconditionally.
findings.suggested_fix: if not alter_token: return self._parse_as_command(start)

findings.explanation: start is a Token (self._prev) but _parse_as_command expects a start index to retreat, so fallback re-parse from partial position is broken.
findings.suggested_fix: save start as self._index-1 or self._curr index and pass index

findings.explanation: Checks self._next instead of self._curr and unconditionally consumes one token, skipping/losing the action keyword or failing at end of input.
findings.suggested_fix: if self._curr: self._advance() only if _curr is expected action start, or use advance=False lookup

findings.explanation: SESSION branch skips the advance, so _prev still points at SESSION and ALTER_PARSERS lookup fails, forcing ALTER SESSION to always become a Command.
findings.suggested_fix: advance to action token for SESSION path too or look up parser on _curr

findings.explanation: self._prev.text.upper() assumes _prev and _prev.text exist; at EOF or after failed advance this raises AttributeError.
findings.suggested_fix: guard with if self._prev and self._prev.text else None

findings.explanation: not_valid/options/cascade parsing is inside if actions:, so option-only ALTER or parser returning None incorrectly falls through to Command.
findings.suggested_fix: parse options outside if actions: and allow Alter with empty actions

findings.explanation: Alter is returned only if not self._curr, so any trailing semicolon or unconsumed token forces a Command even for valid ALTER.
findings.suggested_fix: return Alter without requiring EOF, or allow semicolon/EOF check

findings.explanation: start is set to self._prev, the token before ALTER (or None at the beginning of input), instead of the ALTER token/current token. _parse_as_command(start) will therefore rewind to the wrong position and build the Command from the previous token or fail/misbehave.
findings.suggested_fix: Use the ALTER token as start, e.g. start = self._curr before consuming ALTER-related tokens.

findings.explanation: alter_token becomes False when _match_set(self.ALTERABLES) fails, but lines 26 and 32 unconditionally dereference alter_token.token_type (and line 74 later dereferences alter_token.text). ALTER without a recognized alterable therefore raises AttributeError instead of falling back to _parse_as_command.
findings.suggested_fix: Guard all uses, e.g. if not alter_token: return self._parse_as_command(start), and only check token_type/text when alter_token is a Token.

findings.explanation: The code advances to the action keyword only when self._next exists, not when self._curr exists. If the action keyword is the last token (e.g. an incomplete ALTER TABLE t ADD at EOF), _prev remains the table token, the ALTER_PARSERS lookup on line 44 misses, and parsing incorrectly falls back or misses the action; conversely it can advance when _curr is already exhausted if _next is stale.
findings.suggested_fix: Change the guard to: if self._curr: self._advance()

findings.explanation: self._match(TokenType.COMMA) in the while condition consumes a comma even when the following PROPERTY_PARSERS/ALTER_PARSERS checks then fail and no mixed action is parsed. That silently swallows a trailing/separating comma and changes what the subsequent NOT VALID/properties/cascade parsing sees, instead of leaving the token stream untouched when the loop is not entered.
findings.suggested_fix: Peek for the comma/property/action tokens first without consuming, and only consume the comma after confirming another ALTER_PARSERS action follows.

findings.category: possible crash on missing previous token
findings.explanation: If _match(TokenType.COMMA) returns False, self._prev.token_type is dereferenced without a None check. When _prev is None this raises AttributeError instead of exiting the mixed-actions loop.
findings.suggested_fix: Use: (self._match(TokenType.COMMA) or (self._prev and self._prev.token_type == TokenType.COMMA))

findings.explanation: Using `tags or sys_tags()` treats an explicitly passed empty sequence as falsy and substitutes system tags, so selecting for no tags incorrectly matches system wheels.
findings.suggested_fix: Use `tags if tags is not None else sys_tags()`

findings.explanation: Indexes `environment["python_full_version"]` whenever `environment` is truthy, so a provided partial environment without that key raises KeyError instead of falling back or raising PylockSelectError.
findings.suggested_fix: Use `env.get()` / `environment.get()` with fallback to `default_environment()["python_full_version"]` and wrap invalid versions in PylockSelectError

findings.explanation: Specifier.contains() without prereleases=True rejects prerelease Python versions even when requires-python explicitly allows them.
findings.suggested_fix: Pass `prereleases=True` to `contains()` for both lock-level and package-level requires-python checks

findings.explanation: Lock-level `environments` markers are evaluated against `environment or {}` with context="requirement" instead of the full `env` with extras/dependency_groups and context="lock_file".
findings.suggested_fix: Evaluate with `env_marker.evaluate(env, context="lock_file")`

findings.explanation: Method contains `yield` so it is a generator; requires-python, environments, and marker checks do not run until iteration, deferring errors and allowing partial results.
findings.suggested_fix: Make `select` a regular function returning a list/iterator via an inner generator after eager validation

findings.explanation: parse_wheel_filename() can raise InvalidWheelFilename for a bad wheel filename, escaping as an unexpected exception instead of PylockSelectError.
findings.suggested_fix: Try/except around parse_wheel_filename and raise PylockSelectError

findings.explanation: Testing `if best_wheel:` instead of `is not None` misclassifies a falsy wheel object and obscures that the selector returns an object or None.
findings.suggested_fix: Use `if best_wheel is not None:`

findings.explanation: Duplicate detection uses raw `package.name` as dict key, so differently-cased names for the same normalized package are not detected as conflicting.
findings.suggested_fix: Normalize key, e.g. `canonicalize_name(package.name)`

findings.explanation: Falling through with no installable source raises NotImplementedError instead of the documented PylockSelectError contract.
findings.suggested_fix: Raise `PylockSelectError(...)` for missing sdist/wheels

findings.explanation: Using `or` treats an explicitly supplied empty tags sequence as unspecified and substitutes the host's tags, so callers cannot select with no compatible tags (e.g. to force sdist fallback or an error).
findings.suggested_fix: Use `tags if tags is not None else sys_tags()`.

findings.explanation: If `environment` is a non-empty mapping that omits `python_full_version` (a partial environment, which marker evaluation otherwise supports by filling defaults), this directly indexes the missing key and raises KeyError instead of falling back to the default environment value.
findings.suggested_fix: Merge over defaults first, e.g. `merged = {**default_environment(), **(environment or {})}` and read `merged['python_full_version']` (also reuse `merged` elsewhere).

findings.explanation: `SpecifierSet.contains` excludes prereleases by default, so an environment actually running a prerelease Python (e.g. 3.14.0a1) is wrongly rejected by a specifier such as `>=3.9` even though its version satisfies it.
findings.suggested_fix: Pass `prereleases=True` when testing the concrete environment version: `self.requires_python.contains(env_python_full_version, prereleases=True)`.

findings.explanation: Same prerelease flaw per-package: a prerelease `python_full_version` that satisfies a package's `requires_python` (e.g. `>=3.9`) is reported as unsatisfied and raises PylockSelectError.
findings.suggested_fix: Use `package.requires_python.contains(env_python_full_version, prereleases=True)`.

findings.explanation: `environments` markers are evaluated against the raw `environment` argument instead of the computed `env`, so the selected `extras`/`dependency_groups` (and any defaults merged for marker evaluation) are ignored here while being honoured for package markers, giving inconsistent accept/reject decisions for markers referencing those values.
findings.suggested_fix: Evaluate against the same prepared environment used for package markers (adapting value types for the context), i.e. derive the environment-marker input from `env` rather than `environment or {}`.

findings.explanation: Because selection errors for wheels are raised inside the second, yielding loop, callers consuming the iterator incrementally receive and may act on earlier packages before a later package raises PylockSelectError for having no compatible wheel, instead of the selection failing atomically.
findings.suggested_fix: Resolve every selected package's source (including wheel choice) into a list first, raising on any error, and only then yield the resolved pairs.

findings.explanation: When environment is None the code builds env from {} instead of default_environment(), so all markers evaluate against missing keys.
findings.suggested_fix: dict(default_environment() if environment is None else environment, extras=..., dependency_groups=...)

findings.explanation: Default-groups expression is inverted: (self.default_groups and []) yields [] when defaults exist and yields None when they don't, causing frozenset(None) crash.
findings.suggested_fix: frozenset(dependency_groups if dependency_groups is not None else (self.default_groups or []))

findings.explanation: Uses environment["python_full_version"] directly and `if environment` test, so a provided environment missing the key raises KeyError instead of falling back to default.
findings.suggested_fix: Merge defaults first: merged = {**default_environment(), **(environment or {})} then read merged["python_full_version"] and test `is not None`

findings.explanation: Environments check evaluates against `environment or {}` without default_environment() merge, so valid environments are rejected when environment is None.
findings.suggested_fix: Evaluate against merged default environment, e.g. the same `env` mapping used for package markers

findings.explanation: sys_tags() returns a one-shot iterator; passing it directly lets the selector exhaust it on the first package so later packages see no tags.
findings.suggested_fix: list(sys_tags()) or tuple(sys_tags()) before passing to create_compatible_tags_selector

findings.explanation: parse_wheel_filename() can raise InvalidWheelFilename which escapes as a crash instead of a PylockSelectError.
findings.suggested_fix: try/except InvalidWheelFilename around parsing and raise PylockSelectError or skip invalid wheel

findings.explanation: Tests `if best_wheel:` which relies on truthiness of the wheel object instead of explicit None check.
findings.suggested_fix: if best_wheel is not None:

findings.explanation: SpecifierSet.contains() without prereleases=True rejects pre-release Python versions that should satisfy requires-python.
findings.suggested_fix: self.requires_python.contains(env_python_full_version, prereleases=True) (same at line 113)

findings.explanation: Raises NotImplementedError for a lock entry with no usable source instead of PylockSelectError, breaking the documented error contract.
findings.suggested_fix: raise PylockSelectError(f"No source available for package {package.name!r} ...")

findings.explanation: `self.default_groups and []` always evaluates to an empty list (or to None/False when default_groups is falsy), so the lock file's default groups are never selected; if default_groups is None, frozenset(None) raises TypeError instead of selecting no groups.
findings.suggested_fix: Use frozenset(self.default_groups or [] if dependency_groups is None else dependency_groups).

findings.explanation: If a non-empty environment dict without a 'python_full_version' key is passed, environment['python_full_version'] raises KeyError instead of falling back to the default environment value as Marker evaluation would.
findings.suggested_fix: Use (environment or default_environment()).get('python_full_version') with a default_environment() fallback, e.g. _pep440_python_full_version(env.get('python_full_version', default_environment()['python_full_version'])).

findings.category: wrong marker environment/context for environments check
findings.explanation: self.environments markers are evaluated against the raw caller environment with context='requirement' instead of the prepared env (which sets extras and dependency_groups) in the lock-file context, so markers referencing extras/dependency_groups evaluate incorrectly or raise marker errors and the check disagrees with package marker evaluation.
findings.suggested_fix: Evaluate with env_marker.evaluate(env, context='lock_file').

findings.explanation: SpecifierSet.contains() excludes prereleases by default, so a prerelease interpreter such as 3.14.0rc1 is rejected by a specifier like >=3.9 even though it satisfies the version range.
findings.suggested_fix: Call self.requires_python.contains(env_python_full_version, prereleases=True).

findings.explanation: Same prerelease problem as the top-level check: package.requires_python.contains() without prereleases=True falsely raises PylockSelectError for prerelease Python versions that satisfy the specifier.
findings.suggested_fix: Call package.requires_python.contains(env_python_full_version, prereleases=True).

findings.explanation: parse_wheel_filename() raises InvalidWheelFilename for a malformed wheel filename, which propagates as an unrelated packaging exception instead of a PylockSelectError (or being treated as no compatible wheel with sdist fallback).
findings.suggested_fix: Catch InvalidWheelFilename around wheel parsing/selection and raise PylockSelectError naming the package and index, or skip the invalid wheel and fall back to the sdist.

findings.explanation: Return puts `kind` in the side slot and discards `kind` when `kind_pre` exists. E.g. `ANY INNER JOIN` returns side=INNER, kind=ANY instead of preserving both kinds.
findings.suggested_fix: Return `is_global, kind_pre or kind, side` if tuple is (method,kind,side) or correctly combine strictness/kind without loss, e.g. handle two KIND tokens.

findings.explanation: Hardcodes parse_bracket=True ignoring the caller-supplied parse_bracket argument.
findings.suggested_fix: Pass through: parse_bracket=parse_bracket

findings.explanation: Blindly moves any `method` to `global_` and clears `method`, losing real methods like HASH and storing a string instead of bool.
findings.suggested_fix: Only convert when method indicates GLOBAL, e.g. if method and method.upper()=="GLOBAL": join.set("method", None); join.set("global_", True)

findings.explanation: Replaces every exp.Table inside the Join including ON-clause/subquery tables instead of only the joined table, corrupting the query and losing aliases/catalog.
findings.suggested_fix: Only convert join.this if it is a Table: this=join.this; if isinstance(this, exp.Table): join.set("this", this.to_column())

findings.explanation: Calls table.replace() while iterating the live find_all generator which can skip nodes or crash.
findings.suggested_fix: Iterate over list(join.find_all(exp.Table)) or avoid find_all entirely.

findings.explanation: The parse_bracket argument is ignored and True is always passed to super()._parse_join, so callers explicitly requesting parse_bracket=False get different parsing than requested.
findings.suggested_fix: Pass through the caller value, e.g. super()._parse_join(skip_join_token=skip_join_token, parse_bracket=parse_bracket, alias_tokens=alias_tokens), only forcing True for the specific ARRAY JOIN case if needed.

findings.explanation: It unconditionally clears 'method' and writes its value to 'global_', but exp.Join/generator use the 'global' arg key, so a parsed GLOBAL join is dropped from generated SQL; it also clobbers/corrupts the slot when method is None or holds a legitimate non-GLOBAL method.
findings.suggested_fix: Only when the first join-parts token was GLOBAL, set join.set('global', True) (the Join arg key) and preserve any real method; do not unconditionally overwrite with method/None.

findings.explanation: join.find_all(exp.Table) converts every descendant Table, including tables inside subqueries, nested joins, functions or ON expressions, into Columns, corrupting those constructs instead of only converting the ARRAY JOIN target expression.
findings.suggested_fix: Convert only the direct join target (join.this, and its direct comma/array elements if applicable), not all descendant tables.

findings.explanation: table.replace() mutates the tree while find_all is lazily traversing it, which can skip nodes, revisit nodes, or raise/traverse inconsistently for multiple or nested tables.
findings.suggested_fix: Materialize first, e.g. for table in list(join.find_all(exp.Table)): table.replace(table.to_column()), or better rewrite the direct target without full traversal.

findings.explanation: Table.to_column() drops the table alias (and other table args such as hints), so ARRAY JOIN arr AS a loses the alias that later column references rely on.
findings.suggested_fix: Preserve the alias when replacing, e.g. build the Column and re-attach table.args.get('alias') to it, or handle the aliased case explicitly before conversion.

findings.explanation: Single KIND token is consumed as kind_pre leaving kind=None, so `side or kind` is None and `kind_pre and kind` is None and the kind is lost, e.g. ALL JOIN, INNER JOIN, ANY LEFT JOIN lose ANY/ALL/INNER.
findings.suggested_fix: return method, side, kind_pre or kind

findings.explanation: _parse_join ignores its parse_bracket argument and always passes parse_bracket=True to super, breaking callers that pass False.
findings.suggested_fix: super()._parse_join(skip_join_token=skip_join_token, parse_bracket=parse_bracket, alias_tokens=alias_tokens)

findings.explanation: Converting every exp.Table under the Join corrupts nested subqueries, ON/USING conditions and aliases instead of only the ARRAY JOIN expression itself.
findings.suggested_fix: Only convert join.this if it is a Table, preserving alias: if isinstance(join.this, exp.Table): join.set('this', join.this.to_column())

findings.explanation: `kind_pre and kind` returns a kind only when both a pre-side and post-side kind were matched, so a single kind such as `ANY LEFT JOIN`, `LEFT ANY JOIN`, `INNER JOIN`, or `LEFT SEMI JOIN` is discarded.
findings.suggested_fix: Use `kind_pre or kind` for the kind element, e.g. `return method, side, kind_pre or kind`.

findings.explanation: `side or kind` places a kind token into the side slot when there is no side, e.g. a sequence with two kinds matched around an absent side is returned with the post-side kind as side and duplicated/misclassified, producing invalid or wrong join SQL.
findings.suggested_fix: Return the matched side unchanged: `return method, side, kind_pre or kind`.

findings.explanation: The `parse_bracket` argument is ignored and `True` is always passed to `super()._parse_join`, so callers that explicitly pass `parse_bracket=False` will still consume bracketed expressions as part of the join.
findings.suggested_fix: Pass the parameter through: `parse_bracket=parse_bracket` (or only force it for an ARRAY join after detecting that case).

findings.explanation: For an ARRAY join, `find_all(exp.Table)` converts every descendant Table, including real tables inside subqueries or nested expressions in the join target/ON clause, into Column references instead of only converting the array-join target itself.
findings.suggested_fix: Only convert the direct join target (unwrapping an Alias if present), e.g. check `join.this`/`join.this.this` is a Table and replace that node, rather than traversing all descendants.

findings.explanation: Nodes are replaced while iterating the lazy `find_all` generator over the same tree, which can skip nodes or traverse stale/replaced subtrees when the target contains nested structures.
findings.suggested_fix: Materialize first: `for table in list(join.find_all(exp.Table)): table.replace(table.to_column())` (combined with restricting to the direct target).

findings.category: lost table metadata in ARRAY JOIN
findings.explanation: `Table.to_column()` builds a Column only from the name/qualifier parts and drops table-level metadata such as a table alias, hints, or other table args if they were stored on the Table node, changing the generated ARRAY JOIN.
findings.suggested_fix: Preserve relevant args when converting, or unwrap/retain the alias/hints around the new Column instead of blindly replacing the Table.

findings.explanation: Method is indented with no enclosing class/def, so the module raises IndentationError on import.
findings.suggested_fix: Wrap in enclosing class, e.g. class RSTRenderer: + def block_text...

findings.explanation: Names Dict, Any, BlockState are used in annotations but never imported, causing NameError at definition time.
findings.suggested_fix: Add from typing import Dict, Any and import BlockState

findings.explanation: Concatenating render_children() + "\n" crashes with TypeError if it returns None and emits stray blank line if children is empty.
findings.suggested_fix: (self.render_children(token, state) or '').rstrip('\n') + '\n' with early return '' if empty

findings.explanation: Condition len(lines) > 2 misses the exactly-2-lines case, leaving the internal <linebreak> placeholder in the output.
findings.suggested_fix: Change to if len(lines) > 1:

findings.explanation: Splitting on literal "<linebreak>" corrupts user content that contains that string and leaks internals.
findings.suggested_fix: Use a unique sentinel / escape user text before split, e.g. uuid placeholder or render softbreaks directly.

findings.explanation: Empty lines become "| " with trailing whitespace which editors strip, breaking the line block, and unconditional +"\n" can double newlines or miss block-separating blank line.
findings.suggested_fix: "|" if not line.strip() else "| "+line and return text.rstrip()+"\n\n"

findings.explanation: A text block containing exactly one <linebreak> splits into 2 lines, so the > 2 condition fails to convert it to an RST line block and leaves the literal <linebreak> placeholder in the output.
findings.suggested_fix: Change `if len(lines) > 2:` to `if len(lines) > 1:`

findings.explanation: Subtracting strings with text - "\n" raises TypeError and crashes on every call.
findings.suggested_fix: return text + "\n"

findings.explanation: Strings do not support subtraction, so `text - "\n"` raises TypeError on every call to block_text, regardless of input.
findings.suggested_fix: return text + "\n"

findings.explanation: CAST(... AS TIMESTAMP) strips time zone from timestamptz inputs, giving wrong results across zones/DST.
findings.suggested_fix: CAST to TIMESTAMPTZ or avoid cast and let subtraction handle types

findings.explanation: CAST(float AS BIGINT) rounds in Postgres instead of truncating, so fractional SECOND/MINUTE/HOUR/DAY diffs are off by 1.
findings.suggested_fix: Use FLOOR/TRUNC/DIV, e.g. CAST(FLOOR(EXTRACT(epoch FROM ...) ...) AS BIGINT)

findings.explanation: WEEK computes float division then CAST which rounds instead of truncating toward zero.
findings.suggested_fix: Use FLOOR(EXTRACT(days FROM ...) / 7) or integer DIV

findings.explanation: EXTRACT(month ...)/3 is float division then rounded by outer CAST, e.g. month 5 gives 1.66 -> 2 instead of 1.
findings.suggested_fix: Use FLOOR(EXTRACT(month FROM age)/3) or (EXTRACT(month ...) / 3)::INT with integer division

findings.explanation: AGE counts full months/years, while DATEDIFF counts month/year boundaries, e.g. Jan 31 to Feb 1 gives 0 not 1.
findings.suggested_fix: Compute boundary difference from year/month parts of endpoints, not from AGE()

findings.explanation: Fallback sets unit=age interval then CAST(interval AS BIGINT) which is invalid in Postgres and errors.
findings.suggested_fix: Raise unsupported-unit error or handle remaining units explicitly instead of CAST(age AS BIGINT)

findings.explanation: CAST(numeric AS BIGINT) in Postgres rounds to the nearest integer instead of truncating, so e.g. a 1.9-day difference becomes 2 days rather than 1.
findings.suggested_fix: Wrap the quotient in TRUNC before casting: CAST(TRUNC(EXTRACT(epoch FROM end-start) <factor>) AS BIGINT)

findings.explanation: EXTRACT(days ...)/7 produces a fractional value that the final CAST AS BIGINT rounds, so 13 days becomes 2 weeks instead of 1 (and -13 days becomes -2 instead of -1).
findings.suggested_fix: Use CAST(TRUNC(EXTRACT(days FROM (end-start)) / 7) AS BIGINT) so the division truncates toward zero.

findings.explanation: EXTRACT(month FROM age)/3 is fractional and is only rounded by the final cast, so 2 months yields 1 quarter and 5 months yields 2 quarters instead of 0 and 1 respectively.
findings.suggested_fix: Truncate the month component before adding: EXTRACT(year FROM age) * 4 + TRUNC(EXTRACT(month FROM age) / 3), then cast.

findings.explanation: Any unit not in DATE_DIFF_FACTOR and not WEEK/MONTH/QUARTER/YEAR (e.g. DECADE, CENTURY, or an unrecognized/plural unit) falls through to CAST(AGE(...) AS BIGINT), but Postgres cannot cast an interval to bigint, causing a runtime error.
findings.suggested_fix: Handle additional units explicitly and raise an unsupported-unit error (or singularize/normalize the unit) instead of casting an interval to BIGINT.

findings.explanation: CAST(... AS TIMESTAMP) on a TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE value discards the zone using the session timezone, so epoch/day differences are computed on wall-clock time and are wrong across DST or differing zones.
findings.suggested_fix: Preserve timestamptz semantics, e.g. only cast date-like inputs to TIMESTAMP and compute differences on timestamptz values where the input is timestamptz.

findings.explanation: Using AGE() measures fully elapsed months/quarters/years, whereas DATEDIFF-style semantics in source dialects count unit boundaries crossed, so e.g. 2023-01-31 to 2023-02-01 reports 0 months instead of 1.
findings.suggested_fix: Compute month/quarter/year differences from the year/month fields of end and start (with the dialect's boundary semantics) rather than from AGE().

findings.explanation: DAY boundary branch computes `this + expr` instead of subtraction, inverting/wrong result.
findings.suggested_fix: return self.sql(exp.Paren(this=this.copy() - expr.copy()))

findings.explanation: exp.DType does not exist, should be exp.DataType; also reuses child nodes without copy and exp.paren casing is wrong.
findings.suggested_fix: exp.Cast(this=expression.this.copy(), to=exp.DataType.build('DATE')) and exp.Paren

findings.explanation: exp.paren lowercase does not exist, raises AttributeError.
findings.suggested_fix: Use exp.Paren(this=...) or self.sql(exp.Paren(...))

findings.explanation: Unknown unit falls back to CAST(AGE(...) AS BIGINT) which cannot cast interval to bigint in Postgres.
findings.suggested_fix: Raise UnsupportedError for unknown unit instead of generating invalid CAST

findings.explanation: QUARTER uses float division EXTRACT(month)/3 then CAST truncates toward zero, wrong for negatives and fractional quarters.
findings.suggested_fix: FLOOR((EXTRACT(year FROM age)*12+EXTRACT(month FROM age))/3)

findings.explanation: CAST(... AS TIMESTAMP) strips time zone, and CAST(.../factor AS BIGINT) truncates toward zero instead of floor for negative diffs.
findings.suggested_fix: Preserve TZ (don't cast away timestamptz) and use FLOOR(...)::BIGINT

findings.explanation: The day-boundary branch adds the two DATE casts instead of subtracting them; PostgreSQL has no date + date operator, so this generates invalid SQL and cannot return end-start.
findings.suggested_fix: return self.sql(exp.paren(this - expr))

findings.explanation: date_part_boundary is only honored for DAY. For WEEK, MONTH, QUARTER, or YEAR boundary-counting sources, the code falls through to elapsed AGE/interval arithmetic, e.g. Jan 31 to Feb 1 counts 0 months instead of 1 crossed month boundary.
findings.suggested_fix: Handle boundary semantics for the other units too, e.g. by comparing DATE_TRUNC(unit, end) with DATE_TRUNC(unit, start) before counting.

findings.explanation: EXTRACT(epoch ...) multiplied/divided by DATE_DIFF_FACTOR is fractional, and CAST(numeric AS BIGINT) in PostgreSQL rounds to nearest rather than truncating, so e.g. 1.6 hours becomes 2 instead of 1 (and -1.6 becomes -2 instead of -1).
findings.suggested_fix: Use CAST(TRUNC(EXTRACT(epoch FROM end - start) <factor>) AS BIGINT) to truncate toward zero.

findings.explanation: EXTRACT(days ...) returns numeric, so / 7 is fractional and the final CAST AS BIGINT rounds; 11 days becomes 2 weeks instead of 1, and -11 days becomes -2 instead of -1.
findings.suggested_fix: Use CAST(TRUNC(EXTRACT(days FROM (end - start)) / 7) AS BIGINT).

findings.explanation: EXTRACT(month FROM age) / 3 is numeric division in PostgreSQL, so 2 months yields 0.667 and the outer CAST rounds it to 1 quarter, and 5 months yields 1.667 rounding to 2 quarters instead of 1.
findings.suggested_fix: Truncate the month component first, e.g. EXTRACT(year FROM age) * 4 + TRUNC(EXTRACT(month FROM age) / 3), then cast the total.

findings.explanation: Any unit not in DATE_DIFF_FACTOR and not WEEK/MONTH/QUARTER/YEAR falls through with unit = AGE(...), producing CAST(interval AS BIGINT), which PostgreSQL rejects with 'cannot cast type interval to bigint'.
findings.suggested_fix: Implement or explicitly reject unsupported units (e.g. microsecond/decade) instead of casting an interval; at minimum return a valid expression or raise an unsupported-unit error.

findings.explanation: Casting inputs to TIMESTAMP (without time zone) converts timestamptz values using the session TimeZone and discards offsets, so elapsed epoch/AGE differences across DST changes or differing offsets can be off by the offset delta.
findings.suggested_fix: Preserve timestamptz inputs (subtract them directly or cast to TIMESTAMPTZ) and only cast plain dates/timestamps to TIMESTAMP.

findings.explanation: expression.text("unit").upper() and "DAY" always evaluates to "DAY" when unit is non-empty and to "" when empty, so WEEK/MONTH/QUARTER/YEAR are never honored.
findings.suggested_fix: unit = expression.text("unit").upper() or "DAY"

findings.explanation: self.sql(expression, 'this') passes 'this' as comment flag, not as arg selector, returning full expression SQL and causing infinite recursion / wrong SQL.
findings.suggested_fix: self.sql(expression.this) and self.sql(expression.expression) or self.sql(expression.args.get(...))

findings.explanation: CAST(... AS TIMESTAMP) drops time-zone info for TIMESTAMPTZ inputs and changes semantics vs timestamptz arithmetic.
findings.suggested_fix: CAST(... AS TIMESTAMPTZ) when needed or avoid cast and use proper type coercion

findings.explanation: WEEK/MONTH/QUARTER/YEAR use truncating CAST to BIGINT, so negative intervals truncate toward zero instead of flooring, giving off-by-one results.
findings.suggested_fix: Wrap with FLOOR(...) before CAST, e.g. CAST(FLOOR(... ) AS BIGINT)

findings.explanation: QUARTER computes EXTRACT(year...)*4 + EXTRACT(month...)/3 with separate truncation, which differs from floor((years*12+months)/3) for negatives and edge months.
findings.suggested_fix: FLOOR((EXTRACT(year FROM age)*12 + EXTRACT(month FROM age))/3)

findings.explanation: Fallback unit = age leads to CAST(AGE(...) AS BIGINT) which is not valid Postgres (cannot cast interval to bigint) and crashes for unsupported units.
findings.suggested_fix: Raise/return NULL for unsupported unit or handle via EXTRACT(epoch...) path

findings.explanation: `expression.text("unit").upper() and "DAY"` evaluates to "DAY" for every non-empty unit and "" only when the unit is missing, so all specified units are discarded and the WEEK/MONTH/QUARTER/YEAR branches become unreachable.
findings.suggested_fix: unit = expression.text("unit").upper() or "DAY"

findings.explanation: Because of line 2, a boundary-based MONTH/YEAR/etc. diff also satisfies `unit == "DAY"` and returns a day count; even with line 2 fixed, `date_part_boundary` is only honored for DAY, so boundary-counting MONTH/QUARTER/YEAR diffs fall through to AGE (elapsed whole periods, e.g. Jan 31 to Feb 1 gives 0 months instead of 1).
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the real unit first and add boundary-based branches for MONTH/QUARTER/YEAR (e.g. compare year/month components) when date_part_boundary is set, not only for DAY.

findings.explanation: CAST(x AS BIGINT) in PostgreSQL rounds to nearest instead of truncating, so e.g. a 1.9-day/second epoch difference becomes 2 where datediff semantics truncate toward zero.
findings.suggested_fix: return f"CAST(TRUNC(EXTRACT(epoch FROM {end} - {start}){factor}) AS BIGINT)"

findings.explanation: EXTRACT returns numeric, so `days / 7` is fractional and the final CAST rounds: 13 days yields 13/7=1.857 -> 2 weeks instead of 1 (and -13 days -> -2 instead of -1).
findings.suggested_fix: Use truncation: TRUNC(EXTRACT(days FROM ({end} - {start})) / 7) before the BIGINT cast.

findings.explanation: EXTRACT returns numeric, so `EXTRACT(month FROM age) / 3` is fractional (5 months -> 1.667) and the outer CAST rounds it to 2 quarters instead of the truncated 1; negative ages round away from zero similarly.
findings.suggested_fix: Truncate the month component first, e.g. EXTRACT(year FROM age) * 4 + TRUNC(EXTRACT(month FROM age) / 3), or compute total months then TRUNC(total / 3).

findings.explanation: The else branch assigns an interval (AGE(...)) and generates CAST(interval AS BIGINT), which PostgreSQL rejects with 'cannot cast type interval to bigint'; this is hit for a missing unit (line 2 yields "") and for any unit not covered by DATE_DIFF_FACTOR or the explicit branches.
findings.suggested_fix: Default a missing unit to DAY and raise/handle unsupported units explicitly, or extract a numeric component; never cast the raw interval to BIGINT.

findings.explanation: CAST(x AS TIMESTAMP) on a timestamptz input drops the time zone using the session TimeZone setting, so differences spanning DST changes or differing offsets are computed on wall-clock time and can be off by hours and vary by session.
findings.suggested_fix: Preserve timestamptz inputs (subtract them directly / EXTRACT(epoch FROM this - expression)) and only cast plain date/timestamp inputs to TIMESTAMP.

findings.explanation: PostgreSQL date - date yields INTEGER, so the boundary DAY path returns INTEGER while every other path returns BIGINT, breaking the consistent 64-bit result contract (and risking integer overflow semantics for extreme date ranges).
findings.suggested_fix: return self.sql(exp.paren(exp.cast(this - expr, exp.DType.BIGINT))) or CAST(({this} - {expr}) AS BIGINT)

findings.explanation: Overwrites expression.this and expressions in-place, so the caller's AST is permanently changed on generation.
findings.suggested_fix: Operate on a copy: expression = expression.copy() before mutating, or build SQL without set().

findings.explanation: expressions[0].name == "MAX" misses lowercase / mixed-case max, so VARCHAR(max) is not normalized.
findings.suggested_fix: Compare case-insensitively: expression.expressions[0].name.upper() == "MAX"

findings.explanation: int(size_expression.name) raises ValueError if param is non-numeric e.g. FLOAT(MAX) or empty.
findings.suggested_fix: Guard with try/except ValueError or check .isdigit() before conversion

findings.explanation: Uses size <= 32 but T-SQL FLOAT(n) semantics split at 24: 1-24 is REAL/FLOAT, 25-53 is DOUBLE.
findings.suggested_fix: Use exp.DType.FLOAT if size <= 24 else exp.DType.DOUBLE

findings.explanation: Unconditionally strips all TEMPORAL_TYPES params, dropping TIMESTAMP(p) precision Hive supports.
findings.suggested_fix: Only strip unsupported temporal params or preserve TIMESTAMP precision

findings.explanation: CHAR with no length becomes TEXT/STRING, but Hive CHAR defaults to CHAR(1), losing type info.
findings.suggested_fix: Only map VARCHAR without length to STRING; preserve bare CHAR or default to CHAR(1)

findings.explanation: TEXT with args becomes VARCHAR keeping args, so TEXT(MAX) becomes invalid Hive VARCHAR(MAX).
findings.suggested_fix: When converting TEXT to VARCHAR, drop MAX param or map to STRING

findings.explanation: datatype_sql mutates the caller's DataType node in place, permanently destroying the original type and parameters (e.g. VARCHAR(MAX), TIMESTAMP precision, FLOAT(p)) so subsequent generation, other-dialect transpilation, or reuse of the AST produces wrong SQL.
findings.suggested_fix: Operate on expression.copy() and pass the copy to super().datatype_sql(), or compute the output without calling expression.set() on the input.

findings.explanation: exp.DataType.is_type(exp.DType.TEXT) expands to the whole text type group in sqlglot, so CHAR(n), NCHAR(n) and other text types with parameters are rewritten to VARCHAR(n), changing semantics instead of only converting TEXT(n).
findings.suggested_fix: Use an exact check such as expression.this == exp.DType.TEXT (or expression.is_type with check on this) before converting to VARCHAR.

findings.explanation: is_type is given the lowercase string "float" instead of exp.DType.FLOAT; DType values/group keys are enum/uppercase based, so this does not reliably match FLOAT (and if group expansion applies it can also match REAL/DOUBLE), leaving FLOAT(p) unconverted or mis-converting related types.
findings.suggested_fix: Use expression.this == exp.DType.FLOAT for an exact match, or expression.is_type(exp.DType.FLOAT) if group semantics are intended.

findings.explanation: int(size_expression.name) raises ValueError for non-numeric parameters such as FLOAT(MAX), an empty parameter, or other symbolic precision values that parsers/other dialects can produce.
findings.suggested_fix: Guard with try/except or name.isdigit() check and fall back to a safe default (e.g. DOUBLE) instead of crashing.

findings.explanation: FLOAT(p) precision semantics in source dialects/SQL standard map p<=24 (binary precision) to single precision and larger values to DOUBLE; using 32 misclassifies FLOAT(25)..FLOAT(32) as FLOAT, losing precision.
findings.suggested_fix: Use the correct dialect threshold, e.g. size < 25 for FLOAT else DOUBLE, after confirming the source precision semantics.

findings.explanation: Comparing expressions[0].name directly to "MAX" can miss lowercase/mixed-case 'max' as produced depending on parser normalization, so VARCHAR(max) is emitted to Hive where MAX is unsupported instead of becoming TEXT.
findings.suggested_fix: Compare case-insensitively: expression.expressions[0].name.upper() == "MAX".

findings.explanation: For temporal types such as TIMESTAMP_TZ/TIMESTAMP with time zone, clearing only expressions leaves other args like kind/timezone intact, so super().datatype_sql() can still emit Hive-unsupported timezone/parameter syntax; the elif also silently discards precision without validating the type supports it.
findings.suggested_fix: Also clear/normalize the kind arg and map zoned temporal types to Hive TIMESTAMP, not just expressions.

findings.explanation: TEXT(n) is blindly rewritten to VARCHAR(n) retaining n, but Hive VARCHAR is limited to 65355; TEXT(65536+) or TEXT(0) produces invalid Hive DDL.
findings.suggested_fix: Validate/clamp the length and fall back to TEXT/STRING when n is out of Hive's VARCHAR range.

findings.explanation: expression.find(exp.DataTypeParam) searches all descendants rather than only the type's direct expressions, so a nested/user-defined type containing a parameter could supply the wrong size for the outer FLOAT conversion.
findings.suggested_fix: Inspect expression.expressions directly for a DataTypeParam instead of using find().

findings.explanation: Generator mutates the input AST with expression.set, so caller's tree is permanently changed and later generations differ.
findings.suggested_fix: Copy expression before modifying, e.g. expression = expression.copy()

findings.explanation: Precision is stripped when SUPPORTS_TEMPORAL_PRECISION is true, opposite of intended logic; dialects that support precision lose it.
findings.suggested_fix: Change to `not self.SUPPORTS_TEMPORAL_PRECISION and ...`

findings.explanation: FLOAT(p) maps to DOUBLE only for p>53 or p>24 depending on dialect, not p>32, so e.g. FLOAT(25-32) wrongly stays FLOAT.
findings.suggested_fix: Use `exp.DType.FLOAT if size <= 24 else exp.DType.DOUBLE`

findings.explanation: int(size_expression.name) raises ValueError if precision is non-numeric or empty, crashing generation.
findings.suggested_fix: Guard with try/except ValueError or check isdigit() before conversion

findings.explanation: Comparison to "MAX" is case-sensitive so VARCHAR(max) or Max is missed and not normalized.
findings.suggested_fix: Use `expression.expressions[0].name.upper() == "MAX"`

findings.explanation: datatype_sql mutates the caller's expression via expression.set(), permanently corrupting the parsed AST; generating Hive SQL first then generating for another dialect (or reusing the tree) yields wrong types and lost parameters.
findings.suggested_fix: Work on a copy: expression = expression.copy() at the start, mutate and render the copy only.

findings.explanation: Precision is stripped when SUPPORTS_TEMPORAL_PRECISION is true, i.e. exactly when the dialect can represent it, and is kept (producing unsupported TIMESTAMP(9)-style output) when the dialect cannot represent it.
findings.suggested_fix: Use 'not self.SUPPORTS_TEMPORAL_PRECISION' so precision is dropped only for dialects that do not support it.

findings.explanation: expressions[0].name == "MAX" fails for lowercase/mixed-case input such as VARCHAR(max), which then falls through to the TEXT branch and can be emitted as VARCHAR(MAX), invalid for Hive-like dialects.
findings.suggested_fix: Compare case-insensitively: expression.expressions[0].name.upper() == "MAX".

findings.explanation: int(size_expression.name) raises ValueError/TypeError for non-numeric parameters (e.g. MAX, a placeholder, or an empty/non-literal parameter), crashing generation instead of falling back to rendering the type.
findings.suggested_fix: Guard the conversion: name = size_expression.name; if name.isdigit(): ... else leave the expression unchanged (or map MAX to DOUBLE).

findings.category: Loss of float scale / wrong descendant search
findings.explanation: expression.find() returns the first descendant DataTypeParam and the whole expressions list is discarded, so FLOAT(M, D) loses its scale D and is silently reclassified using only M, changing the type's semantics.
findings.suggested_fix: Inspect expression.expressions directly and only apply the FLOAT/DOUBLE mapping for a single precision parameter; otherwise preserve or explicitly handle precision and scale.

findings.explanation: Any parameterizable text type with no length (e.g. CHAR, which defaults to CHAR(1) in several source dialects, or NVARCHAR) is rewritten to unbounded TEXT, changing fixed-length/padded and national-character semantics.
findings.suggested_fix: Only apply the no-length-to-TEXT rewrite to types whose source semantics are actually unbounded (e.g. VARCHAR without length where the target requires a length), not to CHAR/NCHAR/NVARCHAR.

findings.explanation: OR condition strips parameters from all types when SUPPORTS_TEMPORAL_PRECISION is False, and strips temporal precision even when it is supported.
findings.suggested_fix: if expression.this in exp.DataType.TEMPORAL_TYPES and not self.SUPPORTS_TEMPORAL_PRECISION:

findings.explanation: When SUPPORTS_TEMPORAL_PRECISION is False the previous elif is always True, so float-size mapping is dead code and never runs.
findings.suggested_fix: Fix previous condition to AND and/or move float handling before temporal-precision stripping.

findings.explanation: is_type("float") passes a string while expression.this is a DType enum, so the check never matches.
findings.suggested_fix: expression.is_type(exp.DType.FLOAT)

findings.explanation: int(size_expression.name) raises ValueError on non-numeric sizes like MAX or empty string.
findings.suggested_fix: Guard with try/except ValueError or check s.isdigit() before int()

findings.explanation: Comparison to "MAX" is case-sensitive and misses "max" or mixed case.
findings.suggested_fix: expression.expressions[0].name.upper() == "MAX"

findings.explanation: datatype_sql mutates the caller's DataType node in place (type and expressions), irreversibly destroying the original type so reusing the AST or generating SQL for another dialect afterwards produces wrong output.
findings.suggested_fix: Work on a copy, e.g. expression = expression.copy(), before calling set(), or compute the SQL without mutating the node.

findings.explanation: Using 'or' makes temporal precision always stripped: whenever the type is temporal the branch fires even when SUPPORTS_TEMPORAL_PRECISION is True.
findings.suggested_fix: Use 'not self.SUPPORTS_TEMPORAL_PRECISION and expression.this in exp.DataType.TEMPORAL_TYPES'.

findings.explanation: When SUPPORTS_TEMPORAL_PRECISION is False the condition is true for every remaining type, so it deletes expressions from VARCHAR/CHAR lengths, DECIMAL precision/scale, and complex types such as ARRAY/STRUCT whose expressions hold nested member types, producing wrong or invalid SQL.
findings.suggested_fix: Only clear expressions for temporal types; leave non-temporal, parameterized, and nested types untouched.

findings.explanation: Because the temporal branch is an elif and is true for all types when SUPPORTS_TEMPORAL_PRECISION is False (as in Hive), the float branch below is dead in exactly that configuration, so FLOAT(n) is never rewritten to FLOAT/DOUBLE and its precision is instead silently dropped.
findings.suggested_fix: Make the float conversion an independent if (or move it before the temporal-precision branch) rather than an elif.

findings.explanation: int(size_expression.name) raises an unhandled ValueError for non-numeric or empty size parameters such as FLOAT(MAX) or dialect-specific parameters, crashing generation instead of falling back to a default type.
findings.suggested_fix: Validate with size_expression.name.isdigit() (try/except ValueError) and fall back to FLOAT/DOUBLE or keep the original type on failure.

findings.explanation: expression.find(exp.DataTypeParam) searches all descendants, so for nested/complex types it can pick a nested type's parameter rather than the float's own size parameter, and is_type('float') with a raw string is less strict than using exp.DType.FLOAT.
findings.suggested_fix: Inspect only expression.expressions for a direct DataTypeParam child and use expression.is_type(exp.DType.FLOAT).

findings.explanation: Comparing expressions[0].name == 'MAX' is case-sensitive and assumes the first expression is the size parameter; a lowercase 'max' (depending on input parsing/normalization) misses the conversion and emits unsupported parameterized text SQL.
findings.suggested_fix: Compare case-insensitively, e.g. expression.expressions[0].name.upper() == 'MAX', after confirming the node is a DataTypeParam.

findings.explanation: If EXT_SUFFIX is empty string, isinstance check passes then ext_suffix[0] raises IndexError.
findings.suggested_fix: Check length first, e.g. `if not isinstance(ext_suffix, str) or not ext_suffix.startswith('.')`

findings.explanation: If soabi is 'cpython' with no '-', soabi.split('-')[1] raises IndexError.
findings.suggested_fix: Validate split parts, e.g. `parts = soabi.split('-'); if len(parts)<2: return []`

findings.explanation: For unknown implementations the full SOABI including platform suffix is kept, producing a tag containing platform parts.
findings.suggested_fix: Strip platform suffix like other branches, e.g. keep only first two/three dash components or split off arch/platform

findings.explanation: Invalid/None EXT_SUFFIX raises SystemError instead of gracefully falling back to empty list or _cpython_abis.
findings.suggested_fix: Return [] or fallback to _cpython_abis() instead of raising

findings.explanation: Len<3 fallback unconditionally calls _cpython_abis() even on PyPy/GraalPy/other where CPython ABI is wrong.
findings.suggested_fix: Only fallback to _cpython_abis on CPython, otherwise return []

findings.explanation: If EXT_SUFFIX is an empty string, isinstance passes and ext_suffix[0] raises IndexError instead of the intended SystemError.
findings.suggested_fix: Check emptiness first: `if not isinstance(ext_suffix, str) or not ext_suffix or ext_suffix[0] != ".":`

findings.explanation: startswith("cpython") matches values without a version separator such as 'cpython' or 'cpython310', and soabi.split("-")[1] then raises IndexError; similarly 'cpythonXYZ-foo' is misparsed as abi 'cpfoo'.
findings.suggested_fix: Require the separator: `if soabi.startswith("cpython-"):` and validate the version part before indexing, falling through to the generic branch otherwise.

findings.explanation: For soabi='cpython-' the split yields an empty version and the function returns the bogus ABI tag 'cp' instead of rejecting or ignoring the malformed suffix.
findings.suggested_fix: Validate that split('-')[1] is non-empty/digits (with optional ABI flags) before constructing 'cp'+version; otherwise return [] or raise SystemError.

findings.explanation: If EXT_SUFFIX is missing _get_config_var can return None (or non-str), then ext_suffix.split crashes with AttributeError.
findings.suggested_fix: if not isinstance(ext_suffix, str): return []

findings.explanation: Empty or falsy EXT_SUFFIX splits to len<3 and incorrectly falls back to _cpython_abis instead of returning [].
findings.suggested_fix: if not ext_suffix: return [] before length check

findings.explanation: soabi starting with cpython without '-' makes soabi.split("-")[1] raise IndexError.
findings.suggested_fix: guard split length, e.g. parts = soabi.split('-'); if len(parts)<2: return []; abi='cp'+parts[1]

findings.explanation: _get_config_var can return None (or an empty string); calling .split on None raises AttributeError, and an empty string falls through to the len<3 branch and incorrectly returns CPython ABIs instead of no ABI tag.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a guard after line 16: `if not ext_suffix: return []`

findings.explanation: If soabi is 'cpython' without a '-<version>' component (e.g. EXT_SUFFIX='.cpython.so'), soabi.split('-')[1] raises IndexError instead of falling back or returning no tag.
findings.suggested_fix: Parse defensively, e.g. `bits = soabi.split('-'); abi = 'cp' + bits[1] if len(bits) > 1 and bits[1] else soabi` or return [] when the version component is missing.

findings.explanation: Uses `and` instead of `or`, so non-str EXT_SUFFIX crashes on `.startswith` with AttributeError instead of SystemError, and str not starting with `.` is not rejected.
findings.suggested_fix: if not isinstance(ext_suffix, str) or not ext_suffix.startswith("."):

findings.explanation: The condition uses 'and' instead of 'or': a non-string EXT_SUFFIX evaluates ext_suffix.startswith('.') and crashes with AttributeError instead of SystemError, while a string not starting with '.' is silently accepted and can produce a wrong ABI tag.
findings.suggested_fix: if not isinstance(ext_suffix, str) or not ext_suffix.startswith("."):

findings.explanation: Leading underscore means generator dispatch never calls this method, so the intended DuckDB wrapping is never applied.
findings.suggested_fix: Rename to arrow_json_extract_sql without leading underscore

findings.explanation: Multi-path JSON_EXTRACT is built as JSON_EXTRACT(this, ARRAY(path1, ...)) wrapped in TO_JSON, but DuckDB expects variadic paths, not a single ARRAY argument, so result is wrong / errors.
findings.suggested_fix: Pass paths as separate args: self.func("JSON_EXTRACT", expression.this, expression.expression, *paths) and build JSON array correctly, e.g. via LIST_VALUE / CAST AS JSON

findings.explanation: Condition uses `not same_parent or isinstance(parent, WRAPPED...)` so it wraps when parent already handles wrapping and skips wrapping when needed; logic is inverted.
findings.suggested_fix: Use `if not expression.same_parent and not isinstance(expression.parent, WRAPPED_JSON_EXTRACT_EXPRESSIONS): arrow_sql = self.wrap(arrow_sql)`

findings.explanation: Nests self.func inside self.func, passing already-rendered SQL string as argument which can be quoted as a literal instead of nested call.
findings.suggested_fix: Build nested expression nodes (exp.Anonymous/exp.Cast) first, then generate SQL once, or use self.sql() handling for nested calls

findings.explanation: DuckDB's JSON_EXTRACT with a VARCHAR[] path list already returns a JSON array, so wrapping it in TO_JSON treats that JSON text as a plain string and double-encodes it (e.g. [1, 2] becomes "[1, 2]"), and string/object elements are likewise re-quoted.
findings.suggested_fix: Return self.func("JSON_EXTRACT", expression.this, exp.Array(...)) directly without the TO_JSON wrapper.

findings.explanation: The multi-path branch returns early and bypasses the parenthesization logic below (same_parent / WRAPPED_JSON_EXTRACT_EXPRESSIONS), so in contexts where the single-path arrow form must be wrapped (e.g. nested JSON extraction, index/dot/data-type parents) the generated SQL can parse with the wrong precedence or target.
findings.suggested_fix: Apply the same wrap decision to the multi-path result: compute the TO_JSON/JSON_EXTRACT SQL, then wrap it under the same condition used on lines 16-19 before returning.

findings.explanation: Only exp.JSONExtract is handled; other members of JSON_EXTRACT_TYPE that can carry extra expressions (e.g. JSONBExtract) fall through to arrow_json_extract_sql, which emits only the first path and silently drops the remaining paths.
findings.suggested_fix: Handle every JSON_EXTRACT_TYPE member that supports multiple paths, or explicitly combine all paths for those types instead of falling through to the single-path arrow form.

findings.explanation: The rebuilt JSON_EXTRACT drops expression.args such as 'safe', so a SAFE extraction in the source dialect becomes an unsafe DuckDB call that raises on malformed JSON/paths instead of returning NULL.
findings.suggested_fix: Preserve/handle the safe flag, e.g. wrap in a null-on-error construct or carry the arg through instead of constructing a bare JSON_EXTRACT.

findings.explanation: If the first path is stored only in expressions (expression.expression is None, as in programmatically built ASTs), the code inserts None into the Array, generating ARRAY(, '$.a', ...) which is invalid DuckDB SQL.
findings.suggested_fix: Build the path list from [p for p in [expression.expression, *paths] if p is not None] and fall through to the arrow form when no first path exists.

findings.explanation: For MySQL semantics, JSON_EXTRACT returns SQL NULL when any supplied path is not found, whereas DuckDB's list-path extraction produces an array containing NULL for the missing path, so the transpiled query returns [1, null] instead of NULL.
findings.suggested_fix: Emulate the source semantics, e.g. guard the result so it is NULL when any extracted element/path is missing, rather than unconditionally returning the DuckDB array.

findings.explanation: Splits on first '#' so '#' inside string literals or URLs is treated as comment start, corrupting code.
findings.suggested_fix: Use tokenize or regex that respects strings to locate real comment.

findings.explanation: Pattern r'\b'+escape(splitter)+r'\b' fails for trailing-space splitters before '(' and for '.' surrounded by spaces/non-word chars, so valid splits are missed.
findings.suggested_fix: Drop trailing \b, e.g. r'\bimport ' and handle '.' without \b.

findings.explanation: re.search/split matches splitter inside string literals, incorrectly breaking code.
findings.suggested_fix: Only split outside strings or parse imports.

findings.explanation: next_line appends popped tail parts so splitter.join(next_line) is reversed, producing wrong import order.
findings.suggested_fix: Reverse before join: splitter.join(reversed(next_line)) or next_line.insert(0,...).

findings.explanation: wrap_length or line_length treats wrap_length=0/None the same and cannot distinguish explicit 0.
findings.suggested_fix: Use wrap_length if wrap_length is not None else line_length.

findings.explanation: Length is checked on content without hoisted comment, so final line with hoisted noqa comment can still exceed limit.
findings.suggested_fix: Include len(noqa_comment) in while condition when _hoist_comment_to_paren.

findings.explanation: If while loop never runs next_line is empty, code still emits empty parenthesized continuation.
findings.suggested_fix: If not next_line: return content unchanged.

findings.explanation: Wrapping '.' splitter with parentheses yields 'os.(' which is a syntax error.
findings.suggested_fix: Do not use parentheses mode for '.' splitter; use backslash or split differently.

findings.explanation: cont_line.rstrip() strips line_separator newlines, collapsing recursive multi-line wrap into one line.
findings.suggested_fix: Use rstrip(' \t') or rstrip() only on last segment.

findings.explanation: 'as ' branch never emits hoisted comment, silently dropping it.
findings.suggested_fix: Append noqa_comment to output in 'as ' branch as well.

findings.explanation: Backslash branch ignores _hoist_comment_to_paren, so hoisted comment is dropped entirely.
findings.suggested_fix: Append comment_prefix+comment to first or last line in backslash mode.

findings.explanation: Moving ')' before comment via split and comment[:-1] corrupts comments ending in ')' and matches comment_prefix with 'in' causing false positives.
findings.suggested_fix: Track paren position explicitly instead of string surgery on last line.

findings.explanation: Trailing-comma logic keyed on truthiness of comment disables comma even when comment is embedded elsewhere, inconsistent with hoisted override.
findings.suggested_fix: Decide comma based on syntactic need, not presence of comment.

findings.explanation: Case-sensitive '"# NOQA" not in content' misses '# noqa', '#NOQA', '#  NOQA' and adds duplicate.
findings.suggested_fix: Use case-insensitive regex like r'#\s*noqa\b' with re.IGNORECASE.

findings.explanation: Trailing '#' yields empty comment string which is then dropped, losing the '#'.
findings.suggested_fix: Treat comment is not None rather than truthiness.

findings.explanation: Splitting on the first '#' treats a '#' inside a string literal as a comment, so such a line is truncated and later rejoined incorrectly.
findings.suggested_fix: Parse the comment with a tokenizer/AST-aware scan instead of content.split('#', 1), ignoring '#' inside strings.

findings.explanation: The noqa test is case-sensitive ('noqa' in comment), so the standard uppercase '# NOQA' (used on line 82) is not recognised and is not hoisted to the parenthesis line.
findings.suggested_fix: Use a case-insensitive check, e.g. 'noqa' in comment.lower().

findings.explanation: next_line is built by pop()-ing parts from the end of line_parts, so when more than one part is moved (e.g. a dotted path a.b.c.d) splitter.join(next_line) emits them in reverse order (d.c...), corrupting the name.
findings.suggested_fix: Reverse before joining: splitter.join(reversed(next_line)), or insert at position 0 / pop(0) appropriately.

findings.explanation: For the 'as ' splitter, a hoisted comment was withheld from line_parts (line 29) but is never re-added in this branch, so noqa/other comments silently disappear.
findings.suggested_fix: Append the hoisted comment in the 'as ' branch, e.g. f"{content}{splitter}{cont_line.lstrip()}{config.comment_prefix + comment if _hoist_comment_to_paren else ''}".

findings.explanation: Extending the parenthesised branch to vertical modes applies parenthesisation to the '.' splitter too, producing e.g. 'import very.(\n long)' / 'module.(name)', which is invalid Python; parentheses are only valid after import/cimport.
findings.suggested_fix: Only use the '(' ... ')' construction for 'import '/'cimport ' splitters; fall through to backslash/vertical wrapping for '.'.

findings.explanation: The hoisted branch unconditionally sets _comma=',' when include_trailing_comma is set, without the endswith(',') guard used for _comma_maybe, so a cont_line already ending in ',' gets a duplicate ',,' (syntax error).
findings.suggested_fix: _comma = ',' if config.include_trailing_comma and not cont_line.rstrip().endswith(',') else ''

findings.explanation: This rewrite fires whenever comment_prefix occurs anywhere in the last line and blindly drops comment[:-1]; if the trailing ')' is the comment's own closing character on a line where the generated ')' is on its own separator line or the '#' came from code, it truncates the comment/corrupts the line.
findings.suggested_fix: Only rewrite when a non-hoisted trailing comment is known to be present and the final ')' is the generated one; strip exactly that generated ')' instead of the last comment character.

findings.explanation: The NOQA guard only checks for the exact substring '# NOQA', so a line already carrying '# noqa' or '#noqa' gets a second NOQA comment appended.
findings.suggested_fix: Detect noqa case-insensitively, e.g. re.search(r'#\s*noqa', content, re.I).

findings.explanation: bare is computed to detect `from ... import *` but never used, so wildcard imports are wrapped despite comments saying they must be left untouched.
findings.suggested_fix: if bare.strip().endswith('import *'): return content

findings.explanation: Splitting on `#` treats `#` inside string literals as a comment start, corrupting code and comment handling.
findings.suggested_fix: Use tokenize or existing comment parser to split code vs comment

findings.explanation: Appending `\b` after a trailing space or around `.` prevents matches like `import (` and ` . ` because boundary requires word-char transition.
findings.suggested_fix: Use e.g. r'\bimport\s' and r'(?<!\w)\.(?=\w)' or plain string search

findings.explanation: Popping from the end and joining `next_line` in pop order reverses continuation fragments.
findings.suggested_fix: Reverse before join: splitter.join(reversed(next_line)) or pop(0)

findings.explanation: `len(content)+2` uses original full line including comment then truncated join, and can exit with empty `next_line` producing an empty parenthesized continuation.
findings.suggested_fix: Measure line_without_comment length and guard `if not next_line: return content`

findings.explanation: In `\` continuation mode an embedded `#` comments out the continuation, and a hoisted comment is dropped entirely because `noqa_comment` is only used in the parentheses branch.
findings.suggested_fix: Keep comment on its own trailing line or return unwrapped; never drop comment

findings.explanation: Case-sensitive `"noqa" in comment` misses `NOQA`/`Noqa` and matches substrings, and `comment and (...)` yields non-bool.
findings.suggested_fix: Use `bool(comment) and ('noqa' in comment.lower())` etc.

findings.explanation: Appending `)` after an inline comment then fixing with `comment[:-1]` truncates a comment legitimately ending in `)` and fails with multiple prefixes or whitespace.
findings.suggested_fix: Insert `)` before comment_prefix instead of post-fix string surgery

findings.explanation: Check `"# NOQA" not in content` is case- and spacing-sensitive and misses `#NOQA`, `# noqa`.
findings.suggested_fix: Use case-insensitive regex like r'#\s*noqa\b' with re.I

findings.explanation: `bare` is computed but never used, so `from x import *` lines are still wrapped and `import *` can be moved into parentheses or a continuation, producing invalid Python despite the stated contract.
findings.suggested_fix: Return content unchanged when `bare` matches a wildcard import, e.g. `if re.match(r'from\s+\S+\s+import\s+\*', bare): return content` before wrapping.

findings.explanation: When the while loop pops more than one element, `next_line` accumulates them last-to-first and `splitter.join(next_line)` emits the segments in reverse order, changing the imported names or dotted path.
findings.suggested_fix: Preserve order, e.g. insert at the front (`next_line.insert(0, line_parts.pop())`) or reverse `next_line` before joining.

findings.explanation: If `wrap_length` is larger than `line_length`, the outer test triggers wrapping but the while condition is immediately false, leaving `next_line` empty; the parenthesised branch then appends an empty `()` after the already-complete statement, corrupting it.
findings.suggested_fix: Use the same effective limit for entry and looping, and return `content` unchanged if `next_line` is empty.

findings.explanation: For the `.` splitter (reached by plain `import a.b.c`, since the `import ` splitter is skipped for lines starting with it) the code emits `import a.(\n b.c)`, which is invalid Python; parentheses may only be inserted after `import`, not after a dot.
findings.suggested_fix: Only use the parenthesised form for `import `/`cimport ` splitters; for `.` use the backslash continuation form.

findings.explanation: In the parenthesised/vertical branch an `as ` split is rejoined with `cont_line.lstrip()` onto the same line, undoing the split and returning a single line that still exceeds `line_length` (and discarding the continuation indent).
findings.suggested_fix: Emit a real continuation, e.g. `f"{content}{splitter}({line_separator}{cont_line})"` or the backslash form, instead of rejoining on one line.

findings.explanation: Hoisting only triggers for lowercase `"noqa" in comment`, so common `# NOQA` / `# NoQA` comments are left embedded inside the parentheses where linters do not honour them on the import line.
findings.suggested_fix: Use a case-insensitive match, e.g. `re.search(r'noqa', comment, re.IGNORECASE)`.

findings.explanation: The comma added here (both the initial value and the hoisted-comment override) does not check whether the wrapped content already ends with a comma, unlike the guard at lines 36-44, so an input already ending in `,` produces `,,`, which is invalid.
findings.suggested_fix: Only set `_comma` when `not cont_line.rstrip().endswith(',')`.

findings.explanation: The check only recognises the exact string `# NOQA`, so a line already carrying `# noqa` gets a second marker appended, and if the line already ends with an ordinary comment the appended `comment_prefix + NOQA` is swallowed inside that existing comment instead of acting as a directive.
findings.suggested_fix: Detect noqa case-insensitively anywhere in the existing comment and, when a comment already exists, merge `NOQA` into it rather than appending another comment prefix.

findings.explanation: Splitting on `#` yields `comment == ""` for a line ending in a bare `#`; the truthiness checks then drop the marker entirely, silently altering the source text.
findings.suggested_fix: Track comment presence separately from its text (e.g. `has_comment = '#' in content`) and re-emit the prefix for empty comments.

findings.explanation: If tag does not contain exactly 2 dashes, unpacking to 3 variables raises ValueError instead of documented InvalidTag.
findings.suggested_fix: Check len(component_parts)!=3 and raise InvalidTag before unpacking, or try/except ValueError -> InvalidTag

findings.explanation: Cartesian product of interpreters x abis x platforms allows attacker-controlled tag with many '.' components to cause memory/CPU exhaustion.
findings.suggested_fix: Limit number of '.' components / total expanded tags and raise InvalidTag if exceeded

findings.explanation: Tags with other than three hyphen-separated fields, such as 'py3-none' or 'py3-none-any-extra', leak a bare ValueError from tuple unpacking instead of raising InvalidTag.
findings.suggested_fix: Check len(component_parts) != 3 before unpacking and raise InvalidTag for malformed tags.

findings.explanation: Order and emptiness validation run before structural validation, so a tag with the wrong number of fields can incorrectly raise UnsortedTagsError (or mask the structural defect) when validate_order is enabled.
findings.suggested_fix: Validate that there are exactly three hyphen-separated components before checking compressed-component ordering.

findings.explanation: Plain lexicographic sorted() misorders numeric tag suffixes, e.g. 'cp310' sorts before 'cp39' and 'macosx_10_10' before 'macosx_10_9', so naturally/version-ordered compressed sets can be rejected and reverse orders accepted.
findings.suggested_fix: Compare components using the PEP 425 tag ordering/natural numeric ordering rather than raw string sorted().

findings.explanation: Duplicate compressed members such as 'py3.py3-none-any' satisfy parts == sorted(parts) and are silently collapsed by the frozenset, so validate_order accepts a malformed non-set compressed tag list.
findings.suggested_fix: When validate_order is true, also reject duplicate members in each compressed component.

findings.explanation: No check that tag has exactly 3 dash-separated parts. Unpacking raises ValueError instead of documented InvalidTag for e.g. 'py3-none' or 'a-b-c-d'.
findings.suggested_fix: Check len(component_parts)!=3: raise InvalidTag(...) before other checks.

findings.explanation: Negative limit must raise ValueError per docstring, but code skips the check and raises TooManyTagsError because tag_count>=1 > negative limit.
findings.suggested_fix: Add at top: if limit is not None and limit < 0: raise ValueError(...)

findings.explanation: tag_count uses raw len(parts) product, but return is a frozenset that deduplicates. Duplicates like 'py3.py3-none-any' count as 2 and can falsely trigger TooManyTagsError.
findings.suggested_fix: Deduplicate components first, e.g. use len(set(p)) for counting or build unique lists before counting.

findings.explanation: When limit is None (default) there is no cap on expansion, so a crafted tag like 'a.a...-b.b...-c.c...' causes combinatorial explosion and OOM/hang on set comprehension.
findings.suggested_fix: Enforce a default maximum limit or require limit, and check size before materializing the frozenset.

findings.explanation: Structural arity is validated last via unpack, so empty/order/limit checks run on malformed tags and can raise UnsortedTagsError or TooManyTagsError instead of InvalidTag.
findings.suggested_fix: Validate len(component_parts)==3 immediately after split, before empty/order/limit checks.

findings.explanation: A negative limit is never validated: tag_count is at least 1, so any negative limit raises TooManyTagsError instead of the documented ValueError.
findings.suggested_fix: At the start of the function, add `if limit is not None and limit < 0: raise ValueError(...)` before parsing/counting.

findings.explanation: Tags with fewer or more than three '-'-separated fields fail unpacking with a plain ValueError about unpacking, rather than InvalidTag for a malformed tag.
findings.suggested_fix: Check `len(component_parts) != 3` and raise `InvalidTag(f"Invalid tag: {tag!r}")` before unpacking.

findings.explanation: The limit/tag-count check runs before the three-field structural validation, so a malformed tag with many '.' components can raise TooManyTagsError (or compute a huge count) instead of InvalidTag.
findings.suggested_fix: Validate `len(component_parts) == 3` (raising InvalidTag) before computing tag_count or applying limit.

findings.explanation: tag_count multiplies the lengths of all '-'-separated components without early abort; a malicious tag with many repeated components produces an astronomically large integer (expensive big-int arithmetic/memory) before the limit check, defeating the purpose of limit.
findings.suggested_fix: Multiply incrementally and raise TooManyTagsError as soon as the running product exceeds limit, without computing the full product (and validate field count first).

findings.explanation: tag_count counts duplicate compressed members (e.g. 'py3.py3-none-any' counts 2) even though the returned frozenset deduplicates them to 1 tag, so limit can incorrectly reject tag sets whose actual generated tag count is within the limit.
findings.suggested_fix: Count distinct members per component, e.g. multiply `len(set(parts))` for each component, when enforcing the limit on generated tags.

findings.explanation: tag_count is initialized to 0 and then multiplied, so it stays 0 forever and the limit check never fires.
findings.suggested_fix: Initialize with tag_count = 1

findings.explanation: Code unpacks to exactly 3 dash-separated components without validation, so tags with !=3 parts raise ValueError from unpacking instead of InvalidTag.
findings.suggested_fix: if len(component_parts) != 3: raise InvalidTag(f"..." ) before unpacking

findings.explanation: TooManyTagsError limit check runs before validating there are 3 components, so malformed tags can raise TooManyTagsError instead of InvalidTag.
findings.suggested_fix: Validate len(component_parts)==3 before computing tag_count and checking limit

findings.explanation: tag_count is initialized to 0, so multiplying it by each component length always leaves it at 0. The limit check therefore never triggers and an attacker-controlled compressed tag set can expand without bound.
findings.suggested_fix: Initialize tag_count to 1: tag_count = 1

findings.explanation: If the tag does not contain exactly three '-'-separated fields, the unpacking raises a bare ValueError instead of InvalidTag, breaking the documented error contract; the earlier limit check can also mask this malformed-tag error with TooManyTagsError.
findings.suggested_fix: After splitting, check len(component_parts) != 3 and raise InvalidTag(f"Invalid tag: {tag!r}") before counting or unpacking.

findings.explanation: The count is the raw Cartesian product of component lengths, but the result is a frozenset, so duplicate members within a compressed component (e.g. 'py3.py3-none-any') produce fewer unique tags than counted and can spuriously raise TooManyTagsError at the limit.
findings.suggested_fix: Count unique members per component, e.g. use len(set(parts)) (after any Tag normalization) when computing the product, or compare the deduplicated expansion size against limit.

findings.explanation: self.expression expects an expression class, not an instance. Passing exp.JSONValue(...) will crash or misbehave.
findings.suggested_fix: return self.expression(exp.JSONValue, this=this, path=..., returning=..., on_condition=...)

findings.explanation: When RETURNING is absent the expression evaluates to False instead of None, passing an invalid boolean as returning.
findings.suggested_fix: returning = self._parse_type() if self._match(TokenType.RETURNING) else None

findings.explanation: Return value of _match(COMMA) is ignored so missing comma is silently accepted and path may be None or misparsed.
findings.suggested_fix: Require comma, e.g. self._match(TokenType.COMMA, expressionIndex=None) or check and raise/return None

findings.explanation: If path is missing/None, dialect.to_json_path(path) will crash; no null check before conversion.
findings.suggested_fix: if not path: return None / handle error before calling to_json_path

findings.explanation: Only one ON condition is parsed, but JSON_VALUE supports both ON EMPTY and ON ERROR clauses.
findings.suggested_fix: Parse in a loop / parse twice and combine into list for on_condition

findings.explanation: Using _parse_bitwise truncates logical expressions like OR/AND for the value and path arguments.
findings.suggested_fix: Use _parse_conjunction or _parse_expression for this and path

findings.explanation: When RETURNING is absent, `self._match(...) and self._parse_type()` evaluates to the boolean False rather than None, so the JSONValue node stores False in a slot expected to hold a type expression or None, breaking node equality/repr and any consumer that expects a type.
findings.suggested_fix: returning = self._parse_type() if self._match(TokenType.RETURNING) else None

findings.explanation: The result of matching the separating comma is ignored, so input without a comma (or with only one argument) is silently accepted and the following token is misparsed as the path instead of being rejected or treated as malformed.
findings.suggested_fix: Check the match result and raise/report a parse error (or handle the one-argument form explicitly) when the comma is missing.

findings.explanation: If the path argument is missing or unparseable, `path` is None and is passed to `self.dialect.to_json_path(path)` and into the required `path` slot of JSONValue, which can crash path conversion or produce an invalid node that later crashes the generator.
findings.suggested_fix: Validate that path is not None (raise a parse error otherwise) before calling to_json_path, e.g. only convert when a path expression was actually parsed.

findings.explanation: Both the JSON document and the path are parsed with _parse_bitwise(), which stops at higher-level operators such as AND/OR, comparisons, IS/IN/LIKE and CASE-level constructs, so a legitimate full expression argument is truncated and the remainder is misinterpreted as RETURNING/ON-clause or left as stray tokens.
findings.suggested_fix: Parse both arguments with _parse_conjunction() (which still stops at COMMA/RPAREN) instead of _parse_bitwise().

findings.explanation: The standard JSON_VALUE grammar allows a PASSING clause (and STRICT) between the path and RETURNING, e.g. JSON_VALUE(doc, path PASSING 1 AS x RETURNING INT); this parser attempts RETURNING immediately after the path, so PASSING/STRICT input is not consumed and the rest of the call is misparsed or fails.
findings.suggested_fix: Parse and store the optional PASSING bindings (and STRICT flag) after the path and before RETURNING, adding the corresponding slots to JSONValue if needed.
