findings.explanation: to_json_path is applied unconditionally to whatever expression was parsed as the path; for a non-literal path (column reference, bind parameter, or computed expression) this can rewrite a dynamic path as if it were a literal JSON path, corrupting the generated SQL.
findings.suggested_fix: Only apply to_json_path when the parsed path is a string literal; otherwise keep the original expression unchanged.

findings.explanation: Using `or` makes `returning` a Token when RETURNING matches instead of the parsed type, and parses a type even when RETURNING is absent.
findings.suggested_fix: returning = self._parse_types() if self._match(TokenType.RETURNING) else None

findings.explanation: Return value of _match(COMMA) is ignored, so missing comma is silently accepted and next clause is misparsed as path.
findings.suggested_fix: Require comma between value and path; return None/error if not present

findings.explanation: _parse_bitwise does not include higher-level operators like AND/OR/assignment, so complex value or path expressions are cut off.
findings.suggested_fix: Use _parse_conjunction or _parse_assignment for `this` and `path`

findings.explanation: If comma or second arg is missing, path is None and to_json_path(None) can crash.
findings.suggested_fix: Guard: path=... if path else None before to_json_path

findings.explanation: Only one on_condition is parsed but JSON_VALUE allows both ON EMPTY and ON ERROR plus DEFAULT variants.
findings.suggested_fix: Loop/parse ON EMPTY and ON ERROR separately and combine

findings.explanation: When RETURNING is matched, _match returns True and the `or` short-circuits, so _parse_types is never called and `returning` is set to the boolean True instead of a type expression, producing an invalid JSONValue node and wrong/crashing generation.
findings.suggested_fix: returning = self._parse_types() if self._match(TokenType.RETURNING) else None

findings.explanation: When RETURNING is absent, _parse_types is unconditionally invoked, so a following type-like token can be spuriously consumed and recorded as a RETURNING type even though no RETURNING clause was present.
findings.suggested_fix: Only call _parse_types after successfully matching RETURNING; otherwise leave returning as None.

findings.explanation: pre_alias/post_alias are concatenated without spaces and without leading space, so sample+version merge and merge into table/file_format.
findings.suggested_fix: Add leading space and separator: pre_alias = f" {pre_alias} {version}".strip() pattern or build with spaces

findings.explanation: pivots is placed before post_alias, so TABLESAMPLE/VERSION renders after PIVOT instead of before it.
findings.suggested_fix: Return order ...{hints}{post_alias}{pivots}... with post_alias before pivots

findings.explanation: WITH ORDINALITY is appended at the very end after joins/laterals instead of immediately after the alias.
findings.suggested_fix: Render ordinality right after alias, e.g. f"{alias}{ordinality}" before indexed/hints, not at end

findings.explanation: Ordinality payload is discarded and only flag checked; alias is glued without ensuring separator space.
findings.suggested_fix: Render ordinality expression if present and use f" WITH ORDINALITY {alias}".strip()

findings.explanation: rows_from overwrites table after when was appended to table, silently dropping the WHEN clause when both exist.
findings.suggested_fix: Compute ROWS FROM first then append when, or append when after rows_from branch

findings.explanation: When indexed is boolean True, self.sql(indexed) is called on a bool producing crash or 'TRUE' instead of bare INDEXED.
findings.suggested_fix: Check isinstance bool: if indexed is True: ' INDEXED'; elif indexed is False: ' NOT INDEXED'; else f' INDEXED BY {self.sql(indexed)}'

findings.explanation: When hints exist but TABLE_HINTS is false, hints are silently dropped instead of rendered.
findings.suggested_fix: Always render hints or fall back to standard hint syntax instead of empty string

findings.explanation: WITH ORDINALITY and its embedded alias are appended at the very end of the returned string, after joins, laterals, hints, pivots and post-alias clauses, so a table with any of those emits WITH ORDINALITY in an invalid position (and the alias binds to the wrong construct).
findings.suggested_fix: Emit ordinality (with the alias) immediately after the table/pre-alias part, before indexed/hints/pivots/joins/laterals, instead of at the end of the return f-string.

findings.explanation: Pivots are emitted before post_alias, so when the dialect puts TABLESAMPLE or a version clause after the alias, the output is 'table AS a PIVOT (...) TABLESAMPLE/FOR ...' instead of the sample/version applying to the base table before the pivot.
findings.suggested_fix: Place post_alias (sample/version) before pivots in the return string: ...{alias}{indexed}{hints}{post_alias}{pivots}{joins}...

findings.explanation: rows_from unconditionally replaces table, silently discarding any 'when' clause already folded into table on lines 44-46, while 'only', partition, file_format, sample/version and other table-level clauses are still emitted around ROWS FROM, producing invalid or semantically wrong SQL for combined inputs.
findings.suggested_fix: Only combine ROWS FROM with compatible args: preserve/relocate 'when' if supported and suppress or reject only/partition/file_format/sample for ROWS FROM tables.

findings.explanation: pattern is only emitted inside the file_format branch, so a table that specifies PATTERN without FILE_FORMAT silently loses the PATTERN clause and queries the wrong files.
findings.suggested_fix: Emit pattern independently, e.g. build the parenthesised clause from whichever of file_format/pattern are present: parts = [FILE_FORMAT => .., PATTERN => ..] filtered by presence.

findings.explanation: If 'indexed' is supplied programmatically as a plain string/bool rather than an expression node, self.sql(indexed) will crash or produce an empty name ('INDEXED BY '), because Generator.sql expects an Expression for non-key calls.
findings.suggested_fix: Normalise before rendering: use indexed.name/sql only for expressions, fall back to str(indexed) for strings, and treat True as an error or bare INDEXED BY omission.

findings.explanation: expression.args.get("ordinality") and "" is always falsy, so WITH ORDINALITY is never emitted.
findings.suggested_fix: ordinality = expression.args.get("ordinality")

findings.explanation: sample and version moved to pre_alias/post_alias without leading space and concatenated as f"{pre_alias}{version}" causing e.g. ")TABLESAMPLE" or "tblTABLESAMPLE".
findings.suggested_fix: Add leading space if pre_alias/post_alias non-empty, e.g. pre_alias = f" {pre_alias.strip()} {version.strip()}".strip() pattern

findings.explanation: pivots, joins, laterals use sep="" and are interpolated without leading space, concatenating multiple items and previous token without whitespace.
findings.suggested_fix: Use sep=" " and prefix with space if non-empty, e.g. pivots = f" {pivots}" if pivots else ""

findings.explanation: When rows_from is present table is overwritten, discarding the WHEN clause added on lines 46-48.
findings.suggested_fix: Append WHEN after ROWS FROM handling or include when in rows_from branch

findings.explanation: WITH ORDINALITY plus alias is appended after joins and laterals instead of immediately after the table/alias.
findings.suggested_fix: Emit ordinality right after alias/indexed, before hints/pivots/joins/laterals

findings.explanation: If indexed is True boolean, self.sql(True) is called with non-expression and will crash or misbehave.
findings.suggested_fix: Explicitly handle True/Expression/False cases, e.g. check isinstance before self.sql(indexed)

findings.explanation: `expression.args.get("ordinality") and ""` is always falsy (empty string when ordinality is truthy, the falsy value itself otherwise), so the `if ordinality:` block never runs and `WITH ORDINALITY` (with its alias) is never emitted.
findings.suggested_fix: ordinality = " WITH ORDINALITY" if expression.args.get("ordinality") else ""

findings.explanation: Unlike `partition` and `version`, `sample` is never given a leading space before being stored in `pre_alias`/`post_alias`, so it is concatenated directly onto the table/file-format/pivot text (e.g. `my_tableTABLESAMPLE ...`), producing invalid SQL whenever a table sample is present.
findings.suggested_fix: sample = f" {sample}" if sample else "" right after line 11, before assigning it to pre_alias/post_alias

findings.explanation: When both the sample and version clauses fall on the same side of the alias, version is appended after sample (`{sample}{version}` / post-alias equivalent), yielding `TABLESAMPLE ... FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF ...` whereas the version clause must precede the table-sample clause, producing invalid SQL for dialects using both.
findings.suggested_fix: Build the pre/post alias segment as f"{version}{sample}" (version first, then sample) when both are on the same side of the alias

findings.explanation: self._curr can be None at EOF (e.g. input ends with PUT), so accessing .token_type crashes the parser.
findings.suggested_fix: if not self._curr or self._curr.token_type != TokenType.STRING:

findings.explanation: Guard checks only TokenType.STRING but _parse_string accepts other string-like tokens, so valid PUT sources fall back to unstructured Command.
findings.suggested_fix: Check membership in all string token types or use self._match(TokenType.STRING) / _parse_conjunction fallback logic.

findings.explanation: If target stage path is missing/unparseable _parse_location_path returns None, creating exp.Put with required target=None which fails validation/generation.
findings.suggested_fix: if target is None: return self._parse_as_command(self._prev)

findings.explanation: Snowflake PUT options are space-separated (PARALLEL= AUTO_COMPRESS= OVERWRITE= SOURCE_COMPRESSION=) while _parse_properties handles comma-separated/WITH properties, so options are truncated or left unconsumed.
findings.suggested_fix: Parse PUT options in a loop with _match_texts and EQ instead of _parse_properties()

findings.explanation: Parser.expression() expects an expression class (exp.Put) plus keyword arguments, but it is passed an already-instantiated exp.Put object; calling expression(**opts) on that instance raises TypeError for every PUT statement that reaches this branch.
findings.suggested_fix: return self.expression(exp.Put, this=self._parse_string(), target=self._parse_location_path(), properties=self._parse_properties())

findings.explanation: Snowflake's canonical PUT form uses an unquoted file:// URI (e.g. PUT file:///tmp/data.csv @stage), which is not a single STRING token, so valid PUT statements fall back to an unstructured Command instead of exp.Put and lose their parsed source/target/properties.
findings.suggested_fix: Parse the file:// location (including unquoted paths and file://'quoted path' forms) as the Put source instead of requiring TokenType.STRING, only falling back to Command when no valid source path can be parsed.

findings.explanation: If PUT is the last token (e.g. input is just 'PUT'), self._curr can be None and accessing self._curr.token_type raises AttributeError instead of gracefully producing a Command/fallback parse.
findings.suggested_fix: Guard the check: if not self._curr or self._curr.token_type != TokenType.STRING: return self._parse_as_command(self._prev)

findings.explanation: Uses `self._parse_string() and ..._parse_location_path()` which discards the first parse and consumes two tokens for the single `this` field, shifting `target` and `properties` by one token.
findings.suggested_fix: Parse source once, e.g. `loc = self._parse_location_path(); this = self._parse_string() or (exp.Literal.string(loc.name) if loc else None)` and then parse target once.

findings.explanation: Calls `self._parse_location_path().name` without checking for None, causing AttributeError when parsing fails or input ends.
findings.suggested_fix: Check for None: `loc = self._parse_location_path(); this = exp.Literal.string(loc.name) if loc else None`.

findings.explanation: Guard allows URI_START but `this` uses `_parse_string()` which only handles STRING, so for `PUT file://...` short-circuit makes `this` None and loses the source.
findings.suggested_fix: Handle both token types for source, e.g. parse location path / URI when current token is URI_START.

findings.explanation: _parse_location_path() is called once for 'this' and again for 'target', advancing the token stream twice; target therefore parses the tokens after the real location (or None) and properties are then parsed from the wrong position.
findings.suggested_fix: Parse the location once into a local variable before constructing exp.Put, e.g. target = self._parse_location_path(), and reuse it.

findings.explanation: The result of _parse_string(), which is the PUT source file, is used only as a boolean and discarded; 'this' is instead built from the target location's name, so the parsed source path is lost and source/target are conflated.
findings.suggested_fix: Set this to the parsed source expression, e.g. this=self._parse_string(), and set target separately from the parsed stage location.

findings.explanation: _parse_location_path() can return None when no valid location follows, and calling .name on it raises AttributeError instead of producing a parse result or fallback command.
findings.suggested_fix: Store the location first and guard it, e.g. location.name if location else None, or fall back to _parse_as_command.

findings.explanation: For the URI_START branch _parse_string() may return None, so 'x and ...' yields None for the required 'this' arg and the URI is consumed as target instead of source, producing a Put with missing source and wrong target.
findings.suggested_fix: Handle STRING and URI_START sources explicitly (parse URI as source) rather than relying on 'and' short-circuiting.

findings.explanation: Using only _parse_location_path().name keeps just the final name component, discarding directory/stage prefix information (e.g. @stage/path, namespace, %-table or ~/ prefixes), so the generated SQL cannot reproduce the original location.
findings.suggested_fix: Keep the full parsed location/path expression instead of reducing it to .name in a new string Literal.

findings.explanation: When _parse_string() returns a falsy value, the 'and' expression returns that falsy non-Expression (None/False) as 'this' rather than an exp.Literal, violating exp.Put's arg contract and potentially breaking generation/equality.
findings.suggested_fix: Assign an explicit expression or None based on a conditional expression, not the result of 'and'.

findings.explanation: self.expression expects an expression class, not an instance; passing exp.Drop(...) will try to call the instance and crash.
findings.suggested_fix: self.expression(exp.Drop, tables=[...], kind=...)

findings.explanation: Columns are stored in `tables` arg which is for table references; Drop column actions use `expressions`, so generation and analysis break.
findings.suggested_fix: exp.Drop(expressions=[...], kind="COLUMN")

findings.explanation: kind="COLUMNS" plural does not match the canonical kind="COLUMN" used by generator and other dialects.
findings.suggested_fix: kind="COLUMN"

findings.explanation: _parse_schema parses column definitions with types, not a plain column identifier list like (a, b), causing wrong results or parse failure.
findings.suggested_fix: self._parse_csv(self._parse_field)

findings.explanation: If _parse_schema returns None, tables=[None] creates an invalid Drop instead of failing gracefully.
findings.suggested_fix: Check parsed result for None before building Drop

findings.explanation: Only matches DROP COLUMNS plural but Spark also supports singular DROP COLUMN, so singular statement returns None.
findings.suggested_fix: Accept both COLUMN and COLUMNS, e.g. _match_texts for singular/plural

findings.explanation: exp.Drop has no 'tables' argument in its contract; its target is stored in 'this' and dropped columns in 'expressions', so the generator ignores 'tables', produces a DROP with no target, and loses the parsed schema.
findings.suggested_fix: Use exp.Drop(this=<parsed table>, expressions=<parsed columns>, kind="COLUMNS") via the parser's expression() API.

findings.explanation: _parse_schema() parses a schema definition (a table plus typed column definitions), not a dropped-column list, so bare column names in DROP COLUMNS (a, b) are misinterpreted as schema/type expressions and the ALTER target table is never parsed here.
findings.suggested_fix: Parse the table separately (e.g. _parse_table_parts in the caller) and parse the columns with _parse_wrapped_id_vars()/_parse_id_var().

findings.explanation: If _parse_schema() fails (e.g. missing or malformed column list) it returns None, producing tables=[None]; copying/generating that node later crashes instead of reporting a parse error or falling back.
findings.suggested_fix: Check the parse result and raise/return None or an exp.Command fallback when no valid column list is present.

findings.explanation: Spark/Delta also accept the singular form ALTER TABLE t DROP COLUMN col, which this only-plural match rejects, returning None and leaving valid input unparsed or misparsed by the caller.
findings.suggested_fix: Match both COLUMN and COLUMNS, e.g. try _match_text_seq('DROP','COLUMNS') or _match_text_seq('DROP','COLUMN').

findings.explanation: The Spark grammar allows DROP COLUMN[S] IF EXISTS (...), but IF EXISTS is never consumed or recorded, so _parse_schema() then fails on the IF token and the exists flag is dropped from the AST.
findings.suggested_fix: After matching COLUMN[S], parse optional IF EXISTS and pass exists=True to exp.Drop.

findings.explanation: DROP COLUMN with a single unparenthesized column (and bare column lists) is valid, but routing everything through _parse_schema() assumes a parenthesized schema, so those forms return None/garbage instead of the column name.
findings.suggested_fix: Handle both parenthesized lists via _parse_wrapped_id_vars() and a single bare identifier via _parse_id_var()/ _parse_conjunction().

findings.explanation: The annotation promises exp.Command as a possible result, but once DROP COLUMNS matches, malformed following syntax still yields a bogus Drop node rather than an error or Command fallback, silently corrupting the parse.
findings.suggested_fix: Validate the column list after matching and fall back to self._parse_command() or raise a parse error on malformed input.

findings.explanation: self.expression expects an expression class, not an instance. Passing exp.Drop(...) causes a crash because the instance is not callable.
findings.suggested_fix: self.expression(exp.Drop, kind="COLUMNS", exists=exists, ...)

findings.explanation: With optional=True _parse_wrapped_csv returns None when there are no parentheses, so DROP COLUMN <col> without parens is lost and produces an empty drop.
findings.suggested_fix: Fall back to parsing single column or unwrapped CSV when wrapped parse returns None, e.g. columns = self._parse_wrapped_csv(...) or [self._parse_column()]

findings.explanation: exp.Drop has no tables arg and columns should not be wrapped in exp.Schema; the produced node will not generate correctly.
findings.suggested_fix: Use exp.Drop with this/expressions args, e.g. self.expression(exp.Drop, kind=..., expressions=columns)

findings.explanation: kind is hardcoded to COLUMNS even for singular DROP COLUMN, so decompilation/generation is wrong.
findings.suggested_fix: Set kind to COLUMN vs COLUMNS based on the consumed token.

findings.explanation: _parse_field_def parses typed field definitions, not plain column references, so plain identifiers can fail or misparse.
findings.suggested_fix: Use _parse_column or _parse_id_var / _parse_field_any for drop column names.

findings.explanation: Parser.expression expects an expression class, but an already-instantiated exp.Drop object is passed; it will try to call the instance as a constructor and raise TypeError (or otherwise not attach the supplied arguments).
findings.suggested_fix: Use the class form: return self.expression(exp.Drop, this=..., expressions=..., exists=exists, kind=...)

findings.explanation: exp.Drop has no 'tables' argument in its arg_types (it uses 'this'/'expressions'); the supplied 'tables' entry is ignored by the generator, so the dropped columns are lost from generated SQL.
findings.suggested_fix: Pass the columns via a supported Drop argument, e.g. expressions=columns, and do not use 'tables'.

findings.explanation: Wrapping the column list in exp.Schema is incorrect for a Drop node; Schema represents a table/column-definition schema and will render incorrectly (e.g. as a definition block) instead of a plain list of columns to drop.
findings.suggested_fix: Pass the parsed column expressions directly to exp.Drop, e.g. expressions=columns.

findings.explanation: _parse_field_def parses full column definitions (name plus data type and constraints), so DROP COLUMN a INT is wrongly accepted and the type is retained/re-emitted, and a plain name becomes a ColumnDef rather than a column reference.
findings.suggested_fix: Parse column references instead, e.g. self._parse_wrapped_csv(self._parse_column) or _parse_id_var/_parse_column_def without type consumption as appropriate.

findings.explanation: _parse_wrapped_csv with optional=True only handles a parenthesised CSV or a single unparenthesised item, so an unparenthesised list such as DROP COLUMNS a, b leaves ', b' unparsed and corrupts the rest of the statement parse.
findings.suggested_fix: Handle both forms explicitly: parse _parse_csv(self._parse_column) when not parenthesised, or _parse_wrapped_csv plus comma-separated fallback.

findings.category: missed edge case / silent invalid SQL
findings.explanation: With optional=True and no column present, the parse yields an empty/[None] column list yet still builds a Drop with an empty Schema, silently producing invalid 'DROP COLUMNS ()' style SQL instead of failing or returning None as the return type suggests.
findings.suggested_fix: Validate that at least one real column was parsed; return None or raise/emit a parse error when the list is empty or contains None.

findings.explanation: kind is hard-coded to the plural 'COLUMNS' regardless of whether the source used singular COLUMN, so generation always emits the plural form and any code comparing kind against the singular value will not match.
findings.suggested_fix: Preserve the parsed COLUMN/COLUMNS token as the kind, or use the canonical kind expected by Drop's generator.

findings.explanation: _match_text_seq consumes DROP COLUMNS before delegating, so super()._parse_drop_column() no longer sees those tokens and will mis-parse or return None.
findings.suggested_fix: Check without consuming or just return super()._parse_drop_column() without pre-matching.

findings.explanation: Method never verifies DROP/COLUMN keyword and always returns a Drop, instead of returning None when input is not a drop-column clause.
findings.suggested_fix: Only build Drop if DROP matched; otherwise return None.

findings.explanation: Singular COLUMN token is never consumed, leaving it in the token stream and corrupting subsequent parsing.
findings.suggested_fix: Parse optional COLUMN/COLUMNS keyword after DROP before exists/columns.

findings.explanation: Only wrapped (parenthesized) list is parsed, so bare DROP COLUMN c without parens yields empty/None columns instead of one column.
findings.suggested_fix: If wrapped parse returns None, fall back to parsing a single column or CSV without wrapping.

findings.explanation: Uses _parse_field_def which consumes types/constraints instead of parsing plain column identifiers.
findings.suggested_fix: Use _parse_column or _parse_id_var/_parse_field for column names.

findings.explanation: With optional=True columns can be None, producing exp.Schema(expressions=None) and an invalid Drop instead of returning None.
findings.suggested_fix: If not columns: return None.

findings.explanation: Drop built with tables=[Schema(...)] which is not the Drop arg for column lists; columns are lost on generation/round-trip.
findings.suggested_fix: Use the correct Drop args, e.g. expressions=columns with kind='COLUMN'/'COLUMNS'.

findings.category: missing token consumption / wrong token order
findings.explanation: The fallback never consumes the singular COLUMN keyword, and parses IF EXISTS before it; for DROP COLUMN [IF EXISTS] c the exists check sees COLUMN, the wrapped-column parse then fails, and COLUMN c is left unconsumed.
findings.suggested_fix: Consume COLUMN first, e.g. self._match_text_seq("COLUMN"), then exists = self._parse_exists().

findings.explanation: _parse_field_def parses a column definition (name plus datatype/constraints), not a column reference to drop, so following identifiers/datatypes can be mis-consumed and a spurious type can be stored and regenerated for a plain DROP COLUMN.
findings.suggested_fix: Parse dropped names with self._parse_column or self._parse_id_var / self._parse_conjunction, as the base implementation does.

findings.explanation: _parse_wrapped_csv(..., optional=True) only accepts a parenthesized list, but Spark also allows ALTER TABLE t DROP COLUMN c without parentheses; that form yields no columns and leaves c unconsumed.
findings.suggested_fix: If no opening paren is present, fall back to parsing a single column (or comma-separated columns) without wrapping.

findings.explanation: Because the wrapped parse is optional, columns can be None/empty (e.g. DROP COLUMN with no name, DROP () , or a non-column DROP such as DROP PARTITION reaching this path), yet a Drop node is unconditionally returned instead of None or a parse error, masking invalid SQL and potentially swallowing other DROP forms.
findings.suggested_fix: Return None (or raise) when no column was parsed: if not columns: return None.

findings.explanation: exp.Drop has no 'tables' arg (its arg_types are this/expressions/exists/kind/cascade etc.), so tables=[exp.Schema(...)] is ignored/not rendered by the generator and the required table/column information is lost, producing wrong SQL or a generation failure.
findings.suggested_fix: Build the node using exp.Drop's declared args (e.g. expressions=columns, exists=exists, kind=...) in the same shape as super()._parse_drop_column(), not tables/Schema.

findings.explanation: The fallback is the non-COLUMNS (singular/no-keyword) path but hardcodes kind="COLUMNS", so regeneration can emit the plural parenthesized form for a singular drop and mismatch the parsed syntax/AST contract.
findings.suggested_fix: Use kind="COLUMN" for this branch (and keep "COLUMNS" only for the delegated parenthesized plural branch), matching the generator's expectations.

findings.explanation: `if literal:` treats valid falsy index 0 (and empty-string key) as missing, so e.g. [1,0] silently drops 0.
findings.suggested_fix: if literal is not False and literal is not None: indexes.append(literal)

findings.explanation: Empty segment after comma (trailing comma [a,] or double comma [a,,b]) returns False from _parse_slice but is silently ignored instead of raising ParseError.
findings.suggested_fix: raise ParseError(_error("Cannot have empty segment")) when literal is False after comma

findings.explanation: Single-element type dispatch tests `literal` (last parsed value) instead of `indexes[0]`; after a dropped tail e.g. ['a',0] it misclassifies Key as Subscript.
findings.suggested_fix: if isinstance(indexes[0], str): ... elif isinstance(indexes[0], (exp.JSONPathScript, exp.JSONPathFilter)):

findings.explanation: Union passes raw str/int/slice values in `indexes` unwrapped, while singletons are wrapped in Key/Subscript/Selector, breaking downstream expectations.
findings.suggested_fix: Wrap each element in indexes to JSONPathKey/JSONPathSubscript/JSONPathSelector before building JSONPathUnion

findings.explanation: The union loop uses truthiness (`if literal:`) instead of the `is not False` check used for the first element, so valid falsy indexes such as 0 (and empty-string keys) after a comma are silently dropped, e.g. `[1,0]` becomes `[1]`.
findings.suggested_fix: Use `if isinstance(literal, str) or literal is not False: indexes.append(literal)` in the loop as well.

findings.explanation: An empty segment after a comma (where _parse_slice returns False, e.g. `[1,]` or `[1,,2]`) is silently ignored instead of raising the 'Cannot have empty segment' ParseError that an empty first segment raises, accepting malformed input.
findings.suggested_fix: Raise ParseError on the empty sentinel in the loop: `if literal is False: raise ParseError(_error('Cannot have empty segment'))` before appending.

findings.explanation: When len(indexes)==1 the node type is decided from `literal`, the last value parsed in the comma loop, rather than indexes[0]; if a trailing falsy element was dropped (e.g. `['a',0]` or `[0,'']`), `literal` differs from the sole retained index and a JSONPathKey/JSONPathSubscript/JSONPathSelector is built with a mismatched payload.
findings.suggested_fix: Dispatch on the retained element: `part = indexes[0]` and test `isinstance(part, str)` / `isinstance(part, (exp.JSONPathScript, exp.JSONPathFilter))`, passing `part` to the node constructor.

findings.explanation: Uses `and` instead of `or`, so any valid non-str first element (int index, slice, filter, script) fails the test and raises empty segment.
findings.suggested_fix: if isinstance(literal, str) or literal is not False:

findings.explanation: Failed union member (literal is False) is silently dropped instead of raising, accepting trailing commas and empty members like `['a',]` or `['a',, 'b']`.
findings.suggested_fix: else: raise ParseError(...) when literal is False

findings.explanation: Multi-element union passes raw str/int/parts directly to JSONPathUnion instead of wrapping like single-element path does with JSONPathKey/Subscript/Selector.
findings.suggested_fix: Wrap each index: str->JSONPathKey, Script/Filter->JSONPathSelector, else->JSONPathSubscript before constructing union

findings.explanation: The initial element is accepted only if it is a string, so valid non-string bracket contents returned by _parse_slice such as integer indexes, slices, wildcards, scripts, and filters incorrectly raise 'Cannot have empty segment'.
findings.suggested_fix: Accept any valid parse result, e.g. `if literal is not False:` and reserve the error for the actual empty/invalid sentinel.

findings.explanation: An empty or invalid element after a comma is silently skipped, so inputs such as ['a',] or ['a',,'b'] are accepted instead of raising a parse error, and the resulting index/union silently loses an element.
findings.suggested_fix: Raise ParseError when _parse_slice returns the empty/invalid sentinel inside the comma loop instead of conditionally skipping it.

findings.explanation: JSONPathUnion is built from raw indexes (strings/ints/slices/parts), whereas the single-element path wraps them into JSONPathKey, JSONPathSelector, or JSONPathSubscript; downstream expression handling expects Expression nodes and can crash or generate wrong output for raw values.
findings.suggested_fix: Wrap every union element the same way as the single-element case before constructing JSONPathUnion, e.g. via a helper that maps str->JSONPathKey, script/filter->JSONPathSelector, otherwise->JSONPathSubscript.

findings.explanation: Checks len(indexes)==2 instead of ==1, so single-element brackets become a JSONPathUnion and two-element brackets take only indexes[0] and silently drop indexes[1].
findings.suggested_fix: if len(indexes) == 1:

findings.explanation: If _parse_slice() fails after a comma (returns False) the empty element is silently skipped instead of raising, accepting [1,] or [1,,2].
findings.suggested_fix: else: raise ParseError(_error(...)) when literal is False

findings.explanation: The single-element case is tested as len(indexes) == 2, so a one-element bracket is wrapped in JSONPathUnion while a genuine two-element union discards indexes[1] and is misbuilt as a single key/selector/subscript from indexes[0] only.
findings.suggested_fix: Use len(indexes) == 1 for the single key/selector/subscript branch and len(indexes) > 1 for JSONPathUnion.

findings.explanation: Inside the comma loop an empty segment (literal is False, e.g. $[1,,2] or a trailing comma $[1,]) is silently skipped instead of raising ParseError like an empty first segment does, so invalid JSONPath is accepted and parsed as if the empty element never existed.
findings.suggested_fix: Add an else branch in the loop: raise ParseError(_error("Cannot have empty segment")) when the parsed literal is False/not a string.

findings.explanation: Parser.expression() takes an expression class, not an instance. Passing instance causes a crash.
findings.suggested_fix: Use func = instance or func = self.validate_expression(instance)

findings.explanation: First parens are ClickHouse params and second are args, but code keeps first parens as expressions and stores second as params, swapping them.
findings.suggested_fix: Move anon_func.expressions to params and parse second parens as expressions

findings.explanation: Testing params by truthiness treats empty params f()(x) as no params, picking wrong expression class.
findings.suggested_fix: Test params is not None instead of if params

findings.explanation: Using if params / elif params drops empty params and skips _parse_window, losing OVER clause for f()(x) OVER ...
findings.suggested_fix: Use is not None checks when setting params and parsing window

findings.explanation: When super already parsed a Window, parsing func params afterwards consumes tokens after the window spec instead of between func and window.
findings.suggested_fix: Do not call _parse_func_params when expr is a Window; parse params before window

findings.explanation: When the base parser already returned a Window and ClickHouse parameters are then parsed from a following parenthesized argument list, the OVER clause following that list is never parsed because the Window branch takes precedence over the params branch. The resulting tree keeps a window parsed against the parameter list or leaves the real OVER clause as trailing tokens.
findings.suggested_fix: In the Window branch, after replacing its function and parsing parameters, check for and parse a subsequent window with self._parse_window(func) when params were present, or restructure so the params case always attempts _parse_window.

findings.explanation: Only an immediate exp.Window wrapper is unwrapped before checking for exp.Anonymous. Base _parse_function can also return wrappers such as IgnoreNulls/RespectNulls (and Filter/WithinGroup style wrappers) around the function or window, so suffixed ClickHouse aggregates inside those wrappers are never converted and are left as plain Anonymous nodes.
findings.suggested_fix: Recursively unwrap/traverse the returned expression to find the Anonymous function node, convert it, and reattach it into whichever wrapper(s) were present.

findings.explanation: Existence of parameters is tested by truthiness, so a valid but empty parameter list returned by _parse_func_params is treated as 'no parameters': the non-parameterized expression class is chosen and _parse_window is not called, losing the parameterized form and potentially leaving an OVER clause unparsed.
findings.suggested_fix: Use an explicit sentinel/None check such as `params is not None` instead of `if params` for both class selection and window parsing.

findings.explanation: The replacement node is rebuilt from only anon_func.this and anon_func.expressions. Any other state _parse_func_params or the base parser stored on the Anonymous node (for example wrapped/operator-style args used by ParameterizedAgg) is silently discarded, which can change generation or semantics of parameterized aggregates.
findings.suggested_fix: Copy all relevant arg_types from anon_func into the new instance (or mutate/convert the existing node) and explicitly carry over fields such as params/wrapped in addition to this/expressions.

findings.explanation: Params are parsed after super already consumed first parens as args, so for quantile(0.9)(x) args and params are swapped.
findings.suggested_fix: Parse parameterized form before base call or treat existing expressions as params and newly parsed parens as args.

findings.explanation: Resolved base name and suffixes in parts are never stored; instance reuses full combined name with suffixes.
findings.suggested_fix: Set instance this to parts[0] and set suffix/combinator fields from parts[1]/parts[2].

findings.explanation: self.expression expects a class, not an instance; passing instance will crash or misbehave.
findings.suggested_fix: Use func = instance or self.validate_expression(instance).

findings.explanation: Only exp.Anonymous is checked, so aggregates already mapped by base parser to Sum/Count/etc never get suffix handling.
findings.suggested_fix: Check isinstance(func, exp.Func) and use func.sql_name() for resolution.

findings.explanation: Unconditional parts[2] indexing assumes 3-tuple shape and will IndexError on other shapes.
findings.suggested_fix: Unpack with length check, e.g. check len(parts)==3.

findings.explanation: Params are greedily parsed even for Window case or non-parameterized aggs, consuming following parens that belong to next expression.
findings.suggested_fix: Only call _parse_func_params when syntax indicates parameterized agg and handle Window+params case.

findings.explanation: Parser.expression() expects an expression class plus keyword arguments, but it is passed an already-constructed instance; calling the instance as a constructor will raise TypeError for every resolved ClickHouse aggregate.
findings.suggested_fix: Use the instance directly: `func = instance`, or construct it with `func = self.expression(exp_class, this=anon_func.this, expressions=anon_func.expressions)` and then set params.

findings.explanation: Only a top-level Window is unwrapped. Aggregates wrapped by the base parser in IgnoreNulls/RespectNulls (including Window(this=IgnoreNulls(this=Anonymous(...)))) are not Anonymous at this level, so combined/parameterized ClickHouse aggregates such as those used with IGNORE NULLS are never resolved.
findings.suggested_fix: Recursively unwrap Window and IgnoreNulls/RespectNulls to find the Anonymous node, resolve it, and rebuild all wrappers around the converted function.

findings.explanation: When super()._parse_function() already returned a Window, the token stream is positioned after the window specification, so _parse_func_params() cannot parse the parameter/argument parentheses that preceded OVER and may instead consume an unrelated following '(' as parameters.
findings.suggested_fix: Only call _parse_func_params() when the aggregate was not already consumed as part of a Window, and handle the windowed-parameterized form by parsing parameters before attempting window parsing.

findings.explanation: After parameters block the base parser, this code re-parses only a window. Post-aggregate modifiers that can appear between the second parameter parentheses and the window, notably IGNORE NULLS/RESPECT NULLS, are left unconsumed and cause parse errors or incorrect subsequent parsing.
findings.suggested_fix: After _parse_func_params(), parse ignore/respect-nulls modifiers in the same order as the base parser before parsing the window, e.g. wrap func with _parse_ignore_nulls/_parse_respect_nulls as appropriate and then call _parse_window().

findings.explanation: If the base parser returned a non-Window wrapper around the Anonymous aggregate, the branches either replace expr with the bare converted func or with _parse_window(func), silently discarding that wrapper and changing the query semantics.
findings.suggested_fix: Preserve any non-Window wrapper by setting its child to the converted func instead of replacing the whole expression, and only replace expr when it was exactly the original Anonymous node.

findings.explanation: Ignores with_alias=False: delegates to super with with_alias=False but then still synthesizes a default table/column alias.
findings.suggested_fix: Only apply default aliasing when with_alias is True, e.g. `if unnest and with_alias:`

findings.explanation: When alias has columns but no table name (e.g. column-only alias) the default table name 'unnest' is never applied.
findings.suggested_fix: Also default missing table name: `if not alias.this: alias.set('this', exp.to_identifier('unnest'))`

findings.explanation: The override ignores with_alias=False and always injects a table alias. _parse_unnest(with_alias=False) is used for UNNEST in expression/function contexts, so e.g. SELECT UNNEST(arr) can be regenerated with an invalid table-style alias AS unnest(unnest), changing the query.
findings.suggested_fix: Only apply the StarRocks default alias logic when with_alias is True: `if unnest and with_alias:`.

findings.explanation: Both the no-alias and alias-without-columns branches always create exactly one output column named 'unnest', even when UNNEST has multiple input expressions and therefore multiple output columns. The generated column-alias list has the wrong arity and can be rejected or mis-bind columns.
findings.suggested_fix: Derive the default column list from len(unnest expressions) (e.g. one default name per expression, with distinct names as StarRocks requires) or omit the column list for multi-expression UNNEST.

findings.explanation: If the parsed UNNEST carries ordinality (an extra ordinality output column), adding a single 'unnest' column alias still gives a column-alias list shorter than the actual output arity, misnaming/dropping the ordinality column on generation.
findings.suggested_fix: When ordinality is present, include an additional default column alias for the ordinality column or skip injecting a column-alias list in that case.

findings.explanation: Ignores with_alias=False and still synthesizes a default table alias, violating the caller's request not to parse/add an alias.
findings.suggested_fix: Only add default alias if with_alias is True, e.g. `if unnest and with_alias:`

findings.explanation: Uses `or` instead of `and`, so it overwrites an explicit column alias when there is one expression and adds a single default column when there are multiple expressions with no aliases.
findings.suggested_fix: Change to `if not alias.args.get("columns") and len(unnest.expressions) == 1:`

findings.explanation: Using `or` overwrites an explicitly specified column alias when there is one UNNEST expression: `UNNEST(arr) AS t(x)` becomes `AS t(unnest)`, losing `x`.
findings.suggested_fix: Only add the default when no columns were specified: `if not alias.args.get("columns") and len(unnest.expressions) == 1:`

findings.explanation: Using `or` adds a single `unnest` column alias for multiple UNNEST expressions when no columns were specified, contradicting the comment that none should be added and producing an alias count that does not match the expressions.
findings.suggested_fix: Only add the default when no columns were specified: `if not alias.args.get("columns") and len(unnest.expressions) == 1:`

findings.explanation: The override ignores `with_alias=False`: it still synthesizes and attaches a table/column alias, so callers that explicitly requested no alias get an AST that generates `AS unnest(unnest)` where an alias was not present/allowed.
findings.suggested_fix: Return early or skip default-alias injection when `with_alias` is False: `if unnest and not with_alias: return unnest` before adding defaults.

findings.explanation: Condition len(unnest.expressions) == 0 is backwards; a normal UNNEST has 1+ expressions so default column is never added, and it would be added only for degenerate empty UNNEST.
findings.suggested_fix: Change to len(unnest.expressions) == 1 to add single default column only for single-array UNNEST.

findings.explanation: Default table alias is injected even when with_alias=False, ignoring caller's request not to parse/consume alias.
findings.suggested_fix: Only add default alias/columns if with_alias is True, e.g. if with_alias and not alias:

findings.explanation: The default column alias is added only when there are zero unnested expressions, so the intended single-array case (`len == 1`) never receives the default `unnest` column, while an empty UNNEST incorrectly receives one column alias for no expression. This contradicts the comment that several arrays should receive none and a single array should receive the default.
findings.suggested_fix: Change the condition to `if not alias.args.get("columns") and len(unnest.expressions) == 1:`

findings.explanation: When `with_alias=False`, the caller explicitly requested that no alias be parsed/attached, but this override unconditionally synthesizes and attaches a table alias, causing generated SQL and downstream parsing to contain an alias the caller did not expect.
findings.suggested_fix: Only synthesize the default table/column alias when `with_alias` is true, e.g. guard the defaulting logic with `if with_alias:`

findings.explanation: CAST(float AS BIGINT) rounds in Postgres instead of truncating, so epoch/factor diffs e.g. 1.6 hours become 2.
findings.suggested_fix: Use FLOOR/TRUNC e.g. CAST(FLOOR(EXTRACT(epoch FROM ... ) ... ) AS BIGINT)

findings.explanation: WEEK computes EXTRACT(days ...)/7 as float then CAST rounds, so 11 days yields 2 instead of 1 and negatives are wrong.
findings.suggested_fix: Use TRUNC/DIV: CAST(TRUNC(EXTRACT(epoch FROM ...)/604800) AS BIGINT) or FLOOR for negatives

findings.explanation: QUARTER does EXTRACT(month)/3 in floating point then CAST rounds, so 5 or 8 months round to 2-3 instead of floor to 1-2.
findings.suggested_fix: Use integer division/floor: EXTRACT(year...)*4 + FLOOR(EXTRACT(month...)/3) with TRUNC

findings.explanation: Fallback sets unit=age then CAST(AGE(...) AS BIGINT) but Postgres cannot cast interval to bigint, so DAY without factor and unknown units produce runtime SQL error.
findings.suggested_fix: EXTRACT appropriate field from AGE, e.g. EXTRACT(day...) or raise unsupported unit error

findings.explanation: CAST(... AS TIMESTAMP) strips timezone from timestamptz inputs instead of preserving it, giving wrong wall-clock diffs.
findings.suggested_fix: Don't force TIMESTAMP or cast to TIMESTAMPTZ when input is tz-aware

findings.explanation: CAST(... AS BIGINT) in PostgreSQL rounds to the nearest integer rather than truncating, so e.g. a 36-hour difference computed in DAYs (1.5) becomes 2 instead of 1, and -1.5 similarly rounds away from the truncated result.
findings.suggested_fix: Wrap the scaled epoch value in TRUNC(...) before casting, e.g. CAST(TRUNC(EXTRACT(epoch FROM end-start){factor}) AS BIGINT).

findings.explanation: EXTRACT(days ...)/7 produces a fractional numeric whose CAST to BIGINT rounds, so 13 days becomes 2 weeks instead of 1 (and -13 days becomes -2 instead of -1).
findings.suggested_fix: Use CAST(TRUNC(EXTRACT(days FROM (end - start)) / 7) AS BIGINT).

findings.explanation: EXTRACT returns numeric, so EXTRACT(month)/3 is fractional (5 months -> 1.667) and the final CAST rounds it (to 2 quarters) instead of truncating, also mishandling negative ages.
findings.suggested_fix: Compute total months first and truncate: CAST(TRUNC((EXTRACT(year FROM age)*12 + EXTRACT(month FROM age)) / 3) AS BIGINT).

findings.explanation: Any unit not in DATE_DIFF_FACTOR and not WEEK/MONTH/QUARTER/YEAR (e.g. DECADE, CENTURY, or an unnormalized/plural unit) falls through to CAST(interval AS BIGINT), which PostgreSQL rejects with 'cannot cast type interval to bigint'.
findings.suggested_fix: Raise a clear unsupported-unit error or add explicit handling for the remaining units instead of casting the AGE interval.

findings.explanation: Casting TIMESTAMPTZ inputs to TIMESTAMP discards the zone and reinterprets the wall time in the session TimeZone, so differences spanning DST transitions or differing offsets are off by the offset shift (and epoch extraction no longer reflects absolute elapsed time).
findings.suggested_fix: Do not downcast to plain TIMESTAMP; preserve TIMESTAMPTZ (or compute EXTRACT(epoch FROM this - expression) on the original values) so the subtraction is timezone-aware.

findings.explanation: The date_part_boundary contract (count crossed calendar boundaries, as in MySQL DATEDIFF/TIMESTAMPDIFF) is only honored for DAY; for MONTH/QUARTER/YEAR/WEEK the AGE/elapsed-based formulas return completed elapsed periods, e.g. Jan 31 to Feb 1 yields 0 months instead of the 1 crossed month boundary.
findings.suggested_fix: When date_part_boundary is set, compute boundary counts for every unit (e.g. via DATE_TRUNC differences / year*12+month of the raw dates) rather than only special-casing DAY.

findings.explanation: AGE() borrows days from the preceding month and is sign-symmetric in a calendar-specific way, so MONTH/YEAR results depend on the day-of-month of the endpoints (e.g. Jan 31 to Feb 28 is 0 months) and negative ranges produce component signs that do not equal a truncated elapsed difference; this deviates from the DateDiff semantics used by other dialects even without the boundary flag.
findings.suggested_fix: Derive months/quarters/years from a consistent truncated-elapsed or boundary formula (as other generators do) instead of EXTRACTing components of AGE().

findings.explanation: exp.cast() wraps the original expression.this/expression nodes in place without copying, reparenting children of the input DateDiff node; generating SQL therefore mutates the caller's AST and corrupts reuse or a second generation of the same tree.
findings.suggested_fix: Cast copies: exp.cast(expression.this.copy(), exp.DType.DATE) and likewise for expression.expression.

findings.explanation: Condition `unit == DAY or date_part_boundary` returns DATE subtraction for all units when boundary flag is set, making lines 18-20 dead code, and forces DAY to boundary semantics even for complete-unit dialects.
findings.suggested_fix: Change to `if unit == DAY and expression.args.get(date_part_boundary):` or handle DAY separately from other boundary units.

findings.explanation: self.sql(expression, 'this') passes whole DateDiff with 'this' as comment flag, causing infinite recursion instead of rendering child; should render child expression.
findings.suggested_fix: Use `self.sql(expression.this)` and `self.sql(expression.expression)`.

findings.explanation: end/start are already SQL strings but passed as args to self.func which expects expressions, causing mis-quoting or failure.
findings.suggested_fix: Build string directly e.g. f"DATE_TRUNC('{unit}', {end})" or pass exp.to_identifier/parse expressions.

findings.explanation: EXTRACT result concatenated directly with factor without operator, producing invalid SQL unless factor contains operator.
findings.suggested_fix: Use explicit division e.g. f"CAST(EXTRACT(epoch FROM {end} - {start}) / {factor} AS BIGINT)".

findings.explanation: EXTRACT(days FROM interval) returns day component only, not total days, so WEEK is wrong for intervals spanning months/years.
findings.suggested_fix: Use epoch-based calc e.g. `EXTRACT(epoch FROM ...)/604800` or `FLOOR(EXTRACT(epoch...)/604800)`.

findings.explanation: CAST(... AS BIGINT) truncates toward zero, so negative fractional units are off-by-one versus floor of complete units.
findings.suggested_fix: Use FLOOR for both signs e.g. `CAST(FLOOR(...) AS BIGINT)`.

findings.explanation: Fallback for unknown unit returns CAST(AGE(...) AS BIGINT) which is invalid cast from interval to bigint in Postgres.
findings.suggested_fix: Raise unsupported error or handle remaining units explicitly.

findings.explanation: Unit not normalized for plurals/aliases e.g. DAYS, HOURS, so lookup and comparisons fail and fall through to wrong branch.
findings.suggested_fix: Normalize unit e.g. singularize and map aliases before comparison/lookup.

findings.explanation: The early return triggers for every unit whenever date_part_boundary is set, returning a DATE difference in days instead of the requested unit's boundary count, e.g. a MONTH boundary diff returns elapsed days; this also makes the truncation logic at lines 18-20 dead code.
findings.suggested_fix: Only take this shortcut when unit == "DAY" and date_part_boundary is set; let other boundary units reach the DATE_TRUNC path.

findings.explanation: For unit == "DAY" without date_part_boundary, calendar-date subtraction counts crossed midnights rather than complete 24-hour periods, e.g. 23:00 to 01:00 next day returns 1 instead of 0.
findings.suggested_fix: Use the epoch/factor arithmetic for non-boundary DAY diffs and reserve DATE subtraction for boundary semantics.

findings.explanation: Casting operands to TIMESTAMP (without time zone) silently drops time-zone information and makes results depend on the session TimeZone setting, so diffs of TIMESTAMPTZ values, especially across DST transitions, are wrong.
findings.suggested_fix: Preserve the operand type or cast to TIMESTAMPTZ instead of naive TIMESTAMP.

findings.explanation: CAST(x AS BIGINT) in Postgres rounds to nearest rather than truncating, so fractional factor results are wrong, e.g. 1.9 hours becomes 2 instead of 1 complete hour (and -1.9 becomes -2 instead of -1).
findings.suggested_fix: Wrap the quotient in TRUNC(...) before casting, e.g. CAST(TRUNC(EXTRACT(epoch FROM end - start){factor}) AS BIGINT).

findings.explanation: EXTRACT(days ...)/7 yields a fractional numeric (13 days -> 1.857) and the outer CAST AS BIGINT rounds it, returning 2 weeks instead of 1 complete week; WEEK with date_part_boundary also gets complete weeks rather than week-boundary crossings.
findings.suggested_fix: Use integer truncation, e.g. CAST(TRUNC(EXTRACT(days FROM (end - start)) / 7) AS BIGINT), and handle boundary WEEK semantics explicitly.

findings.explanation: EXTRACT(month FROM age)/3 is fractional numeric division, so 2 months gives 0.667 and 5 months gives 1.667, which the rounding CAST turns into 1 and 2 quarters instead of 0 and 1 complete quarters.
findings.suggested_fix: Truncate the month component before/while dividing, e.g. EXTRACT(year FROM age) * 4 + TRUNC(EXTRACT(month FROM age) / 3).

findings.explanation: Any unit not covered by the factor map or WEEK/MONTH/QUARTER/YEAR (e.g. DECADE, CENTURY, or an unrecognized unit) falls through to CAST(AGE(...) AS BIGINT), and Postgres cannot cast an interval to bigint, producing a runtime error instead of a result.
findings.suggested_fix: Handle remaining units explicitly or raise a clear unsupported-unit error at generation time rather than emitting invalid SQL.

findings.explanation: factor is fetched from DATE_DIFF_FACTOR but never used, so DAY (non-boundary), HOUR, MINUTE, SECOND etc fall to else and do CAST(AGE(...) AS BIGINT) which Postgres rejects because interval cannot cast to bigint.
findings.suggested_fix: Use factor with EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM age)/factor, e.g. CAST(FLOOR(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM age)/factor) AS BIGINT)

findings.explanation: EXTRACT(days FROM ...) uses plural field name and extracts only the days component of an interval, so differences spanning months/years are wrong and Postgres expects DAY.
findings.suggested_fix: Use EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (end - start))/86400/7 e.g. FLOOR(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM ...)/604800)

findings.explanation: WEEK is excluded from DATE_TRUNC boundary handling, so dialects counting boundary crossings get complete-week counts instead.
findings.suggested_fix: Handle WEEK boundaries explicitly accounting for dialect week-start day instead of leaving it out

findings.explanation: QUARTER uses floating division EXTRACT(month)/3 then CAST truncates toward zero, giving wrong result for negative intervals where floor is required.
findings.suggested_fix: Use FLOOR division, e.g. FLOOR((year*12+month)/3)

findings.explanation: CAST(... AS TIMESTAMP) strips time zone, so timestamptz inputs lose offset/DST information.
findings.suggested_fix: CAST to TIMESTAMPTZ or preserve original type instead of TIMESTAMP

findings.explanation: DATE_DIFF_FACTOR is looked up but never used, and the fallback sets unit to AGE(...), so DAY and sub-day units generate CAST(AGE(...) AS BIGINT); PostgreSQL cannot cast an interval to BIGINT and this SQL fails at runtime.
findings.suggested_fix: Use the factor for epoch-based units, e.g. return CAST(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM end - start) / factor AS BIGINT) with truncation, and handle DAY similarly via total days/epoch.

findings.explanation: EXTRACT returns numeric, so days/7 is fractional and the outer CAST(... AS BIGINT) rounds instead of truncating; e.g. 13 days becomes 2 weeks instead of 1, and negative spans round away from zero.
findings.suggested_fix: Use CAST(TRUNC(EXTRACT(days FROM (end - start)) / 7) AS BIGINT) or integer truncation toward zero.

findings.explanation: EXTRACT(month FROM age)/3 is numeric division and CAST(... AS BIGINT) rounds, so e.g. 5 complete months yields 2 quarters instead of 1 (and negative spans are similarly wrong).
findings.suggested_fix: Truncate the month component before/while dividing, e.g. CAST(EXTRACT(year FROM age) * 4 + TRUNC(EXTRACT(month FROM age) / 3) AS BIGINT).

findings.explanation: When date_part_boundary is set, WEEK is excluded from DATE_TRUNC truncation, so the WEEK branch counts complete 7-day periods rather than crossed week boundaries as required by boundary-counting dialects, giving e.g. 0 instead of 1 across a week boundary.
findings.suggested_fix: Implement week-boundary counting explicitly using the source dialect's week-start convention, or truncate/align both operands to that week start before dividing.

findings.explanation: The DAY boundary fast path returns a bare DATE-DATE subtraction, which in PostgreSQL yields INTEGER, while every other path returns BIGINT, breaking the expected result-type contract and risking overflow differences for large spans.
findings.suggested_fix: Wrap the fast path as CAST((CAST(this AS DATE) - CAST(expression AS DATE)) AS BIGINT).

findings.explanation: An unknown, plural, or abbreviated unit (e.g. DAYS, MS, FORTNIGHT) misses DATE_DIFF_FACTOR/DATE_DIFF_BOUNDARY_UNITS lookups and silently falls through to the invalid CAST(AGE(...) AS BIGINT) or an invalid DATE_TRUNC field instead of being normalized or rejected.
findings.suggested_fix: Normalize units to canonical singular names and raise/return a clear unsupported-unit error when the unit is not in the supported maps.

findings.explanation: Component form TIMESTAMP_FROM_PARTS(year, month, day, ...) also has `this` and `expression` non-None, so it is misclassified as DATE+TIME form and returns year+month.
findings.suggested_fix: Only take DATE+TIME path when no other component args (year/month/day/hour/minute/sec/milli/micro/nano/zone) are present.

findings.explanation: milli is an Expression, not a list; milli.pop() is wrong API and crashes, and leaves milli arg on parent expression.
findings.suggested_fix: Use expression.set("milli", None) or expression.args.pop("milli", None) to remove it.

findings.explanation: Same bug for nano: nano.pop() crashes/misuses API and leaves nano arg behind.
findings.suggested_fix: Use expression.set("nano", None) to clear it.

findings.explanation: Python + / += on Expression nodes does not build SQL AST and raises TypeError.
findings.suggested_fix: Build exp.Add(this=sec, expression=exp.Div(this=milli, expression=exp.to_literal(1000))) etc.

findings.explanation: Merged fractional seconds are passed along with leftover milli/nano args to MAKE_TIMESTAMP, which does not accept them, producing wrong arity/SQL.
findings.suggested_fix: Clear milli/nano (and micro/zone) from the copied expression before rename_func("MAKE_TIMESTAMP").

findings.explanation: milli/1000.0 and nano/1e9 in DOUBLE loses precision, especially nanoseconds, causing wrong timestamps.
findings.suggested_fix: Use precise decimal/interval arithmetic or CAST to DOUBLE only at end.

findings.explanation: Other TimestampFromParts args like micro/microseconds and timezone are ignored, silently dropped or passed to MAKE_TIMESTAMP which rejects them.
findings.suggested_fix: Handle micro like milli/nano and map timezone to MAKE_TIMESTAMPTZ or error.

findings.explanation: When sec is None (seconds omitted/default 0) it forwards missing sec to MAKE_TIMESTAMP instead of defaulting to 0.
findings.suggested_fix: Default sec to exp.to_literal(0) when absent.

findings.explanation: Condition uses truthiness of Expression objects (if milli or nano) instead of is-not-None checks and mutates input expression in place.
findings.suggested_fix: Check if milli is not None or nano is not None and operate on expression.copy().

findings.explanation: Embedding date_expr/time_expr directly in a new Add node re-parents/reuses the original children without copying, mutating the input expression tree and breaking its invariants for later generation or reuse.
findings.suggested_fix: Use copied nodes, e.g. self.sql(exp.Add(this=date_expr.copy(), expression=time_expr.copy())), or generate without constructing a new parent node.

findings.explanation: DuckDB DATE + TIME is not always equivalent to Snowflake TIMESTAMP_FROM_PARTS(date,time[,zone]): a timezone/zone argument if present is silently dropped, and if the first argument is already a timestamp/datetime rather than a date the addition has different/error semantics.
findings.suggested_fix: Preserve/handle expression.args.get('zone') (e.g. cast/AT TIME ZONE) and only use DATE+TIME when this is known to be a DATE, otherwise cast to TIMESTAMP first.

findings.explanation: Valid TIMESTAMP_FROM_PARTS forms can omit seconds (e.g. only year..minute, with sec defaulting in the source dialect); falling back to MAKE_TIMESTAMP with a missing sec argument then emits MAKE_TIMESTAMP with too few/wrong arguments instead of supplying 0 seconds.
findings.suggested_fix: Default sec to exp.Literal.number(0) instead of assuming sec is always present; don't rename an incomplete arg set to MAKE_TIMESTAMP.

findings.explanation: milli is a single Expression node (not a list) in TimestampFromParts.args, so milli.pop() raises AttributeError; the same applies to nano.pop() on line 22.
findings.suggested_fix: Use milli directly without pop: sec = sec + milli / exp.Literal.number(1000.0) (relying on Expression operator overloads or exp.Div).

findings.explanation: If milli/nano were lists, .pop() and sec+= in-place operations mutate the caller's original expression; generating SQL twice or reusing the tree yields different (fraction-lost or double-counted) SQL and corrupts parent links.
findings.suggested_fix: Work on expression.copy() and build a new sec expression with exp.Add/exp.Div instead of += and pop().

findings.explanation: sec is an exp.Expression; sec += expr / exp.Literal.number(...) relies on Expression.__truediv__/__add__ not producing a proper Div/Add node (and float literal construction via Literal.number may produce an invalid literal), so this can raise TypeError or generate non-numeric text instead of fractional seconds.
findings.suggested_fix: Build nodes explicitly: exp.Div(this=milli.copy(), expression=exp.to_identifier('1000') or exp.Literal(this='1000.0', is_string=False)) and exp.Add(this=sec, expression=...); verify with a literal sec.

findings.explanation: After folding milli/nano into sec, the milli/nano entries are never removed from expression.args, so rename_func('MAKE_TIMESTAMP') via function_fallback_sql emits them as extra trailing arguments to DuckDB MAKE_TIMESTAMP (too many arguments / double-counted fractional seconds).
findings.suggested_fix: On the copied expression, clear them: expression.set('milli', None); expression.set('nano', None) (or pop the arg keys) before calling rename_func.

findings.explanation: If milli/nano are lists, the preceding pop() empties them, so `if milli or nano:` is False and the updated sec is never written back, silently losing fractional seconds; if they are expressions the check also reflects original presence after mutation inconsistently when only one was popped/processed.
findings.suggested_fix: Capture had_milli/had_nano booleans before any mutation and set sec unconditionally when either was present.

findings.explanation: Converting milli/nano to fractional seconds via binary float division (1000.0/1000000000.0) and adding to sec loses exactness for nanosecond values and for non-literal sec expressions, and can render long float literals that DuckDB rounds to microseconds anyway in a wrong value.
findings.suggested_fix: Use decimal/exact arithmetic for literal sec (or MAKE_TIMESTAMP_NS / interval arithmetic for nano) and avoid float literals for nano; at minimum use string Decimal division.

findings.explanation: The date/time form is detected merely by this and expression both being non-None, but the component form also stores year in `this` and month in `expression`, so a 2+-component call can be misrouted to DATE+TIME unless the parser guarantees a distinct marker; relying on both being present does not distinguish the two forms.
findings.suggested_fix: Distinguish using the actual discriminator used by the parser (e.g. presence of 'expressions'/sec/milli/nano args or a dedicated date arg), not just this/expression non-None.

findings.explanation: milli is a single expression node, not a list, so milli.pop() is invalid and will crash or remove the node from its parent incorrectly.
findings.suggested_fix: Use milli directly, e.g. sec + milli / exp.Literal.number(1000), and remove with expression.set("milli", None)

findings.explanation: nano is a single expression node, so nano.pop() is invalid and will crash or corrupt the AST.
findings.suggested_fix: Use nano directly and remove with expression.set("nano", None)

findings.explanation: After folding milli/nano into sec the milli/nano args are left on expression, so MAKE_TIMESTAMP receives extra unsupported arguments.
findings.suggested_fix: After folding do expression.set("milli", None); expression.set("nano", None)

findings.explanation: expression.set("sec", sec) mutates the caller's AST inside a generator; generators must not have side effects.
findings.suggested_fix: Copy/build a new TimestampFromParts or Func node instead of mutating expression

findings.explanation: Folding with float division by 1000.0 and 1000000000.0 loses precision for milliseconds/nanoseconds and forces DOUBLE seconds.
findings.suggested_fix: Use exact numeric/decimal arithmetic or DuckDB interval arithmetic to preserve fractional seconds

findings.explanation: Timezone/zone argument of TIMESTAMP_FROM_PARTS is silently dropped in both the DATE+TIME path and the MAKE_TIMESTAMP path.
findings.suggested_fix: Handle zone explicitly, e.g. wrap result with timezone cast or reject unsupported zone

findings.explanation: Only handles date+time when both parts present; single date or time part falls through to component form where date is misinterpreted as year.
findings.suggested_fix: Distinguish overloads by arg count/types and handle partial date/time or fall back explicitly

findings.explanation: milli is a single Expression (not a list), so milli.pop() raises AttributeError on transpilation of any TIMESTAMP_FROM_PARTS with a milli argument; the same applies to nano.pop().
findings.suggested_fix: Use milli directly without pop(): sec = sec + milli / exp.Literal.number(1000)

findings.explanation: sec += milli/exp.Literal... and sec += ... rely on Expression.__add__/__truediv__ overloads that build anonymous/binary nodes, not numeric literals; dividing an Expression by a float Literal via / creates an invalid node / does not produce sec + milli/1000 SQL as intended and may raise or generate wrong SQL.
findings.suggested_fix: Build explicitly: exp.Add(this=sec, expression=exp.Div(this=milli, expression=exp.Literal.number(1000))) (and analogously for nano)

findings.explanation: sec is the original expression node from expression.args; doing sec += ... rebinds/mutates the shared node and, together with expression.set on line 25, mutates the caller's AST during generation, so repeated generation or reuse of the tree yields different/corrupted SQL.
findings.suggested_fix: Copy nodes first (sec = sec.copy(), milli = milli.copy()) and construct a new Add node instead of += on the original args.

findings.explanation: If milli/nano were lists, .pop() mutates expression.args in place, removing the argument permanently; generating SQL twice or inspecting the AST afterwards loses milli/nano and produces a different (truncated) MAKE_TIMESTAMP.
findings.suggested_fix: Do not pop; read the value non-destructively and clear/overwrite args explicitly via expression.set('milli', None) if needed.

findings.explanation: After folding milli/nano into sec, the original milli and nano args are left on the expression, so rename_func('MAKE_TIMESTAMP') will still emit them as extra positional arguments to DuckDB MAKE_TIMESTAMP(year,month,day,hour,min,sec[,...]), producing wrong arity/semantics or double-counting fractional seconds.
findings.suggested_fix: Clear them before delegating: expression.set('milli', None); expression.set('nano', None) (and pop from args if list-valued).

findings.explanation: if milli or nano relies on Expression/list truthiness; a non-empty Expression may be falsy/truthy inconsistently (e.g. Literal 0) and an emptied list from pop() is falsy, so sec is not updated when only milli/nano was present or when its value is 0, silently dropping fractional seconds.
findings.suggested_fix: Use explicit None checks: if milli is not None or nano is not None: expression.set('sec', sec)

findings.explanation: The early return on sec is None bypasses milli/nano handling, but valid component forms can have milli/nano without sec in some dialects, and conversely if sec is present but is not a numeric literal the float division 1000.0 introduces floating-point imprecision for nano (1e9) losing sub-microsecond precision DuckDB supports.
findings.suggested_fix: Default sec to Literal 0 if missing when milli/nano present, and use integer/rational arithmetic or MAKE_TIMESTAMP with separate micros argument instead of float division.

findings.explanation: Returning self.sql(exp.Add(this=date_expr, expression=time_expr)) reuses the original date/time child nodes without copying, mutating/aliasing the original TimestampFromParts tree, and Add has lower precedence handling that can generate unparenthesized 'date + time' losing any zone/safe semantics stored in other args (e.g. zone is ignored).
findings.suggested_fix: Use copied nodes: exp.Add(this=date_expr.copy(), expression=time_expr.copy()), wrap as needed, and handle/preserve expression.args.get('zone') or fall through to MAKE_TIMESTAMP when zone/safe present.

findings.explanation: The two-arg form is detected only when both this and expression are non-None, but the component form also sets this/expression (year/month), so a component call with only year+month populated or a two-arg call in other arg slots mis-routes; conversely a 2-component partial call is incorrectly treated as date+time.
findings.suggested_fix: Discriminate by presence of component args (year/month/day/sec etc.) or an explicit flag/arg count, not merely this/expression non-None.

findings.explanation: When sec is missing the code silently emits MAKE_TIMESTAMP with the original TimestampFromParts args, which DuckDB will reject or misinterpret (different arg names/order), masking an invalid AST instead of supplying default sec=0 or failing clearly.
findings.suggested_fix: Set sec to exp.Literal.number(0) and continue with milli/nano handling, or raise/emit MAKE_TIMESTAMP with explicit year..second args in correct order.

findings.explanation: milli is an expression node, calling milli.pop() with no key is wrong and crashes or corrupts the node instead of removing the arg from parent.
findings.suggested_fix: Use expression.args.pop("milli") to get and remove the arg

findings.explanation: Nanoseconds conversion is inverted: computes 1e9 / nano instead of nano / 1e9, producing wildly wrong seconds.
findings.suggested_fix: sec = exp.Div(this=nano_value, expression=exp.Literal.number(1000000000))

findings.explanation: Consumed milli/nano args are never removed from expression.args, so MAKE_TIMESTAMP receives unsupported extra args.
findings.suggested_fix: Pop milli/nano from expression.args and only set merged sec

findings.explanation: Zone is not removed from inner expression and zone.pop() is wrong value, so generating AtTimeZone(this=expression) re-invokes same function forever.
findings.suggested_fix: zone_value = expression.args.pop("zone"); return self.sql(exp.AtTimeZone(this=expression.copy() or rebuilt, zone=zone_value))

findings.explanation: Date+time form ignores optional zone argument, dropping timezone information.
findings.suggested_fix: Handle zone in this branch too, e.g. wrap DATE+TIME in AtTimeZone when zone present

findings.explanation: The component form also populates `this`/`expression` (first/second components), so this check can misclassify TIMESTAMP_FROM_PARTS(year, month, ...) as date+time and emit year+month, making the component branch unreachable for that representation.
findings.suggested_fix: Distinguish the two forms by arity/arg keys (e.g. presence of sec/expressions), not merely by this/expression being non-None.

findings.explanation: milli is a single Expression node in TimestampFromParts args, not a list, so milli.pop() raises AttributeError for any input with milliseconds; same pattern is used for nano and zone.
findings.suggested_fix: Use the expression directly, e.g. sec = sec + milli / exp.Literal.number('1000.0'), and clear the arg via expression.set('milli', None) if needed.

findings.explanation: Nanosecond conversion is inverted: it computes 1000000000.0 / nano instead of nano / 1000000000.0, giving wildly wrong fractional seconds and a division-by-zero in generated SQL when nano=0.
findings.suggested_fix: sec += nano / exp.Literal.number('1000000000.0')

findings.explanation: pop() on milli/nano/zone mutates the original AST, so generating SQL twice, or reusing/transpiling the same parsed tree, silently loses fractional seconds and timezone on subsequent generations.
findings.suggested_fix: Do not pop from the input expression; copy the expression or build a new TimestampFromParts/MAKE_TIMESTAMP node with the consumed args removed.

findings.explanation: After pop() the milli/nano lists are emptied, so `if milli or nano:` is falsy and expression.set('sec', sec) is skipped, discarding the computed fractional seconds before MAKE_TIMESTAMP is emitted.
findings.suggested_fix: Track presence before consuming, e.g. has_frac = milli is not None or nano is not None, then set sec unconditionally when has_frac.

findings.explanation: Wrapping the still-unconverted TimestampFromParts in AtTimeZone and calling self.sql re-enters timestampfromparts_sql on the same mutated node; it only terminates because zone was popped, and any non-list zone raises AttributeError, while MAKE_TIMESTAMP fallback rendering can still include leftover zone/milli/nano args as extra positional arguments.
findings.suggested_fix: First build the MAKE_TIMESTAMP expression with fractional seconds applied and zone/milli/nano removed, then wrap that converted node in AtTimeZone.

findings.explanation: When sec is absent (valid forms such as date-only TIMESTAMP_FROM_PARTS or omitted seconds), it falls back to rename_func MAKE_TIMESTAMP with missing/mismatched arguments, emitting DuckDB SQL with wrong arity instead of defaulting seconds to 0.
findings.suggested_fix: Default missing time components to 0 or handle the date-only form explicitly before the MAKE_TIMESTAMP fallback.

findings.explanation: Returning bare date_expr + time_expr reuses the original child nodes and relies on DuckDB DATE+TIME semantics without a cast; for TIMESTAMP/DATE expressions or non-DATE/TIME operand types this can produce DATE/INTERVAL arithmetic or a type error rather than a TIMESTAMP.
findings.suggested_fix: Emit CAST(date_expr AS TIMESTAMP) + time_expr (on a copied node) or CAST(date_expr + time_expr AS TIMESTAMP) after validating operand forms.

findings.explanation: this and unit are swapped: TIMESTAMP_TRUNC(timestamp, unit) means this should be args[0] and unit args[1], but code uses the reverse causing wrong results and None this on single-arg calls.
findings.suggested_fix: return exp.TimestampTrunc(this=seq_get(args, 0), unit=seq_get(args, 1))

findings.explanation: TIMESTAMP_TRUNC is parsed as TIMESTAMP_TRUNC(timestamp, unit) in the dialects using this builder, but the code assigns args[1] to this and args[0] to unit, swapping the timestamp and granularity and producing wrong/invalid SQL on generation.
findings.suggested_fix: return exp.TimestampTrunc(this=seq_get(args, 0), unit=seq_get(args, 1))

findings.explanation: zone reuses seq_get(args, 1), so it duplicates `this` instead of reading the optional third time-zone argument, losing the timezone and sharing one node in two fields.
findings.suggested_fix: zone=seq_get(args, 2)

findings.explanation: zone is populated with seq_get(args, 1), duplicating the timestamp argument instead of using the third argument; any timezone is ignored and even two-argument calls incorrectly gain a zone equal to the timestamp, producing wrong/invalid generated SQL.
findings.suggested_fix: zone=seq_get(args, 2)

findings.explanation: LOCAL is matched unconditionally but only used for DIRECTORY. For a normal INSERT it is consumed and silently discarded.
findings.suggested_fix: Only match LOCAL inside the DIRECTORY branch or add it to Insert when not DIRECTORY.

findings.explanation: Early return for FIRST/ALL discards already parsed hint, overwrite, ignore, local and never parses outer Insert wrapper.
findings.suggested_fix: Pass hint/overwrite/ignore/etc to _parse_multitable_inserts or build Insert around it.

findings.explanation: alternative becomes False when OR is matched but text is not in INSERT_ALTERNATIVES, and a stray OR is silently consumed.
findings.suggested_fix: if self._match(TokenType.OR): alternative=self._parse_var(any_token=True); validate against INSERT_ALTERNATIVES else raise.

findings.explanation: If table/function parsing returns None the code continues with this=None and builds an invalid Insert instead of raising.
findings.suggested_fix: Check if this is None: self.raise_error('Expected table.')

findings.explanation: columns.append(target.this) drops table/db qualifier and if value: uses truthiness instead of is not None.
findings.suggested_fix: Append target (or target.copy()) and test if value is not None.

findings.explanation: Empty SET list creates empty Schema/Values instead of error, and alias is parsed after SET where ON CONFLICT/RETURNING/SELECT can be mis-consumed as alias.
findings.suggested_fix: Raise if columns empty and remove alias parsing from set_values.

findings.explanation: STORED/BY NAME use match and parse; if keyword matched but parse fails the token is lost with no error and value becomes False.
findings.suggested_fix: if self._match_text_seq('STORED'): stored=self._parse_stored() or raise; same for BY NAME.

findings.explanation: REPLACE is consumed even when neither WHERE nor USING follows, silently dropping it instead of error.
findings.suggested_fix: Only consume REPLACE when followed by WHERE/USING, else raise or don't match.
